$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{2x}+\frac{x-4}{2x} & =\frac{5x-6}{2x} \\ 2x\cdot (\frac{x-2}{2x}+\frac{x-4}{2x}) & =n\cdot (\frac{5x-6}{2x}) \\ 2x\cdot \frac{x-2}{2x}+2x\cdot \frac{x-4}{2x} & =2x\cdot \frac{5x-6}{2x} \\ \cancel{2x}\cdot \frac{x-2}{\cancel{2x}}+\cancel{2x}\cdot \frac{x-4}{\cancel{2x}} & =\cancel{2x}\cdot \frac{5x-6}{\cancel{2x}} \\ x-2+x-4 & =5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2+x-4 & =5x-6 \\ 2x-6 & =5x-6 \\ 5x-2x & =-6+6 \\ 3x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. We multiply both sides of the equation by $b,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{b+5}{b}+\frac{b-7}{b} & =6 \\ b\cdot (\frac{b+5}{b}+\frac{b-7}{b}) & =b\cdot 6 \\ b\cdot \frac{b+5}{b}+b\cdot \frac{b-7}{b} & =b\cdot 6 \\ \cancel{b}\cdot \frac{b+5}{\cancel{b}}+\cancel{b}\cdot \frac{b-7}{\cancel{b}} & =b\cdot 6 \\ b+5+b-7 & =6b\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $b,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}b+5+b-7 & =6b \\ 2b-2 & =6b \\ -4b & =2 \\ b & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $b=0$ as a solution. The equation has the denominators $x$ and $3x.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(x,3x)=3x.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $3x,$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x\cdot (\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{x}) & =3x\cdot (\frac{3-x}{3x}) \\ 3x\cdot \frac{2}{3}+3x\cdot \frac{1}{x} & =3x\cdot \frac{3-x}{3x} \\ \cancel{3}x\cdot \frac{2}{\cancel{3}}+3\cancel{x}\cdot \frac{1}{\cancel{x}} & =\cancel{3x}\cdot \frac{3-x}{\cancel{3x}} \\ x\cdot (2)+3\cdot (1) & =3-x \\ 2x+3 & =3-x\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+3 & =3-x \\ 2x+x & =3-3 \\ 3x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. Since $x=0,$ we conclude that there is no solution." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0e75216d-bcd6-569a-b621-c249dcbf26bb"] :db/ensure The equation has the denominators $3q$ and $4q.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(3q,4q)=12q.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $12q,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2q-1}{4q} & =\frac{q+1}{3q}-1 \\ 12q\cdot (\frac{2q-1}{4q}) & =12q\cdot (\frac{q+1}{3q}-1) \\ 12q\cdot \frac{2q-1}{4q} & =12q\cdot \frac{q+1}{3q}-12q\cdot 1 \\ 3\cdot \cancel{4q}\cdot (\frac{2q-1}{\cancel{4q}}) & =4\cdot \cancel{3q}\cdot (\frac{q+1}{\cancel{3q}})-12q \\ 3(2q-1) & =4(q+1)-12q\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $q,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3(2q-1) & =4(q+1)-12q \\ 6q-3 & =4q+4-12q \\ 6q-3 & =-8q+4 \\ 6q+8q & =4+3 \\ 14q & =7 \\ q & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $q=0$ as a solution. But since $q=\frac{1}{2}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $q=\frac{1}{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields #uuid "f095dc29-06a2-59bf-8997-6e524951d317" :question/math-academy-id "q-75936" :question/problem "Which value of $m$ satisfies the equation $\frac{4m+1}{3m}-\frac{m-1}{6m}=\frac{1}{9m}?$" :question/worked-solution "We note that $m=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $3m,6m,$ and $9m.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(3m,6m,9m)=18m.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $18m,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4m+1}{3m}-\frac{m-1}{6m} & =\frac{1}{9m} \\ 18m\cdot (\frac{4m+1}{3m}-\frac{m-1}{6m}) & =18m\cdot (\frac{1}{9m}) \\ 18m\cdot (\frac{4m+1}{3m})-18m\cdot (\frac{m-1}{6m}) & =18m\cdot (\frac{1}{9m}) \\ 6\cdot 3m\cdot (\frac{4m+1}{3m})-3\cdot 6m\cdot (\frac{m-1}{6m}) & =2\cdot 9m\cdot (\frac{1}{9m}) \\ 6\cdot \cancel{3m}\cdot (\frac{4m+1}{\cancel{3m}})-3\cdot \cancel{6m}\cdot (\frac{m-1}{\cancel{6m}}) & =2\cdot \cancel{9m}\cdot (\frac{1}{\cancel{9m}}) \\ 6(4m+1)-3(m-1) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $m,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6(4m+1)-3(m-1) & =2 \\ 24m+6-3m+3 & =2 \\ 21m+9 & =2 \\ 21m & =-7 \\ m & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $m=0$ as a solution. But since $m=-\frac{1}{3}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $m=-\frac{1}{3}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields #uuid "f7541a79-898f-52f6-9741-385d5ef8e2c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-75955" :question/problem "Which value of $n$ satisfies the equation $\frac{3}{2n}-\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}=\frac{7}{3n}?$" :question/worked-solution "We note that $n=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $2n,$ ${n}^{2},$ and $3n.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(2n,{n}^{2},3n)=6{n}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $6{n}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2n}-\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}} & =\frac{7}{3n} \\ 6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2n}-\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}) & =6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{7}{3n}) \\ 6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2n})-6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}) & =6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{7}{3n}) \\ 3n\cdot 2n\cdot (\frac{3}{2n})-6\cdot {n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}) & =2n\cdot 3n\cdot (\frac{7}{3n}) \\ 3n\cdot \cancel{2n}\cdot (\frac{3}{\cancel{2n}})-6\cdot \cancel{{n}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1-n}{\cancel{{n}^{2}}}) & =2n\cdot \cancel{3n}\cdot (\frac{7}{\cancel{3n}}) \\ 3n\cdot (3)-6\cdot (1-n) & =2n\cdot (7) \\ 9n-6(1-n) & =14n\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $n,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}9n-6(1-n) & =14n \\ 15n-6 & =14n \\ n & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $n=0$ as a solution. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We note that $v=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $6v,\,{v}^{2},$ and $2{v}^{2}.$ First, we find the denominators' least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$). We have that

$$
\text{LCM}(6v,{v}^{2},2{v}^{2})=6{v}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $6{v}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{v+4}{{v}^{2}}-\frac{7}{6v} & =\frac{5}{2{v}^{2}} \\ 6{v}^{2}(\frac{v+4}{{v}^{2}}-\frac{7}{6v}) & =6{v}^{2}(\frac{5}{2{v}^{2}}) \\ 6{v}^{2}\cdot \frac{v+4}{{v}^{2}}-6{v}^{2}\cdot \frac{7}{6v} & =6{v}^{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2{v}^{2}} \\ 6\cdot {v}^{2}\cdot \frac{v+4}{{v}^{2}}-6v\cdot v\cdot \frac{7}{6v} & =3\cdot 2{v}^{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2{v}^{2}} \\ 6\cdot \cancel{{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{v+4}{\cancel{{v}^{2}}}-\cancel{6v}\cdot v\cdot \frac{7}{\cancel{6v}} & =3\cdot \cancel{2{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{5}{\cancel{2{v}^{2}}} \\ 6(v+4)-v\cdot (7) & =3\cdot 5 \\ 6(v+4)-7v & =15\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $v,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6(v+4)-7v & =15 \\ 6v+24-7v & =15 \\ -v+24 & =15 \\ -v & =-9 \\ v & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $v=0$ as a solution. But since $v=9\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $v=9.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-787aa0da-04c6-5397-99c2-28c45379391c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-787aa0da-04c6-5397-99c2-28c45379391c" :answer-field/id #uuid "787aa0da-04c6-5397-99c2-28c45379391c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-38875fd2-c051-51ae-9cd4-a572e31fc61c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-38875fd2-c051-51ae-9cd4-a572e31fc61c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-38875fd2-c051-51ae-9cd4-a572e31fc61c" :answer/id #uuid "38875fd2-c051-51ae-9cd4-a572e31fc61c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068969 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133789 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-cc66ebbe-2cca-5407-87bc-772df677089f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-cc66ebbe-2cca-5407-87bc-772df677089f" :question/id #uuid "cc66ebbe-2cca-5407-87bc-772df677089f" :question/math-academy-id "q-86762" :question/problem "Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

Therefore, we get the following projection:

\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the Pythagorean identity 

$$
\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x= 1.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic Pythagorean identity

$$
\cosh^2x -\sinh^2x=1
$$

which we can write as

$$
1+\sinh^2x=\cosh^2x.
$$

Additionally, we have

$$
\sech x = \dfrac{1}{\cosh x}.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x})}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166796 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a49f44d3-1abb-5067-966c-70ae50d2155e" "question-9ddcb9f3-50a1-505b-ae57-c8a55dc1f652" "question-6c61796b-b24c-5403-8a9e-cd8bda63e7c0" "question-7461b1f3-1aea-5d09-ab06-c9f25cb75e4f" "question-4e26e540-b6e1-55b9-88da-a99de2917513"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166634 :question/problem "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}

\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\ln 2} \dfrac{\tanh{x}-\tanh^3{x}}{\sech{x}} \, \textrm{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the secant-tangent identity 

$$
1 + \tan^2 x= \sec^2{x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic secant-tangent identity

$$
1-\tanh^2x=\sech^2{x}.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the integral and evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{\operatorname{tanh}⁡x-{tanh}^{3}⁡x}{\operatorname{sech}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{(1-{tanh}^{2}⁡x)\operatorname{tanh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sech}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{{sech}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sech}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =-\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+\operatorname{sech}⁡0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}+\frac{2}{{e}^{0}+{e}^{0}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{(2+\frac{1}{2})}+1 \\  & =-\frac{2}{(\frac{5}{2})}+1 \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic cosecant-cotangent identity

$$
\coth^2x - 1=\csch^2{x}.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the integral and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\eqalign{

			&= \cosh{x} \Big|_{\ln 3}^{\ln 6}\[5pt]
			&= \cosh(\ln 6) - \cosh(\ln 3)\[5pt]
			&= \left(\dfrac{e^{\ln 6}+e^{-\ln 6}}{2}\right) - \left(\dfrac{e^{\ln 3}+e^{-\ln 3}}{2}\right)\[5pt]
			&= \left(\dfrac{6 + \dfrac{1}{6}}{2}\right) - \left(\dfrac{3 + \dfrac{1}{3}}{2}\right)\[5pt]

            &= \dfrac{17}{12}
	}

$$

Setting $\theta = 2x + 1,$ we get 

$$
\cosh^2 (2x+1) - \sinh^2(2x+1) = 1
$$

which can be written as

$$
\cosh^2 (2x+1) -1 = \sinh^2(2x+1).

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-007da683-6a06-5103-8ccf-d7e5e491284b" :question/id #uuid "007da683-6a06-5103-8ccf-d7e5e491284b" :question/math-academy-id "q-96324" :question/problem "Calculate $\int \frac{1}{1-{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the Pythagorean identity

We use Osborn's rule to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity. 

Osborn's rule states that to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity, we

- replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function, and

- for any product of two trigonometric sines, change the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

$\displaystyle 
        \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

For example, suppose we want to calculate the following integral:

$$
\int \cosh^2{x} - \sinh^2{x} \: \textrm{d}x
$$

First, we recall the Pythagorean identity

$$
\cos^2{x} + \sin^2{x} = 1.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the corresponding hyperbolic identity

$$
\cosh^2{x} - \sinh^2{x} = 1.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {{{cosh}^{2}⁡x-{sinh}^{2}⁡x}_{⏟}}_{1}\,\text{d}x=\int 1\,\text{d}x=x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's see another example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168119 :tutorial/content "$\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}

        \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$We can use Osborn's rule to write down the hyperbolic equivalents of the sectant-tangent and cotangent-cosecant identities.

From the secant-tangent identity

$$
1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x
$$

we have the equivalent hyperbolic identity

$$
1 - \tanh^2 x = \sech^2 x.
$$

Similarly, from the cotangent-cosecant identity

$$
1+\cot^2 x = \csc^2 x
$$

we have the equivalent hyperbolic identity

$$
1-\coth^2 x  = -\csch^2 x
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\coth^2 x - 1 = \csch^2 x.
$$

These identities can be used to solve certain integrals involving the expressions $\tanh^2{x},$ $\coth^2 x,$ $\sech^2 x,$ or $\csch^2{x}.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167027 :activity/expected-seconds 1500.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167733 :step/math-academy-id 639523 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167630 :step/math-academy-id 639524 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167734 :step/math-academy-id 639527 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167631 :step/math-academy-id 639528 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167632 :step/math-academy-id 639531 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167633 :step/math-academy-id 639535 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192832 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-cd69e9f7-e929-5fe2-b3bb-4bb36c948590" "question-dcb3950f-e511-5b2b-8452-0fa93d40b2ff"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-cd69e9f7-e929-5fe2-b3bb-4bb36c948590" :question/id #uuid "cd69e9f7-e929-5fe2-b3bb-4bb36c948590" :question/math-academy-id "q-345553" :question/problem "$$

Consider the matrices $U$ and $V$ above. Let $X$ be a $2\times 3$ standardized observation matrix, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature. Given that $X=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $X,$ what is the third principal component of the data?" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>{\lambda }_{3}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- the $3$rd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to the $3$rd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}.$

Notice that the covariance matrix corresponding to $X$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}V{Σ}^{T}({U}^{T}U)Σ{V}^{T} \\  & =V(\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ){V}^{T},\end{aligned}
$$

where the final expression represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C.$ Notice that:

- $\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ$ is a diagonal $3\times 3$ matrix, where the entries on the main diagonal are the eigenvalues (written in descending order) of the covariance matrix $C$, and

- $V$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix, whose columns are the corresponding unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$

Therefore, the columns of $V$ are the principal components of the data.
So, the third principal component is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].

The singular values of $X$ are 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=5,\,{\sigma }_{2}=2,\,{\sigma }_{3}=1,\,{\sigma }_{4}=0.5,\,{\sigma }_{5}=0.1.
$$

The scientist then converted the original observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ using the equation $Y=X{V}_{2},$ where ${V}_{2}$ is the $5\times 2$ matrix consisting of the first two principal components of the data. What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix $Y$ compared to the initial observation matrix $X?$" :question/worked-solution "Let $V$ be the matrix of principal components. Then, applying the change of variables

$$
Y=XV
$$

we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}$ are uncorrelated),

- the features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance, and

- the squares of the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}^{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2},…,{\sigma }_{5}^{2}$ represent the variances in the respective features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}.$

Now, the total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(5)^{2}+(2)^{2}+(1)^{2}+(0.5)^{2}+(0.1)^{2} \\  & =30.26\end{aligned}
$$

Since the scientist used only the first two principal components, the remaining variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Remaining} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(5)^{2}+(2)^{2} \\  & =29.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{Remaining}}{\text{Total}} & =\frac{29}{30.26} \\  & ≈0.958 \\  & =95.8%.\end{aligned}

planes $x=-1,$ $x=1,$ $y=0,$ $y=1,$ $z=0,$ $z=1.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $F=2xz\,i+({x}^{2}+z)\,j+2\,k,$ find the flux of $F$ across $S.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xz)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+z)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2) \\  & =2z+0+0 \\  & =2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}2z\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}2z\,\text{d}z \\  & =(1-(-1))\cdot (1-0)\cdot [{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=1} \\  & =2({1}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130990 :answer-field/correct 17592186130992 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133930 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d1625297-e3fd-57e3-914d-8b51c40eca40" "question-65b5959b-427f-58b2-a1ab-3381594e4750"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d1625297-e3fd-57e3-914d-8b51c40eca40" :question/id #uuid "d1625297-e3fd-57e3-914d-8b51c40eca40" :question/math-academy-id "q-162576" :question/problem "Consider the positively (outward) oriented surface $S$ given by $(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}+(z+3)^{2}=16$ and the vector field $F=(x+2y)\,i+(4z-y)\,j+(z+xy)\,k.$ Use the divergence theorem to find the flux of $F$ across $S.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+2y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(4z-y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z+xy) \\  & =1+(-1)+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid sphere of radius $4$ enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}1\,\text{d}V \\  & =1{∭}_{R}\,\text{d}V \\  & ={∭}_{R}\,\text{d}V \\  & =\text{Volume}(R) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\pi \cdot {4}^{3} \\  & =\frac{256\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-669b5857-9476-53d2-a3ba-83114e28734b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{3})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xz\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}) \\  & =0+(-2xz\operatorname{sin}⁡y)+0 \\  & =-2xz\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}(-2xz\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{2}^{4}(-2xz\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{2}^{4}z\,\text{d}z \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=1}\cdot [\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{y=0}^{y=\pi }\cdot {[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=2}^{z=4} \\  & =({1}^{2}-{0}^{2})\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0)\cdot (\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot (-2)\cdot 6 \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-69fd017c-8fd8-594c-96db-bb6def0c9f0a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

:question/id #uuid "6b8e59d5-6b05-50ce-8455-191b0c2a0b7a" :question/math-academy-id "q-73776" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{2}+5x+4?$

I. $x=4$ is a root of $f(x)$

II. $(x-4)$ is a factor of $f(x)$

III. $(x-4)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder" :question/worked-solution "The factor theorem states that $(x-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=r$ is also a root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(x-4).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-4 & =0 \\ x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

We now check each of the statements, in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, $x=4$ is not a root of $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4) & ={4}^{2}+5(4)+4 \\  & =16+20+4 \\  & =40 \\  & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. According to the factor theorem, since $x=4$ is not a root of $f(x),$ then $(x-4)$ is not a factor of $f(x).$

- Statement III is false. Since $(x-4)$ is not a factor of $f(x),$ then it does not divide $f(x)$ with zero remainder.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-63b70b6a-3c22-5376-9d31-4b93eb63027c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-63b70b6a-3c22-5376-9d31-4b93eb63027c" :answer-field/id #uuid "63b70b6a-3c22-5376-9d31-4b93eb63027c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-b074b252-d948-500c-8a9b-b0d2c27004f1" :answer-field/choices ["answer-6fc2e5c4-3531-5d25-8436-a4eb1e7ccd7a" "answer-f2645d9f-4118-565c-be24-6f9684808038" "answer-002539d9-f83f-5f8a-821f-f91ec24993f6" "answer-17a8904d-7494-54a8-9cf6-42abe4eadb2e" "answer-b074b252-d948-500c-8a9b-b0d2c27004f1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6fc2e5c4-3531-5d25-8436-a4eb1e7ccd7a" :answer/id #uuid "6fc2e5c4-3531-5d25-8436-a4eb1e7ccd7a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f2645d9f-4118-565c-be24-6f9684808038" :answer/id #uuid "f2645d9f-4118-565c-be24-6f9684808038" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-002539d9-f83f-5f8a-821f-f91ec24993f6" :answer/id #uuid "002539d9-f83f-5f8a-821f-f91ec24993f6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-17a8904d-7494-54a8-9cf6-42abe4eadb2e" :answer/id #uuid "17a8904d-7494-54a8-9cf6-42abe4eadb2e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b074b252-d948-500c-8a9b-b0d2c27004f1" :answer/id #uuid "b074b252-d948-500c-8a9b-b0d2c27004f1" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "None" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-7c34a96f-d461-5b11-9cb5-80d7557e52d7" :question/id #uuid "7c34a96f-d461-5b11-9cb5-80d7557e52d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-73777" :question/problem "For which of the following polynomials is $(x+1)$ a factor?

I. $f(x)={x}^{2}+3x+2$

II. $g(x)={x}^{2}+8x+7$

III. $h(x)=-{x}^{2}+x$" :question/worked-solution "The factor theorem states that $(x-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=r$ is also a root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(x+1).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =0 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

According to the factor theorem, $(x+1)$ is a factor of $p(x)$ if the root $x=-1$ is a root of $p(x).$ 

So now, we will check if $x=-1$ is a root of the polynomials $f,$ $g$ and $h.$

- Evaluating $x=-1$ at $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1) & =(-1)^{2}+3(-1)+2 \\  & =1-3+2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that $(x+1)$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$

- Now, evaluating $x=-1$ at $g(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-1) & =(-1)^{2}+8(-1)+7 \\  & =1-8+7 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that $(x+1)$ is indeed a factor of $g(x).$

- Finally, evaluating $x=-1$ at $h(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-1) & =-(-1)^{2}+(-1) \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e9167685-de61-5642-a6f3-e2034b8507d4"] :db/ensure and solve the equation." :question/worked-solution "We first move the constant to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-10x+50 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-10x & =-50\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-10x & =-50 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 5x+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =-50 \\ (x-5)^{2}-25 & =-50 \\ (x-5)^{2} & =-25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-5,\,q=-25,$ and $p+q=-30.$

We now solve the equation using the square root method.

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-5)^{2} & =-25 \\ x-5 & =\pm \sqrt{-25} \\ x-5 & =\pm 5\,\text{i} \\ x & =5\pm 5\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=5+5\,\text{i}$ and $x=5-5\,\text{i}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["question-7f361b6d-88da-56f4-bb4f-1191d0218d94"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101196 :question/problem "A cinema hall can hold $120$ people. The price of each ticket is $$10.$ The cost of maintaining the cinema is made up of a fixed cost of $$400$ plus a cost of $$0.25$ per person. How many tickets should the cinema sell to maximize its profit?" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

First, note that for selling $x$ tickets, the cinema has a revenue (in dollars) of 

$$
R(x)=10\cdot x=10x
$$

and a cost (in dollars) of 

$$
C(x)={{400}_{⏟}}_{\text{fixed cost}}\,\,+{{0.25x.}_{⏟}}_{\text{variable cost}}
$$

Therefore, the profit function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =R(x)-C(x) \\  & =10x-(400+0.25x) \\  & =9.75x-400.\end{aligned}
$$

We note that the permitted domain is $0\le x\le 120.$ Therefore, $x=0$ and $x=120$ are candidates for the global maxima of $P(x).$

We need to find the critical points of $P(x)$ for $0<x<120.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=9.75.
$$

We can see that the equation ${P}^{′}(x)=0$ has no solutions.

Our candidates are $x=0$ and $x=120.$ Computing $P(x)$ at each of these values, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0) & =9.75(0)-400=-400 \\ P(120) & =9.75(120)-400=770\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the cinema will have a maximum profit level when it sells $120$ tickets." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186098511 :answer-field/correct 17592186098514 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101018 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-da64bda4-339a-50c3-828b-c79ac0fe60b0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-da64bda4-339a-50c3-828b-c79ac0fe60b0" :question/id #uuid "da64bda4-339a-50c3-828b-c79ac0fe60b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-87576" :question/problem "A daycare center can take care of between $10$ and $20$ children. The fee that parents must pay each month depends on the number of children enrolled in the center. If there are $10$ children enrolled, parents must pay $$40.$ On the other hand, if there are more than $10$ children enrolled, the price drops by $$2$ for each child. All the parents pay the same monthly fee.

How many children must enroll for the center to maximize its revenue?" :question/worked-solution "First, note that if there are $10+x$ children enrolled, then the monthly fee is $40-2x.$ So, the total revenue is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & ={{(10+x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{number of children enrolled}}\times \,\,\,\,\,\,{{(40-2x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{monthly fee}} \\  & =(10+x)(40-2x) \\  & =400-20x+40x-2{x}^{2} \\  & =400+20x-2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the center can only take care between $10$ and $20$ children, the permitted domain for $x$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & \le x+10\le 20 \\ 0 & \le x\le 10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=0$ and $x=10$ are both candidates for the global maxima of $R(x).$

We need to find the critical points of $R(x)$ for $0<x<10.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{R}^{′}(x)=20-4x,
$$

and solving ${R}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 20-4x & =0 \\ 4x & =20 \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $x=5$ lies in the interval $0<x<10.$ All that's left now is to confirm that $x=5$ does indeed give a maximum value of $R(x).$ To do this, we compute the second derivative:

$$
{R}^{″}(x)=-4<0
$$

Since the second derivative is negative, the point $x=5$ is indeed a local maximum of $R(x).$ And since $R(x)$ is quadratic, we conclude that $x=5$ is a global maximum of $R(x).$ 

Therefore, the center must have $10+5=15$ children enrolled to maximize its revenue." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields :question/id #uuid "4cb999cb-e9bf-5cd0-a21c-a3857e783014" :question/math-academy-id "q-87593" :question/problem "A factory spends $C(x)=100-47x+21{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}$ thousand dollars per month to manufacture $x$ units of a certain product. The factory sells the product for $$100\,000$ per unit. Given that the factory can produce between $1$ and $10$ items per month, what is the maximum monthly profit it can make?" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

First, note that for selling $x$ units of the product per month, the factory has a monthly revenue (income) of $R(x)=100\cdot x=100x$ thousand dollars. 

Therefore, the profit function (in thousands of dollars) is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =R(x)-C(x) \\  & =100x-(100-47x+21{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}) \\  & ={x}^{3}-21{x}^{2}+147x-100.\end{aligned}
$$

We note that the permitted domain is $1\le x\le 10.$ Therefore, $x=1$ and $x=10$ are both candidates for the global maxima of $P(x).$

We need to find the critical points of $P(x)$ for $1<x<10.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=3{x}^{2}-42x+147,
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-42x+147 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-14x+49 & =0 \\ (x-7)^{2} & =0 \\ x & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check if $x=7$ gives a maximum value of $P(x).$ To do this, we compute the second derivative:

$$
{P}^{″}(x)=6x-42.
$$

Evaluating ${P}^{″}(x)$ at the critical point, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{″}(7)=6(7)-42=0,\end{aligned}
$$

which does not confirm or deny that $x=7$ is a maximum of $P(x).$ Therefore, we should consider $x=7$ as one of the candidates.

Our candidates are $x=1,$ $x=7$ and $x=10.$ Computing $P(x)$ at each of these values, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1) & =(1)^{3}-21(1)^{2}+147(1)-100=27 \\ P(7) & =(7)^{3}-21(7)^{2}+147(7)-100=243 \\ P(10) & =(10)^{3}-21(10)^{2}+147(10)-100=270\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

"A company spends $C(x)=0.01{x}^{2}+4x+680$ dollars to produce $x$ units of a certain product. The company sells the product for $$12$ per unit. Given that the company can produce at most $500$ units per month, how many units should the company produce per month to maximize its monthly profit?" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

First, note that for selling $x$ units of the product per month, the company has a monthly revenue (income) of $R(x)=12\cdot x=12x$ dollars. 

Therefore, the profit function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =R(x)-C(x) \\  & =12x-(0.01{x}^{2}+4x+680) \\  & =8x-0.01{x}^{2}-680.\end{aligned}
$$

We note that the permitted domain is $0\le x\le 500.$ 

We need to find the critical points of $P(x)$ for $0<x<500.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=8-0.02x,
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 8-0.02x & =0 \\ x & =400\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $x=400$ lies in the interval $0<x<500.$ All that's left now is to confirm that $x=400$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(x).$ To do this, we compute the second derivative:

$$
{P}^{″}(x)=-0.02<0
$$

Since the second derivative is negative, the point $x=400$ is indeed a local maximum of $P(x).$ And since $P(x)$ is quadratic, we conclude that $x=400$ is a global maximum of $P(x).$ 

Therefore, we conclude that the company will have a maximum monthly profit when it produces $400$ units per month." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields "A tutoring center offers private lesson packages. When the price of a package is $$40,$ the center books all $80$ available sessions. For every $$4$ increase in the package price, one fewer session is booked. If the cost of providing each session is $$16,$ what price should the center charge to maximize its profit?

To maximize profit, the center should charge $$$
{{field-1}}
per session." :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

Let $x$ represent the number of unbooked sessions. Then the number of **booked** sessions is $(80-x),$ and the **price per session** is $(40+4x).$

So, the total revenue is

$$
R(x)=(80-x)(40+4x).
$$

Expanding, we get

$$
R(x)=-4{x}^{2}+280x+3200.
$$

The cost of providing each booked session is $$16,$ so the total cost is

$$
C(x)=16(80-x)=1280-16x.
$$

Therefore, the profit function is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =R(x)-C(x) \\  & =(-4{x}^{2}+280x+3200)-(1280-16x) \\  & =-4{x}^{2}+296x+1920.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given the domain $0\le x\le 80.$

To find the maximum, we take the derivative:

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=-8x+296.
$$

Solving ${P}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get:

$$
x=37.
$$

Since ${P}^{″}(x)=-8<0,$ this point is a maximum. Since $P(x)$ is quadratic, this maximum is global.

Now, if $x=37$ sessions are unbooked, then the price is:

$$
40+4(37)=188.
$$

Therefore, to maximize profit, the center should charge $$\,\,188$ per session." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨4x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $x$-component of $F=⟨4x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $x$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the front and back sides. 

![](images/dc/dc37a067eb8070ecbdfea53c1ede3e221e1873a192b50fcbf07234f33c183787.png)

  

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=3$ for $0\le y\le 2$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=3$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨4x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨12{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =12{y}^{2}{z}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}12{y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}12{y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}12{y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[4{y}^{3}{z}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}32{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[8{z}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for $0\le y\le 2$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨4x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =8+0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8118e8d0-ad36-5eed-a94c-c49d91624022"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087431 :question/problem "Given that $f(x) = x^2,$ what is $f'(x)$ according to the definition of the derivative?" :question/worked-solution "The derivative $f '(x)$ is given by the limit 

$$
\lim_{h\to 0} \dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} .
$$

Since $f(x) = x^2$,  we have that $f(x+h) = (x+h)^2.$ Hence,  we get

$$
\displaystyle f'(x)=\lim_{h\to 0} \dfrac{(x+h)^2-x^2}{h} .
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087881 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-779ee099-0fc5-5dca-bd3b-ce3793ba0e8c" "question-a35127e9-e5f3-508e-9d5a-b3279aa78b1a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087432 :question/problem "Given $y =x^2,$ calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ using the limit of a difference quotient." :question/worked-solution "We let $y=f(x)$ and apply the formula for the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(x+h)^{2}-{x}^{2}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}+2xh+{h}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{2xh+{h}^{2}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{2xh}{h}+\frac{{h}^{2}}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(2x+h) \\  & =2x+0 \\  & =2x\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-ab9ad28a-3195-5102-ad22-90c2dc511297" :question/id #uuid "ab9ad28a-3195-5102-ad22-90c2dc511297" :question/math-academy-id "q-101957" :question/problem "Given that $f(x)=2x+1$, what is ${f}^{′}(x)$ according to the definition of the derivative?" :question/worked-solution "The derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ is given by the limit 

$$
{lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}).
$$

Since $f(x)=2x+1$,  we have that $f(x+h)=2(x+h)+1.$ Hence,  we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{2(x+h)+1-(2x+1)}{h}).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f4d0ff0d-7860-5a8a-a6e6-4fb8f62ae866"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The definition of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying this to $f(x)=-4{x}^{2}+5x$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{-4(x+h)^{2}+5(x+h)-(-4{x}^{2}+5x)}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{-4({x}^{2}+2xh+{h}^{2})+5x+5h+4{x}^{2}-5x}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{-4{x}^{2}-8xh-4{h}^{2}+5x+5h+4{x}^{2}-5x}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{-8xh-4{h}^{2}+5h}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{h(-8x-4h+5)}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(-8x-4h+5) \\  & =-8x+5.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a93c79b4-53dc-5d15-9856-ca96c8afc783"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a93c79b4-53dc-5d15-9856-ca96c8afc783" :answer-field/id #uuid "a93c79b4-53dc-5d15-9856-ca96c8afc783" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f05b0eb8-1f64-572b-9eb7-f009dba2ee76" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f05b0eb8-1f64-572b-9eb7-f009dba2ee76"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f05b0eb8-1f64-572b-9eb7-f009dba2ee76" :answer/id #uuid "f05b0eb8-1f64-572b-9eb7-f009dba2ee76" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-8x+5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186088899 :tutorial/content "The instantaneous rate of change of a function $f(x)$ at the point $x=a,$ denoted $f'(a),$ is given by the limit

$$
f'(a) = \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}.
$$

This formula works for a specific point $x=a.$ If we want a method that works for a *general* point $x,$ then we substitute $a=x$ in the formula and get

$$
f'(x) = \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}.
$$

The function $f'(x)$ is called the **derivative of $f(x)$ with respect to $x$**. It gives the slope of the tangent line to the curve $y=f(x)$ at a general point with coordinates $(x,f(x)).$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186088900 :tutorial/content "For a given curve $y=f(x),$ the derivative can be represented using several different notations. They are

$$
f'(x),\qquad y'(x), \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

In words, the term $y'(x)$  is said like

- "$y$ prime of $x$," or

- "$y$ prime," or sometimes

- "$y$ dash."

The term $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ is said like "dee $y$ by dee $x$."

The important thing to remember is that they all represent the same thing, the derivative." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087898 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133882 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-40abd682-d4fa-55d0-8dea-db00bcc211a6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-40abd682-d4fa-55d0-8dea-db00bcc211a6" :question/id #uuid "40abd682-d4fa-55d0-8dea-db00bcc211a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-109131" :question/problem "Consider the triangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(0,0),(1,1)$ and $(0,1),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ According to Green's theorem,

Calculate the function $f(x,y).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/56/5673a3eadfa3c01dbb9e2c8bf497b17f34a834d950621afa7d480af625ce1e18.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=xy+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+(xy+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}[y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)]\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=y.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a172fe47-3553-5b48-9c9c-d02e78168ac3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{k}\cdot {10}^{1+x/2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{k}\cdot {10}^{1+y/2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{k}\cdot {10}^{1+y/2}+1 \\ \frac{1}{k}\cdot {10}^{1+y/2} & =x-1 \\ {10}^{1+y/2} & =kx-k \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{1+y/2}) & =\operatorname{log}⁡(kx-k) \\ 1+\frac{y}{2} & =\operatorname{log}⁡(kx-k) \\ \frac{y}{2} & =\operatorname{log}⁡(kx-k)-1 \\ y & =2\operatorname{log}⁡(kx-k)-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is ${f}^{-1}(x)=2\operatorname{log}⁡(kx-k)-2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{2}{3}-{5}^{2x-k}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{2}{3}-{5}^{2y-k}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{2}{3}-{5}^{2y-k} \\ {5}^{2y-k} & =\frac{2}{3}-x \\ {5}^{2y-k} & =\frac{2-3x}{3} \\ {log}_{5}⁡({5}^{2y-k}) & ={log}_{5}⁡(\frac{2-3x}{3}) \\ 2y-k & ={log}_{5}⁡(\frac{2-3x}{3}) \\ 2y & ={log}_{5}⁡(\frac{2-3x}{3})+k \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}{log}_{5}⁡(\frac{2-3x}{3})+\frac{k}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is ${f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{2}{log}_{5}⁡(\frac{2-3x}{3})+\frac{k}{2}$

$$
f(x)=2^{5x}+1
$$

and we wish to find the inverse function $f^{-1}(x).$ We can do this using the following three steps.

**Step 1:** We start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={2}^{5x}+1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Then, we interchange $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={2}^{5y}+1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={2}^{5y}+1 \\ x-1 & ={2}^{5y} \\ {log}_{2}⁡(x-1) & ={log}_{2}⁡({2}^{5y}) \\ {log}_{2}⁡(x-1) & =5y \\ 5y & ={log}_{2}⁡(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{5}{log}_{2}⁡(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{5}\log_2{(x-1)}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186111881 :tutorial/content "Now suppose we wish to find the inverse of the logarithmic function

$$

**Step 2:** Then, we interchange $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
x = 3\log_{2}(y-1)+1
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{log}_{2}⁡(y-1)+1 & =x \\ 3{log}_{2}⁡(y-1) & =x-1 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(y-1) & =\frac{x-1}{3} \\ {2}^{{log}_{2}⁡(y-1)} & ={2}^{(x-1)/3} \\ y-1 & ={2}^{(x-1)/3} \\ y & ={2}^{(x-1)/3}+1\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is

"affed96b-3c3d-54a9-a279-f8432cb1a012" :question/math-academy-id "q-114073" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{2}{5+20{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "Note that we can write this integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{2}{5+20{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $4{x}^{2}=(2x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{2}{5+20{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{1+(2x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{20}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5596b996-55c7-584d-a670-904b75102451"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "543d7533-dccc-5fe7-9798-fd9513ac4953" :question/math-academy-id "q-88456" :question/problem "What is the product of solutions of the equation $2{x}^{2}\cdot {5}^{x+2}-32\cdot {5}^{x+2}=0?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}\cdot {5}^{x+2}-32\cdot {5}^{x+2} & =0 \\ (2{x}^{2}-32)\cdot {5}^{x+2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
2{x}^{2}-32=0\,\text{and}\,{5}^{x+2}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation $2{x}^{2}-32=0$ can be factored as

$$
\begin{aligned}2({x}^{2}-16) & =0 \\ 2(x+4)(x-4) & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-4,4.$

- The equation $2=0$ is not a possible solution because it's a false statement.

- The equation ${5}^{x+2}=0$ has no solutions because ${5}^{x+2}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

Therefore, the original equation has the solutions $x=-4,4,$ and their product is $(-4)\cdot 4=-16.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot {5}^{x-2} & ={x}^{2}\cdot {5}^{x-2} \\ 4\cdot {5}^{x-2}-{x}^{2}\cdot {5}^{x-2} & =0 \\ (4-{x}^{2}){5}^{x-2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
4-{x}^{2}=0\,\text{and}\,{5}^{x-2}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation $4-{x}^{2}=0$ can be factored as

$$
(2+x)(2-x)=0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-2,2.$

- The equation ${5}^{x-2}=0$ has no solutions because ${5}^{x-2}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

:question/id #uuid "af0d631e-6f1f-57fd-bd84-ccd6cde384ee" :question/math-academy-id "q-126546" :question/problem "Given that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $F(x,y)=⟨y+{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},\,x{y}^{2}⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(y+{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})\,dx+x{y}^{2}\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/0c/0cb340ef33d4cc38081e3796b4c8e076f1499760c0a3ffeecb8123a41fefeec8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y+{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ and $Q(x,y)=x{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(y+{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})\,dx+x{y}^{2}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}-1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cf819579-d6fd-53c1-af84-bcfb66bf0607"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-cf819579-d6fd-53c1-af84-bcfb66bf0607" :answer-field/id #uuid "cf819579-d6fd-53c1-af84-bcfb66bf0607" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1e31ec7e-c4a0-5af1-a007-a5f374623cde" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4697b16a-b954-5ce9-9fdc-2eb3d67c270a" "answer-4a79f07c-c8a1-549a-81cf-2a1164ba3d60" "answer-307eac12-8ffa-5b27-b7eb-9fa2f8ffbd12" "answer-656fd776-3d31-5e32-af9a-81ea6f3a0abf" "answer-1e31ec7e-c4a0-5af1-a007-a5f374623cde"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4697b16a-b954-5ce9-9fdc-2eb3d67c270a" :answer/id #uuid "4697b16a-b954-5ce9-9fdc-2eb3d67c270a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4a79f07c-c8a1-549a-81cf-2a1164ba3d60" :answer/id #uuid "4a79f07c-c8a1-549a-81cf-2a1164ba3d60" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-307eac12-8ffa-5b27-b7eb-9fa2f8ffbd12" :answer/id #uuid "307eac12-8ffa-5b27-b7eb-9fa2f8ffbd12" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta -r" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-656fd776-3d31-5e32-af9a-81ea6f3a0abf" :answer/id #uuid "656fd776-3d31-5e32-af9a-81ea6f3a0abf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -r" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1e31ec7e-c4a0-5af1-a007-a5f374623cde" :answer/id #uuid "1e31ec7e-c4a0-5af1-a007-a5f374623cde" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -r" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176311 :question/problem "Given that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $F(x,y)=⟨x{y}^{2},\,x+{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡y}⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+(x+{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡y})\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/d8/d831c7fb805d16ec7a2dc2462813ea79b78d888ed2121330ed5d823b590d3c4f.png)

Since $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=x+{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+(x+{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2xy)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-2xy)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r-{r}^{3}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}r-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186174124 :answer-field/correct "answer-da61f6d3-ed49-54d2-b863-5a31a5f2ff0f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e9bae659-b917-5899-868d-3dd4b4436e04" "answer-dce15c84-2fee-5b91-8d2e-70aabd4925cc" "answer-da61f6d3-ed49-54d2-b863-5a31a5f2ff0f" "answer-6763f71a-2f1e-5e1a-b5b0-80171e8077f0" "answer-eb7dfd07-1378-5021-b284-61af5aa9f83b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e9bae659-b917-5899-868d-3dd4b4436e04" :answer/id #uuid "e9bae659-b917-5899-868d-3dd4b4436e04" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "r+{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dce15c84-2fee-5b91-8d2e-70aabd4925cc" :answer/id #uuid "dce15c84-2fee-5b91-8d2e-70aabd4925cc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "r-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-da61f6d3-ed49-54d2-b863-5a31a5f2ff0f" :answer/id #uuid "da61f6d3-ed49-54d2-b863-5a31a5f2ff0f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "r-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6763f71a-2f1e-5e1a-b5b0-80171e8077f0" :answer/id #uuid "6763f71a-2f1e-5e1a-b5b0-80171e8077f0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "r{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }-r{sin}^{2}⁡\theta " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-eb7dfd07-1378-5021-b284-61af5aa9f83b" :answer/id #uuid "eb7dfd07-1378-5021-b284-61af5aa9f83b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-37e413b5-1ec6-5915-aa78-dfcf790b6b22" :question/id #uuid "37e413b5-1ec6-5915-aa78-dfcf790b6b22" :question/math-academy-id "q-126519" :question/problem "Given that 

$$
{∮}_{C}{y}^{3}\,dx-{x}^{3}\,dy={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?" :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/79/798665574b8f0e11d991bb0d934efd01bdeb65840c2e86498be4edbc59578439.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=-{x}^{3},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{3}\,dx-{x}^{3}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(-3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(-3\cdot (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-3\cdot (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}(-3{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -3{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}-3{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}-3{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-600ccac0-481d-5135-af9b-c1f28719ac01"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-600ccac0-481d-5135-af9b-c1f28719ac01" :answer-field/id #uuid "600ccac0-481d-5135-af9b-c1f28719ac01" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-9e873ca7-af38-5f44-9341-1fb3e1ea8712" :answer-field/choices ["answer-eb337268-12ae-51d7-ad27-55abc1397eb5" "answer-1f8a5c91-67b1-5ae9-83b6-a14d25c55b45" "answer-9e873ca7-af38-5f44-9341-1fb3e1ea8712" "answer-0c5d1032-d8df-5131-9315-d27ce3d12daa" "answer-46824a5c-5d89-5cc0-92ba-1b68ec6d9595"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-eb337268-12ae-51d7-ad27-55abc1397eb5" :answer/id #uuid "eb337268-12ae-51d7-ad27-55abc1397eb5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3{r}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1f8a5c91-67b1-5ae9-83b6-a14d25c55b45" :answer/id #uuid "1f8a5c91-67b1-5ae9-83b6-a14d25c55b45" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9e873ca7-af38-5f44-9341-1fb3e1ea8712" :answer/id #uuid "9e873ca7-af38-5f44-9341-1fb3e1ea8712" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3{r}^{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0c5d1032-d8df-5131-9315-d27ce3d12daa" :answer/id #uuid "0c5d1032-d8df-5131-9315-d27ce3d12daa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3{r}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-46824a5c-5d89-5cc0-92ba-1b68ec6d9595" :answer/id #uuid "46824a5c-5d89-5cc0-92ba-1b68ec6d9595" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176223 :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/de/deeb5648e328ecc93cf6c1de620e103da0f7677705d1e89e4654deff8d411f66.png)

Since $P(x,y)=3y-{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ and $Q(x,y)=7x+\sqrt{y+5},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=7.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(3y-{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\,dx+(7x+\sqrt{y+5})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(7-3)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{2}4r\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186416109 :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(-xy)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/e1/e1c053e1cc4b4304c1302da2c57278200931b84e4ba687269d0ea89a99b523b8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=x+y$ and $Q(x,y)=-xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(-xy)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y-1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y-1)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 6,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

 

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(-y-1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{6}(-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186416112 :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/77/7724df0035511419dcb5117ba8aa337380325af22ee235d206a954aa12c62fe9.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{3}-x$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{3}+{e}^{1/y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{3}-x)\,dx+({x}^{3}+{e}^{1/y})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}3({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}3{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186262637 :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})\,dx+(xy+y{e}^{y})\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/23/232ced663dcac27ce2775af66dd2ef215ed937e0f4eb5e3e6fb008a3d82dc069.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}+{x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=xy+y{e}^{y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})\,dx+(xy+y{e}^{y})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,-\pi \le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{0}\,{\int }_{0}^{1}-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054628 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ae7dac11-f018-50fc-a556-53f9ec9e3fc0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-ae7dac11-f018-50fc-a556-53f9ec9e3fc0" :question/id #uuid "ae7dac11-f018-50fc-a556-53f9ec9e3fc0" :question/math-academy-id "q-13587" :question/problem "If $f(x)=-3x-5$ and $g(x)=-5x+12,$ then $(f-g)(x)=$" :question/worked-solution "The notation $(f-g)(x)$ means the difference of the functions $f(x)$ and $g(x).$

To find the difference of the two functions, we subtract $g(x)$ from $f(x):$

$\displaystyle \int 4\sinh 2x \cosh 2x \, \textrm{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\sin {2\theta}=2\sin \theta \cos \theta
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the double-angle formula for the hyperbolic sine:

$$
\sinh {2\theta} =2\sinh \theta \cosh \theta
$$

 

Letting $\theta= 2x,$ we get

$$
\sinh {4x} =2\sinh 2x \cosh 2x.
$$

 

Rearranging the above formula, we get

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\sinh {4x}= \sinh 2x \cosh 2x.
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =\int 4\cdot \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \operatorname{sinh}⁡4x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cosh}⁡4x+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡4x+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166803 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1212fe46-96e8-51be-81fa-22f7749ff713" "question-7b5373c3-faa7-5442-9a9c-2d5aebc96c49" "question-216e3ef8-6751-5e3e-9d7f-5d48b7476c3e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166641 :question/problem "Calculate $\displaystyle \int \cosh^2{x} + \sinh^2{x}\ \, \textrm{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the following double-angle formula for cosine: 

$$
\cos{2x}= \cos^2{x}-\sin^2{x}
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the following double-angle formula for the hyperbolic cosine:

$$
\cosh 2x = \cosh^2{x} + \sinh^2{x}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {cosh}^{2}⁡x+{sinh}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166804 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6b367b19-8f35-5f68-a044-eb7b9764c38d" "question-1ebb4c16-c258-518a-a825-ce276a761a9f" "question-cf4092b0-8e64-55b4-94ba-2a8ea4d2ac81" "question-12efb8aa-cbcc-5328-91fe-5d769b12ac7b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166642 :question/problem "Calculate $\displaystyle \int 2\cosh^2 x \, \textrm{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the following double-angle formula for cosine: 

$$
\cos{2x} =2\cos^2 x -1.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the following double-angle formula for the hyperbolic cosine:

$$
\cosh{2x} =2\cosh^2 x -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
\cosh^2 x = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\cosh 2x +1 \right).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{cosh}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x+x+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166805 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d0857a55-78b2-5e38-b682-a21c51974c3c" "question-1ddb9340-9af2-51a6-8581-bb4c21f42fab" "question-4b85bc81-6104-5328-b444-83c8973655d4" "question-bc295d1d-76d5-5f67-a844-a3b5be954577" "question-12bc09cc-29a3-5e9b-995b-e577844956a7"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166643 :question/problem "Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\ln 2} 8\sinh^2{x} \, \textrm{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the following double-angle formula for cosine: 

$$
\cos {2x}=1-2\sin^2x.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the following double-angle formula for the hyperbolic cosine:

$$
\cosh{2x} = 1+ 2\sinh^2{x}
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\sinh^2x = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\cosh {2x} -1\right ).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}8{sinh}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}8\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}4\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x-4\,\text{d}x \\  & =(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x-4x)\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-(2\operatorname{sinh}⁡0-4\cdot 0) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\  & =({2}^{2}-{2}^{-2})-4\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\  & =\frac{15}{4}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-e9856d89-c407-5a27-9255-59fdcff13d87" :question/id #uuid "e9856d89-c407-5a27-9255-59fdcff13d87" :question/math-academy-id "q-165868" :question/problem "Calculate

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the double-angle formula for the hyperbolic sine:

$$

$$

[:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168120 :tutorial/content "We can compute integrals containing hyperbolic functions using the hyperbolic counterparts of the trigonometric double-angle formulas. We use Osborn's rule to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity. 

Osborn's rule states that to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity, we

- replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function, and

- for any product of two trigonometric sines, change the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

$\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\sinh}{\mathop{\rm sinh}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\cosh}{\mathop{\rm cosh}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\tanh}{\mathop{\rm tanh}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

For example, let's consider the following integral:

$$
\displaystyle{\int} \sinh x \cosh x \, \textrm{d}x
$$

  

Notice that the corresponding trigonometric integral is

$$
\displaystyle{\int} \sin x \cos x \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

  

One way of solving this trigonometric integral is to use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\sin 2x = 2\sin x \cos x
$$

Applying Osborn's rule, we get an equivalent hyperbolic identity:

$$
\sinh 2x = 2\sinh x \cosh x
$$

Rearranging the above formula, we get

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\sinh {2x}= \sinh x \cosh x.
$$

 

Therefore, we can calculate our original integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sinh}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sinh}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cosh}⁡2x+C\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167028 :activity/expected-seconds 1260.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186051482 :answer-field/choices 17592186051483] [:db/retract 17592186051482 :answer-field/choices 17592186051484] [:db/retract 17592186051482 :answer-field/choices 17592186051485] [:db/retract 17592186051482 :answer-field/choices 17592186051486] [:db/retract 17592186051482 :answer-field/choices 17592186051487] {:db/id 17592186054664 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e75342f3-2efc-5d3d-a3c3-d44c19646c04"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054992 :question/problem "![](images/ae/aee38b4fa46a403ee9517fc5a087434c8205b6553a4ebefa43be74ba7babfbc0.png)

moment $\text{E}[XY]=4,$ and second raw moments $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=8$ and $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]=15.$ Find the variance of $5X+2Y.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y]+2ab\,\text{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find $\text{Var}[X]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =8-{2}^{2} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =15-{3}^{2} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =4-2\cdot 3 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[5X+2Y] & ={5}^{2}\cdot 4+{2}^{2}\cdot 6+2\cdot 5\cdot 2\cdot (-2) \\  & =100+24-40 \\  & =84.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ea6f32d4-0004-5767-8eca-1a4a4e3083fd"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id
