"![](images/32/321c16127ae1999e4ec42024f35cd076930618588fe378b9ca16a4ee4eabd58a.png)

Consider the vector field $F=-0.5x\,i-0.5y\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $8$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across all four sides of the square.*" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/ab/abe90a592e098a4656577f3a2303669dccc126baff738397836c8f96c26b5389.png)

First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-0.5x\,i-0.5y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-0.5{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=4\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-4,4].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-0.5{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-0.5{\int }_{-4}^{4}4\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{-4}^{4}\text{d}t \\  & =-2(4-(-4)) \\  & =(-2)\cdot 8 \\  & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides ${C}_{2},{C}_{3},$ and ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=4\cdot (-16)=-64.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a8f6c78e-2502-540d-9f7b-11049bb63129"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a8f6c78e-2502-540d-9f7b-11049bb63129" :answer-field/id #uuid "a8f6c78e-2502-540d-9f7b-11049bb63129" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-5a4b60e3-cd37-51c5-b631-37359cad927c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e63d7042-0452-51d5-8e47-47acba03407b" "answer-4fce93da-e871-5c72-9d09-6eb4bf2aae2b" "answer-7ae15837-c155-5657-9cbb-e2ad0a708b49" "answer-cb15f9d8-3a05-5c26-bc50-d85a868e79fa" "answer-5a4b60e3-cd37-51c5-b631-37359cad927c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e63d7042-0452-51d5-8e47-47acba03407b" :answer/id #uuid "e63d7042-0452-51d5-8e47-47acba03407b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-16" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4fce93da-e871-5c72-9d09-6eb4bf2aae2b" :answer/id #uuid "4fce93da-e871-5c72-9d09-6eb4bf2aae2b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-24" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7ae15837-c155-5657-9cbb-e2ad0a708b49" :answer/id #uuid "7ae15837-c155-5657-9cbb-e2ad0a708b49" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-32" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cb15f9d8-3a05-5c26-bc50-d85a868e79fa" :answer/id #uuid "cb15f9d8-3a05-5c26-bc50-d85a868e79fa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-36" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5a4b60e3-cd37-51c5-b631-37359cad927c" :answer/id #uuid "5a4b60e3-cd37-51c5-b631-37359cad927c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-64" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-90bd3eab-412f-52dc-83f5-2f8877931db1" :question/id #uuid "90bd3eab-412f-52dc-83f5-2f8877931db1" :question/math-academy-id "q-127193" :question/problem "![](images/32/32d4722f4a1dd1cfae3fb22cde7399dcb66623e484bcd5989fd2de246a905b51.png)

Consider the vector field $F=-3\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/3b/3bd953b7fb02b90a55a29bea6f58ff9bd8bab77d62b1df1c547ca899656d37a3.png)

Now, since the vector field $F=-3\,j$ is parallel to ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{3},$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s.
$$

Now, since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through ${C}_{2}$ will cancel with the net outflow through ${C}_{4}.$ That is

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s=-{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s\,⟹\,{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8bc18207-a6fd-5437-a68d-b3d6fef6d67e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8bc18207-a6fd-5437-a68d-b3d6fef6d67e" :answer-field/id #uuid "8bc18207-a6fd-5437-a68d-b3d6fef6d67e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1add2c2e-a167-5c2c-b545-a5f1eb517140" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d3235a30-a18e-50b4-a05b-6c1309b09270" "answer-91c49acb-1fa6-5ddc-9050-3b83a7f4c764" "answer-1add2c2e-a167-5c2c-b545-a5f1eb517140" "answer-ba10258f-f51b-5e95-9c08-2bf569bcb880" "answer-28b45251-3b7f-5715-8789-20bd83838a64"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d3235a30-a18e-50b4-a05b-6c1309b09270" :answer/id #uuid "d3235a30-a18e-50b4-a05b-6c1309b09270" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-91c49acb-1fa6-5ddc-9050-3b83a7f4c764" :answer/id #uuid "91c49acb-1fa6-5ddc-9050-3b83a7f4c764" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1add2c2e-a167-5c2c-b545-a5f1eb517140" :answer/id #uuid "1add2c2e-a167-5c2c-b545-a5f1eb517140" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ba10258f-f51b-5e95-9c08-2bf569bcb880" :answer/id #uuid "ba10258f-f51b-5e95-9c08-2bf569bcb880" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-28b45251-3b7f-5715-8789-20bd83838a64" :answer/id #uuid "28b45251-3b7f-5715-8789-20bd83838a64" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]}]

$\frac{x-2}{2x}+\frac{x-4}{2x}=\frac{5x-6}{2x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $x=0$ is an excluded solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

We multiply both sides of the equation by $2x,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{2x}+\frac{x-4}{2x} & =\frac{5x-6}{2x} \\ 2x\cdot (\frac{x-2}{2x}+\frac{x-4}{2x}) & =n\cdot (\frac{5x-6}{2x}) \\ 2x\cdot \frac{x-2}{2x}+2x\cdot \frac{x-4}{2x} & =2x\cdot \frac{5x-6}{2x} \\ \cancel{2x}\cdot \frac{x-2}{\cancel{2x}}+\cancel{2x}\cdot \frac{x-4}{\cancel{2x}} & =\cancel{2x}\cdot \frac{5x-6}{\cancel{2x}} \\ x-2+x-4 & =5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2+x-4 & =5x-6 \\ 2x-6 & =5x-6 \\ 5x-2x & =-6+6 \\ 3x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. Therefore, we conclude that there is no solution." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c8e3c1c2-59cd-57ee-a592-7d15bb5c605d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c8e3c1c2-59cd-57ee-a592-7d15bb5c605d" :answer-field/id #uuid "c8e3c1c2-59cd-57ee-a592-7d15bb5c605d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1df39945-f17e-5051-9124-626d55bf8a1a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-64742e1b-bec8-5682-b5ee-105f5d4f7a68" "answer-abfebc27-8159-524d-9a6e-cdfd59eb0187" "answer-7532c4d0-18e0-53bb-a6b7-c9f7c5d650eb" "answer-befbf0c7-7d19-5ffd-943e-139e02963d23" "answer-1df39945-f17e-5051-9124-626d55bf8a1a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-64742e1b-bec8-5682-b5ee-105f5d4f7a68" :answer/id #uuid "64742e1b-bec8-5682-b5ee-105f5d4f7a68" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-abfebc27-8159-524d-9a6e-cdfd59eb0187" :answer/id #uuid "abfebc27-8159-524d-9a6e-cdfd59eb0187" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7532c4d0-18e0-53bb-a6b7-c9f7c5d650eb" :answer/id #uuid "7532c4d0-18e0-53bb-a6b7-c9f7c5d650eb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-befbf0c7-7d19-5ffd-943e-139e02963d23" :answer/id #uuid "befbf0c7-7d19-5ffd-943e-139e02963d23" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1df39945-f17e-5051-9124-626d55bf8a1a" :answer/id #uuid "1df39945-f17e-5051-9124-626d55bf8a1a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "No solution" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-21325d3f-ea32-5619-afd8-5e491ef497e5" :question/id #uuid "21325d3f-ea32-5619-afd8-5e491ef497e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-270354" :question/problem "Solve for $b$ where $\frac{b+5}{b}+\frac{b-7}{b}=6.$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $b=0$ is an excluded solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

We multiply both sides of the equation by $b,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{b+5}{b}+\frac{b-7}{b} & =6 \\ b\cdot (\frac{b+5}{b}+\frac{b-7}{b}) & =b\cdot 6 \\ b\cdot \frac{b+5}{b}+b\cdot \frac{b-7}{b} & =b\cdot 6 \\ \cancel{b}\cdot \frac{b+5}{\cancel{b}}+\cancel{b}\cdot \frac{b-7}{\cancel{b}} & =b\cdot 6 \\ b+5+b-7 & =6b\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $b,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}b+5+b-7 & =6b \\ 2b-2 & =6b \\ -4b & =2 \\ b & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $b=0$ as a solution. However, since $b=-\frac{1}{2}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $b=-\frac{1}{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1e7444c8-c4e7-5947-a2ec-fcf6d2b56070"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1e7444c8-c4e7-5947-a2ec-fcf6d2b56070" :answer-field/id #uuid "1e7444c8-c4e7-5947-a2ec-fcf6d2b56070" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-c78e8f45-6241-530a-8e86-768b85aa828e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c78e8f45-6241-530a-8e86-768b85aa828e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c78e8f45-6241-530a-8e86-768b85aa828e" :answer/id #uuid "c78e8f45-6241-530a-8e86-768b85aa828e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-a581df95-2d51-59ad-a71c-d2138e307e87" :question/id #uuid "a581df95-2d51-59ad-a71c-d2138e307e87" :question/math-academy-id "q-3518" :question/problem "Solve for $x$ where $\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{x}=\frac{3-x}{3x}.$" :question/worked-solution "We note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined.

The equation has the denominators $x$ and $3x.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(x,3x)=3x.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $3x,$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x\cdot (\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{x}) & =3x\cdot (\frac{3-x}{3x}) \\ 3x\cdot \frac{2}{3}+3x\cdot \frac{1}{x} & =3x\cdot \frac{3-x}{3x} \\ \cancel{3}x\cdot \frac{2}{\cancel{3}}+3\cancel{x}\cdot \frac{1}{\cancel{x}} & =\cancel{3x}\cdot \frac{3-x}{\cancel{3x}} \\ x\cdot (2)+3\cdot (1) & =3-x \\ 2x+3 & =3-x\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+3 & =3-x \\ 2x+x & =3-3 \\ 3x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. Since $x=0,$ we conclude that there is no solution." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0e75216d-bcd6-569a-b621-c249dcbf26bb"] :db/ensure The equation has the denominators $3q$ and $4q.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(3q,4q)=12q.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $12q,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2q-1}{4q} & =\frac{q+1}{3q}-1 \\ 12q\cdot (\frac{2q-1}{4q}) & =12q\cdot (\frac{q+1}{3q}-1) \\ 12q\cdot \frac{2q-1}{4q} & =12q\cdot \frac{q+1}{3q}-12q\cdot 1 \\ 3\cdot \cancel{4q}\cdot (\frac{2q-1}{\cancel{4q}}) & =4\cdot \cancel{3q}\cdot (\frac{q+1}{\cancel{3q}})-12q \\ 3(2q-1) & =4(q+1)-12q\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $q,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3(2q-1) & =4(q+1)-12q \\ 6q-3 & =4q+4-12q \\ 6q-3 & =-8q+4 \\ 6q+8q & =4+3 \\ 14q & =7 \\ q & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $q=0$ as a solution. :question/worked-solution "We note that $m=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $3m,6m,$ and $9m.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(3m,6m,9m)=18m.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $18m,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4m+1}{3m}-\frac{m-1}{6m} & =\frac{1}{9m} \\ 18m\cdot (\frac{4m+1}{3m}-\frac{m-1}{6m}) & =18m\cdot (\frac{1}{9m}) \\ 18m\cdot (\frac{4m+1}{3m})-18m\cdot (\frac{m-1}{6m}) & =18m\cdot (\frac{1}{9m}) \\ 6\cdot 3m\cdot (\frac{4m+1}{3m})-3\cdot 6m\cdot (\frac{m-1}{6m}) & =2\cdot 9m\cdot (\frac{1}{9m}) \\ 6\cdot \cancel{3m}\cdot (\frac{4m+1}{\cancel{3m}})-3\cdot \cancel{6m}\cdot (\frac{m-1}{\cancel{6m}}) & =2\cdot \cancel{9m}\cdot (\frac{1}{\cancel{9m}}) \\ 6(4m+1)-3(m-1) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $m,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6(4m+1)-3(m-1) & =2 \\ 24m+6-3m+3 & =2 \\ 21m+9 & =2 \\ 21m & =-7 \\ m & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $m=0$ as a solution. :question/worked-solution "We note that $n=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $2n,$ ${n}^{2},$ and $3n.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(2n,{n}^{2},3n)=6{n}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $6{n}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2n}-\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}} & =\frac{7}{3n} \\ 6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2n}-\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}) & =6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{7}{3n}) \\ 6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2n})-6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}) & =6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{7}{3n}) \\ 3n\cdot 2n\cdot (\frac{3}{2n})-6\cdot {n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}) & =2n\cdot 3n\cdot (\frac{7}{3n}) \\ 3n\cdot \cancel{2n}\cdot (\frac{3}{\cancel{2n}})-6\cdot \cancel{{n}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1-n}{\cancel{{n}^{2}}}) & =2n\cdot \cancel{3n}\cdot (\frac{7}{\cancel{3n}}) \\ 3n\cdot (3)-6\cdot (1-n) & =2n\cdot (7) \\ 9n-6(1-n) & =14n\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $n,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}9n-6(1-n) & =14n \\ 15n-6 & =14n \\ n & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $n=0$ as a solution. But since $n=6\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $n=6.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-efc35caa-71e9-53b2-85d0-1e3c73992105"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-efc35caa-71e9-53b2-85d0-1e3c73992105" :answer-field/id #uuid "efc35caa-71e9-53b2-85d0-1e3c73992105" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-2db04f8a-deb3-5e11-91d5-eea128cb749d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b61f0de4-08b9-5e89-9aaa-a012a63e7f6f" "answer-c71bf5dc-237a-5908-9987-a1df036cb19a" "answer-cf71e830-8356-5e8d-bce8-f9b93f8cc125" "answer-2db04f8a-deb3-5e11-91d5-eea128cb749d" "answer-0b7a2e99-60fa-5845-b485-7f1ecf41d0a7"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b61f0de4-08b9-5e89-9aaa-a012a63e7f6f" :answer/id #uuid "b61f0de4-08b9-5e89-9aaa-a012a63e7f6f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c71bf5dc-237a-5908-9987-a1df036cb19a" :answer/id #uuid "c71bf5dc-237a-5908-9987-a1df036cb19a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cf71e830-8356-5e8d-bce8-f9b93f8cc125" :answer/id #uuid "cf71e830-8356-5e8d-bce8-f9b93f8cc125" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2db04f8a-deb3-5e11-91d5-eea128cb749d" :answer/id #uuid "2db04f8a-deb3-5e11-91d5-eea128cb749d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0b7a2e99-60fa-5845-b485-7f1ecf41d0a7" :answer/id #uuid "0b7a2e99-60fa-5845-b485-7f1ecf41d0a7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ff75b330-ecd4-5fa0-b36d-564d6c66e864" :question/id #uuid "ff75b330-ecd4-5fa0-b36d-564d6c66e864" :question/math-academy-id "q-276869" :question/problem "Solve for $v$ where $\frac{v+4}{{v}^{2}}-\frac{7}{6v}=\frac{5}{2{v}^{2}}.$

$$

\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the Pythagorean identity 

$$
\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x= 1.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic Pythagorean identity

$$
\cosh^2x -\sinh^2x=1
$$

which we can write as

$$
1+\sinh^2x=\cosh^2x.
$$

Additionally, we have

$$
\sech x = \dfrac{1}{\cosh x}.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x})}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166796 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a49f44d3-1abb-5067-966c-70ae50d2155e" "question-9ddcb9f3-50a1-505b-ae57-c8a55dc1f652" "question-6c61796b-b24c-5403-8a9e-cd8bda63e7c0" "question-7461b1f3-1aea-5d09-ab06-c9f25cb75e4f" "question-4e26e540-b6e1-55b9-88da-a99de2917513"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166634 :question/problem "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}

\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\ln 2} \dfrac{\tanh{x}-\tanh^3{x}}{\sech{x}} \, \textrm{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}

\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the secant-tangent identity 

$$
1 + \tan^2 x= \sec^2{x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic secant-tangent identity

$$
1-\tanh^2x=\sech^2{x}.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the integral and evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{\operatorname{tanh}⁡x-{tanh}^{3}⁡x}{\operatorname{sech}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{(1-{tanh}^{2}⁡x)\operatorname{tanh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sech}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{{sech}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sech}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =-\operatorname{sech}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+\operatorname{sech}⁡0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}+\frac{2}{{e}^{0}+{e}^{0}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{(2+\frac{1}{2})}+1 \\  & =-\frac{2}{(\frac{5}{2})}+1 \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166797 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-36b4a778-aa5a-54d9-9b61-eb9431bef188" "question-d50512b3-2d0b-53b0-a169-ed8ad3f44908" "question-70e33acb-bebf-51b2-9607-6c52a3430a18" "question-fe6b40d3-8971-55c8-aabc-4ac03f347ec4" "question-9ea30f92-f367-5355-89e8-50b8c17d0449"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166635 :question/problem "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}

\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_{\ln 3}^{\ln 6} \dfrac{\csch{x}}{\coth^2{x} - 1} \, \textrm{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the cosecant-cotangent identity 

$$

\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
1 + \cot^2 x= \csc^2{x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic cosecant-cotangent identity

$$
\coth^2x - 1=\csch^2{x}.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the integral and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		\int_{\ln 3}^{\ln 6} \dfrac{\csch{x}}{\coth^2{x} - 1} \, \textrm{d}x
			&= \int_{\ln 3}^{\ln 6} \dfrac{\csch{x}}{\csch^2{x}} \, \textrm{d}x \[5pt]
			&= \int_{\ln 3}^{\ln 6} \sinh{x} \, \textrm{d}x \[5pt]
			&= \cosh{x} \Big|_{\ln 3}^{\ln 6}\[5pt]
			&= \cosh(\ln 6) - \cosh(\ln 3)\[5pt]
			&= \left(\dfrac{e^{\ln 6}+e^{-\ln 6}}{2}\right) - \left(\dfrac{e^{\ln 3}+e^{-\ln 3}}{2}\right)\[5pt]
			&= \left(\dfrac{6 + \dfrac{1}{6}}{2}\right) - \left(\dfrac{3 + \dfrac{1}{3}}{2}\right)\[5pt]
			&= \dfrac{37}{12} - \dfrac{5}{3}\[5pt]
			&= \dfrac{37}{12} - \dfrac{20}{12} \[5pt]
            &= \dfrac{17}{12}
	}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166798 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c7a3ee0b-1bd5-5d07-b45d-54312bc57611" "question-f321e82d-23c7-5f15-828b-dbb232e439d7" "question-7649fd25-c8c5-5938-a768-41b9d4f9aa06" "question-1c959d7c-d68c-591a-a3b7-ea71063de12e" "question-56c765b2-a04b-54c3-b2ad-79e20147ade9"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166636 :question/problem "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}

$$
\cosh^2 (2x+1) - \sinh^2(2x+1) = 1

$$
\cosh^2 (2x+1) -1 = \sinh^2(2x+1).

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic Pythagorean identity

$$
{cosh}^{2}⁡x-{sinh}^{2}⁡x=1.
$$

Additionally, we have

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{coth}^{2}⁡x}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{{coth}^{2}⁡x}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x-1+1}\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{{coth}^{2}⁡x}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{(\frac{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x})}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{coth}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186165656 :answer-field/correct "answer-744490d1-9896-5ac5-9b5a-97aeb15a3238" :answer-field/choices ["answer-744490d1-9896-5ac5-9b5a-97aeb15a3238" "answer-421b7a92-fb82-5fac-b1cf-0b831b760fd1" "answer-84be6896-bcea-56cf-8b32-6d72991af814" "answer-94e81827-f57f-549f-8221-d7c1a9b3c0c3" "answer-cc34c6ea-57ba-59bc-8e55-253f0cdf1126"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-744490d1-9896-5ac5-9b5a-97aeb15a3238" :answer/id #uuid "744490d1-9896-5ac5-9b5a-97aeb15a3238" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\operatorname{coth}⁡x+C" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-421b7a92-fb82-5fac-b1cf-0b831b760fd1" :answer/id #uuid "421b7a92-fb82-5fac-b1cf-0b831b760fd1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\operatorname{coth}⁡x+\operatorname{cosh}⁡x+C" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-84be6896-bcea-56cf-8b32-6d72991af814" :answer/id #uuid "84be6896-bcea-56cf-8b32-6d72991af814" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\operatorname{sech}⁡x-\operatorname{sinh}⁡x+C" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-94e81827-f57f-549f-8221-d7c1a9b3c0c3" :answer/id #uuid "94e81827-f57f-549f-8221-d7c1a9b3c0c3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{coth}⁡x+C" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cc34c6ea-57ba-59bc-8e55-253f0cdf1126" :answer/id #uuid "cc34c6ea-57ba-59bc-8e55-253f0cdf1126" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{sech}⁡x+C" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-a49f44d3-1abb-5067-966c-70ae50d2155e" :question/id #uuid "a49f44d3-1abb-5067-966c-70ae50d2155e" :question/math-academy-id "q-96429" :question/problem "Evaluate ${\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{2-2{tanh}^{4}⁡x}{1+{tanh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the secant-tangent identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic secant-tangent identity

$$
1-{tanh}^{2}⁡x={sech}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the integral and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{2-2{tanh}^{4}⁡x}{1+{tanh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{1-{tanh}^{4}⁡x}{1+{tanh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{(1-{tanh}^{2}⁡x)(1+{tanh}^{2}⁡x)}{1+{tanh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(1-{tanh}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{tanh}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =2\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-2\operatorname{tanh}⁡0 \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-1}{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+1}-2\cdot \frac{{e}^{0}-1}{{e}^{0}+1} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{2}^{2}-1}{{2}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-58f1aa97-2aa4-5f57-8fa7-34a54ff2bfe8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-58f1aa97-2aa4-5f57-8fa7-34a54ff2bfe8" :answer-field/id #uuid "58f1aa97-2aa4-5f57-8fa7-34a54ff2bfe8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-2efeda09-6488-58c8-b51d-5cb115113e8b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-bd388afb-e318-5bb0-ad11-815dec250e03" "answer-3694787f-4267-5b85-9a9d-c811b7ca8c3f" "answer-5c2f505b-06f8-527d-b1b4-f411adee504d" "answer-ee6a0a2b-3a0c-5024-a882-d244026f8d60" "answer-2efeda09-6488-58c8-b51d-5cb115113e8b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bd388afb-e318-5bb0-ad11-815dec250e03" :answer/id #uuid "bd388afb-e318-5bb0-ad11-815dec250e03" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3694787f-4267-5b85-9a9d-c811b7ca8c3f" :answer/id #uuid "3694787f-4267-5b85-9a9d-c811b7ca8c3f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5c2f505b-06f8-527d-b1b4-f411adee504d" :answer/id #uuid "5c2f505b-06f8-527d-b1b4-f411adee504d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ee6a0a2b-3a0c-5024-a882-d244026f8d60" :answer/id #uuid "ee6a0a2b-3a0c-5024-a882-d244026f8d60" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2efeda09-6488-58c8-b51d-5cb115113e8b" :answer/id #uuid "2efeda09-6488-58c8-b51d-5cb115113e8b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{6}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-9ddcb9f3-50a1-505b-ae57-c8a55dc1f652" :question/id #uuid "9ddcb9f3-50a1-505b-ae57-c8a55dc1f652" :question/math-academy-id "q-347992" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the secant-tangent identity 

$$
{sec}^{2}⁡x-1={tan}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic secant-tangent identity

$$
1-{sech}^{2}⁡x={tanh}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the integral and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\frac{{sech}^{2}⁡x}{1-{sech}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\frac{{sech}^{2}⁡x}{{tanh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{sech}^{2}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{tanh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\frac{1}{{sinh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{coth}⁡x{|}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\  & =-(\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)-\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)) \\  & =\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡4) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}-\frac{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡4}}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡4}} \\  & =\frac{2+{2}^{-1}}{2-{2}^{-1}}-\frac{4+{4}^{-1}}{4-{4}^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}-\frac{17}{15} \\  & =\frac{8}{15}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6cecfe57-733c-5892-b9ce-085b5206a4dd"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-6cecfe57-733c-5892-b9ce-085b5206a4dd" :answer-field/id #uuid "6cecfe57-733c-5892-b9ce-085b5206a4dd" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-5ba324a1-6779-572b-99bc-3815b4a02bbf" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5ba324a1-6779-572b-99bc-3815b4a02bbf"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5ba324a1-6779-572b-99bc-3815b4a02bbf" :answer/id #uuid "5ba324a1-6779-572b-99bc-3815b4a02bbf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{8}{15}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-6c61796b-b24c-5403-8a9e-cd8bda63e7c0" :question/id #uuid "6c61796b-b24c-5403-8a9e-cd8bda63e7c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-96405" :question/problem "Calculate $\int \frac{1-\operatorname{tanh}⁡x}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x(1-{tanh}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the secant-tangent identity

We use Osborn's rule to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity. 

Osborn's rule states that to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity, we

- replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function, and

- for any product of two trigonometric sines, change the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

$\displaystyle 
        \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

For example, suppose we want to calculate the following integral:

$$
\int \cosh^2{x} - \sinh^2{x} \: \textrm{d}x
$$

First, we recall the Pythagorean identity

$$
\cos^2{x} + \sin^2{x} = 1.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the corresponding hyperbolic identity

$$
\cosh^2{x} - \sinh^2{x} = 1.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {{{cosh}^{2}⁡x-{sinh}^{2}⁡x}_{⏟}}_{1}\,\text{d}x=\int 1\,\text{d}x=x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's see another example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168119 :tutorial/content "$\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
        \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$We can use Osborn's rule to write down the hyperbolic equivalents of the sectant-tangent and cotangent-cosecant identities.

From the secant-tangent identity

$$
1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x
$$

we have the equivalent hyperbolic identity

$$
1 - \tanh^2 x = \sech^2 x.
$$

Similarly, from the cotangent-cosecant identity

$$
1+\cot^2 x = \csc^2 x
$$

we have the equivalent hyperbolic identity

$$
1-\coth^2 x  = -\csch^2 x
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\coth^2 x - 1 = \csch^2 x.

$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- the $3$rd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to the $3$rd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}.$

Notice that the covariance matrix corresponding to $X$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}V{Σ}^{T}({U}^{T}U)Σ{V}^{T} \\  & =V(\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ){V}^{T},\end{aligned}
$$

where the final expression represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C.$ Notice that:

- $\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ$ is a diagonal $3\times 3$ matrix, where the entries on the main diagonal are the eigenvalues (written in descending order) of the covariance matrix $C$, and

- $V$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix, whose columns are the corresponding unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$

Therefore, the columns of $V$ are the principal components of the data.
So, the third principal component is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].

"question-6923f3da-7346-5c88-a6fe-bd6d1873e88f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193317 :question/problem "A scientist measured $5$ particular features, ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{5},$ for each athlete among a group of athletes. The collected data was stored in the standardized observation matrix $X,$ where each row contains measurements for a particular athlete.
The singular values of $X$ are 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=5,\,{\sigma }_{2}=2,\,{\sigma }_{3}=1,\,{\sigma }_{4}=0.5,\,{\sigma }_{5}=0.1.
$$

The scientist then converted the original observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ using the equation $Y=X{V}_{2},$ where ${V}_{2}$ is the $5\times 2$ matrix consisting of the first two principal components of the data. What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix $Y$ compared to the initial observation matrix $X?$" :question/worked-solution "Let $V$ be the matrix of principal components. Then, applying the change of variables

$$
Y=XV
$$

we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}$ are uncorrelated),

- the features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance, and

- the squares of the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}^{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2},…,{\sigma }_{5}^{2}$ represent the variances in the respective features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}.$

Now, the total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(5)^{2}+(2)^{2}+(1)^{2}+(0.5)^{2}+(0.1)^{2} \\  & =30.26\end{aligned}
$$

Since the scientist used only the first two principal components, the remaining variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Remaining} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(5)^{2}+(2)^{2} \\  & =29.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{Remaining}}{\text{Total}} & =\frac{29}{30.26} \\  & ≈0.958 \\  & =95.8%.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186191829 :answer-field/correct 17592186191832 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-a62d30b2-87c9-5394-8f0b-7a8e71495548" :question/id #uuid "a62d30b2-87c9-5394-8f0b-7a8e71495548" :question/math-academy-id "q-345594" :question/problem "An epidemiologist measured $4$ particular features, ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4},$ for each disease affecting a specific population. $$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xz)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+z)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2) \\  & =2z+0+0 \\  & =2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}2z\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}2z\,\text{d}z \\  & =(1-(-1))\cdot (1-0)\cdot [{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=1} \\  & =2({1}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130990 :answer-field/correct 17592186130992 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133930 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d1625297-e3fd-57e3-914d-8b51c40eca40" "question-65b5959b-427f-58b2-a1ab-3381594e4750"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d1625297-e3fd-57e3-914d-8b51c40eca40" :question/id #uuid "d1625297-e3fd-57e3-914d-8b51c40eca40" :question/math-academy-id "q-162576" :question/problem "Consider the positively (outward) oriented surface $S$ given by $(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}+(z+3)^{2}=16$ and the vector field $F=(x+2y)\,i+(4z-y)\,j+(z+xy)\,k.$ Use the divergence theorem to find the flux of $F$ across $S.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. $$
24÷4=6\,\text{R}0.

:question/id #uuid "6b8e59d5-6b05-50ce-8455-191b0c2a0b7a" :question/math-academy-id "q-73776" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{2}+5x+4?$

I. $x=4$ is a root of $f(x)$

II. $(x-4)$ is a factor of $f(x)$

III. $(x-4)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder" :question/worked-solution "The factor theorem states that $(x-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=r$ is also a root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(x-4).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-4 & =0 \\ x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

We now check each of the statements, in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, $x=4$ is not a root of $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4) & ={4}^{2}+5(4)+4 \\  & =16+20+4 \\  & =40 \\  & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. According to the factor theorem, since $x=4$ is not a root of $f(x),$ then $(x-4)$ is not a factor of $f(x).$

- Statement III is false. Since $(x-4)$ is not a factor of $f(x),$ then it does not divide $f(x)$ with zero remainder.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-63b70b6a-3c22-5376-9d31-4b93eb63027c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-63b70b6a-3c22-5376-9d31-4b93eb63027c" :answer-field/id #uuid "63b70b6a-3c22-5376-9d31-4b93eb63027c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-b074b252-d948-500c-8a9b-b0d2c27004f1" :answer-field/choices ["answer-6fc2e5c4-3531-5d25-8436-a4eb1e7ccd7a" "answer-f2645d9f-4118-565c-be24-6f9684808038" "answer-002539d9-f83f-5f8a-821f-f91ec24993f6" "answer-17a8904d-7494-54a8-9cf6-42abe4eadb2e" "answer-b074b252-d948-500c-8a9b-b0d2c27004f1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6fc2e5c4-3531-5d25-8436-a4eb1e7ccd7a" :answer/id #uuid "6fc2e5c4-3531-5d25-8436-a4eb1e7ccd7a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f2645d9f-4118-565c-be24-6f9684808038" :answer/id #uuid "f2645d9f-4118-565c-be24-6f9684808038" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-002539d9-f83f-5f8a-821f-f91ec24993f6" :answer/id #uuid "002539d9-f83f-5f8a-821f-f91ec24993f6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-17a8904d-7494-54a8-9cf6-42abe4eadb2e" :answer/id #uuid "17a8904d-7494-54a8-9cf6-42abe4eadb2e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b074b252-d948-500c-8a9b-b0d2c27004f1" :answer/id #uuid "b074b252-d948-500c-8a9b-b0d2c27004f1" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "None" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-7c34a96f-d461-5b11-9cb5-80d7557e52d7" :question/id #uuid "7c34a96f-d461-5b11-9cb5-80d7557e52d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-73777" :question/problem "For which of the following polynomials is $(x+1)$ a factor?

I. $f(x)={x}^{2}+3x+2$

II. $g(x)={x}^{2}+8x+7$

III. $h(x)=-{x}^{2}+x$" :question/worked-solution "The factor theorem states that $(x-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=r$ is also a root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(x+1).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =0 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

According to the factor theorem, $(x+1)$ is a factor of $p(x)$ if the root $x=-1$ is a root of $p(x).$ 

So now, we will check if $x=-1$ is a root of the polynomials $f,$ $g$ and $h.$

- Evaluating $x=-1$ at $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1) & =(-1)^{2}+3(-1)+2 \\  & =1-3+2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that $(x+1)$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$

- Now, evaluating $x=-1$ at $g(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-1) & =(-1)^{2}+8(-1)+7 \\  & =1-8+7 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, by the factor theorem, we conclude that $(x+1)$ is indeed a factor of $g(x).$

- Finally, evaluating $x=-1$ at $h(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-1) & =-(-1)^{2}+(-1) \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e9167685-de61-5642-a6f3-e2034b8507d4"] :db/ensure :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}-64?$

I. $x=-4$ is a root of $f(x)$

II. $(x+4)$ is a factor of $f(x)$

III. $(x+4)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder" :question/worked-solution "The factor theorem states that $(x-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=r$ is also a root of $p(x).$ 

Here, we are considering $(x+4).$ The root of this expression can be found by setting the expression equal to $0$ and solving:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4 & =0 \\ x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

We now check each of the statements, in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, $x=-4$ is not a root of $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-4) & =(-4)^{3}-64 \\  & =-64-64 \\  & =-128 \\  & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. According to the factor theorem, since $x=-4$ is not a root of $f(x),$ then $(x+4)$ is not a factor of $f(x).$

- Statement III is false. Since $(x+4)$ is not a factor of $f(x),$ then it does not divide $f(x)$ with zero remainder.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b4b04c50-0203-5dfc-9b1a-8237ab5897f1"] :question/id #uuid "b2554883-e4a0-51fb-ab55-70bbe918132c" :question/math-academy-id "q-66431" :question/problem "The equation ${x}^{2}-10x+50=0$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation." :question/worked-solution "We first move the constant to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-10x+50 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-10x & =-50\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-10x & =-50 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 5x+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =-50 \\ (x-5)^{2}-25 & =-50 \\ (x-5)^{2} & =-25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-5,\,q=-25,$ and $p+q=-30.$

We now solve the equation using the square root method.

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-5)^{2} & =-25 \\ x-5 & =\pm \sqrt{-25} \\ x-5 & =\pm 5\,\text{i} \\ x & =5\pm 5\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=5+5\,\text{i}$ and $x=5-5\,\text{i}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields The price of each ticket is $$10.$ The cost of maintaining the cinema is made up of a fixed cost of $$400$ plus a cost of $$0.25$ per person. How many tickets should the cinema sell to maximize its profit?" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

First, note that for selling $x$ tickets, the cinema has a revenue (in dollars) of 

$$
R(x)=10\cdot x=10x
$$

and a cost (in dollars) of 

$$
C(x)={{400}_{⏟}}_{\text{fixed cost}}\,\,+{{0.25x.}_{⏟}}_{\text{variable cost}}
$$

Therefore, the profit function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =R(x)-C(x) \\  & =10x-(400+0.25x) \\  & =9.75x-400.\end{aligned}
$$

We note that the permitted domain is $0\le x\le 120.$ Therefore, $x=0$ and $x=120$ are candidates for the global maxima of $P(x).$

We need to find the critical points of $P(x)$ for $0<x<120.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=9.75.
$$

We can see that the equation ${P}^{′}(x)=0$ has no solutions.

Our candidates are $x=0$ and $x=120.$ Computing $P(x)$ at each of these values, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0) & =9.75(0)-400=-400 \\ P(120) & =9.75(120)-400=770\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the cinema will have a maximum profit level when it sells $120$ tickets." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186098511 :answer-field/correct 17592186098514 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101018 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-da64bda4-339a-50c3-828b-c79ac0fe60b0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-da64bda4-339a-50c3-828b-c79ac0fe60b0" :question/id #uuid "da64bda4-339a-50c3-828b-c79ac0fe60b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-87576" :question/problem "A daycare center can take care of between $10$ and $20$ children. The fee that parents must pay each month depends on the number of children enrolled in the center. If there are $10$ children enrolled, parents must pay $$40.$ On the other hand, if there are more than $10$ children enrolled, the price drops by $$2$ for each child. All the parents pay the same monthly fee.

How many children must enroll for the center to maximize its revenue?" :question/worked-solution "First, note that if there are $10+x$ children enrolled, then the monthly fee is $40-2x.$ So, the total revenue is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & ={{(10+x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{number of children enrolled}}\times \,\,\,\,\,\,{{(40-2x)}_{⏟}}_{\text{monthly fee}} \\  & =(10+x)(40-2x) \\  & =400-20x+40x-2{x}^{2} \\  & =400+20x-2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the center can only take care between $10$ and $20$ children, the permitted domain for $x$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & \le x+10\le 20 \\ 0 & \le x\le 10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=0$ and $x=10$ are both candidates for the global maxima of $R(x).$

We need to find the critical points of $R(x)$ for $0<x<10.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{R}^{′}(x)=20-4x,
$$

and solving ${R}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 20-4x & =0 \\ 4x & =20 \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $x=5$ lies in the interval $0<x<10.$ All that's left now is to confirm that $x=5$ does indeed give a maximum value of $R(x).$ To do this, we compute the second derivative:

$$
{R}^{″}(x)=-4<0
$$

Since the second derivative is negative, the point $x=5$ is indeed a local maximum of $R(x).$ And since $R(x)$ is quadratic, we conclude that $x=5$ is a global maximum of $R(x).$

:question/id #uuid "4cb999cb-e9bf-5cd0-a21c-a3857e783014" :question/math-academy-id "q-87593" :question/problem "A factory spends $C(x)=100-47x+21{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}$ thousand dollars per month to manufacture $x$ units of a certain product. The factory sells the product for $$100\,000$ per unit. Given that the factory can produce between $1$ and $10$ items per month, what is the maximum monthly profit it can make?" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

First, note that for selling $x$ units of the product per month, the factory has a monthly revenue (income) of $R(x)=100\cdot x=100x$ thousand dollars. 

Therefore, the profit function (in thousands of dollars) is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =R(x)-C(x) \\  & =100x-(100-47x+21{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}) \\  & ={x}^{3}-21{x}^{2}+147x-100.\end{aligned}
$$

We note that the permitted domain is $1\le x\le 10.$ Therefore, $x=1$ and $x=10$ are both candidates for the global maxima of $P(x).$

We need to find the critical points of $P(x)$ for $1<x<10.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=3{x}^{2}-42x+147,
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-42x+147 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-14x+49 & =0 \\ (x-7)^{2} & =0 \\ x & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check if $x=7$ gives a maximum value of $P(x).$ To do this, we compute the second derivative:

$$
{P}^{″}(x)=6x-42.
$$

Evaluating ${P}^{″}(x)$ at the critical point, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{″}(7)=6(7)-42=0,\end{aligned}
$$

which does not confirm or deny that $x=7$ is a maximum of $P(x).$ Therefore, we should consider $x=7$ as one of the candidates.

Our candidates are $x=1,$ $x=7$ and $x=10.$ Computing $P(x)$ at each of these values, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1) & =(1)^{3}-21(1)^{2}+147(1)-100=27 \\ P(7) & =(7)^{3}-21(7)^{2}+147(7)-100=243 \\ P(10) & =(10)^{3}-21(10)^{2}+147(10)-100=270\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum monthly profit is $270\cdot $1\,000=$270\,000.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cbe295f2-3c78-53d7-a4bc-8cad7afb171c"] "A company spends $C(x)=0.01{x}^{2}+4x+680$ dollars to produce $x$ units of a certain product. The company sells the product for $$12$ per unit. Given that the company can produce at most $500$ units per month, how many units should the company produce per month to maximize its monthly profit?" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

First, note that for selling $x$ units of the product per month, the company has a monthly revenue (income) of $R(x)=12\cdot x=12x$ dollars. 

Therefore, the profit function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =R(x)-C(x) \\  & =12x-(0.01{x}^{2}+4x+680) \\  & =8x-0.01{x}^{2}-680.\end{aligned}
$$

We note that the permitted domain is $0\le x\le 500.$ 

We need to find the critical points of $P(x)$ for $0<x<500.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=8-0.02x,
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 8-0.02x & =0 \\ x & =400\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $x=400$ lies in the interval $0<x<500.$ All that's left now is to confirm that $x=400$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(x).$ To do this, we compute the second derivative:

$$
{P}^{″}(x)=-0.02<0
$$

Since the second derivative is negative, the point $x=400$ is indeed a local maximum of $P(x).$ And since $P(x)$ is quadratic, we conclude that $x=400$ is a global maximum of $P(x).$ 

Therefore, we conclude that the company will have a maximum monthly profit when it produces $400$ units per month." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields "A tutoring center offers private lesson packages. When the price of a package is $$40,$ the center books all $80$ available sessions. For every $$4$ increase in the package price, one fewer session is booked. If the cost of providing each session is $$16,$ what price should the center charge to maximize its profit?

To maximize profit, the center should charge $$$
{{field-1}}
per session." :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we apply the candidates test.

Let $x$ represent the number of unbooked sessions. Then the number of **booked** sessions is $(80-x),$ and the **price per session** is $(40+4x).$

So, the total revenue is

$$
R(x)=(80-x)(40+4x).
$$

Expanding, we get

$$
R(x)=-4{x}^{2}+280x+3200.
$$

The cost of providing each booked session is $$16,$ so the total cost is

$$
C(x)=16(80-x)=1280-16x.
$$

Therefore, the profit function is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =R(x)-C(x) \\  & =(-4{x}^{2}+280x+3200)-(1280-16x) \\  & =-4{x}^{2}+296x+1920.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given the domain $0\le x\le 80.$

To find the maximum, we take the derivative:

$$
{P}^{′}(x)=-8x+296.
$$

Solving ${P}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get:

$$
x=37.
$$

Since ${P}^{″}(x)=-8<0,$ this point is a maximum. Since $P(x)$ is quadratic, this maximum is global.

Now, if $x=37$ sessions are unbooked, then the price is:

$$
40+4(37)=188.
$$

Therefore, to maximize profit, the center should charge $$\,\,188$ per session." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields 17592186059514 :question/problem "The angle $\theta =  \dfrac {8\pi}3$ is represented in the coordinate plane in the usual way. In which quadrant does it lie?" :question/worked-solution "First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $\dfrac {8\pi}3$ by *subtracting* integer multiples of $2\pi$ until we get a coterminal angle that lies in the range $[0, 2\pi).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8\pi }{3}-2\pi =\frac{2\pi }{3}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So the angle $\dfrac {2\pi}3$ is coterminal with $\dfrac {8\pi}3.$ Let's draw this coterminal angle in the coordinate plane.

![](images/23/2360ed202deeca403c4631c319b69df30a9f0268b7ef270a8e436103c0ac3edb.png)

We see that $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ lies in quadrant II. Therefore, $\dfrac{8\pi}{3}$ also lies in this quadrant." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059685 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1327ffff-07aa-5bea-93ff-453e6c9d98a5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059513 :question/problem "The angle $\theta =  -435^\circ$ is represented in the coordinate plane in the usual way. In which quadrant does it lie?" :question/worked-solution "First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $-435^\circ$ by *adding* integer multiples of $360^\circ$ until we get a coterminal angle that lies in the range $[0^\circ, 360^\circ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}-{435}^{∘}+{360}^{∘} & =-{75}^{∘} \\ -{75}^{∘}+{360}^{∘} & ={285}^{∘}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So the angle $285^\circ$ is coterminal with $-435^\circ.$ Let's draw this coterminal angle in the coordinate plane.

![](images/4f/4f3fc79c2fc99478c407a63352d9113ef9cbef6a93a6feb62bd284d5f443bed5.png)

We see that $285^\circ$ lies in quadrant IV. Therefore, $-435^\circ$ also lies in this quadrant." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059683 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a22714ba-933f-5202-894c-587dd0012788" "question-a369ef6f-b58e-5e3b-af34-1de431b7ed56"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059511 :question/problem "Which angles are coterminal with $240^\circ?$

$$
600^\circ, \quad 300^\circ, \quad -480^\circ.
$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the coterminal angles of a given angle $\theta,$ we add and subtract integer multiples of $360^\circ\mathbin{.}$

Let's start by adding multiples of $360^\circ$ to $240^\circ\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{240}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}={600}^{∘}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

There are no answer choices larger than $600^\circ,$ so we can stop here.

Now, let's subtract multiples of $360^\circ$ from $240^\circ\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{240}^{∘}-{360}^{∘} & =-{120}^{∘} \\ {240}^{∘}-2\cdot ({360}^{∘}) & =-{480}^{∘}\,✓\end{aligned}

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨4x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $x$-component of $F=⟨4x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $x$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the front and back sides. 

![](images/dc/dc37a067eb8070ecbdfea53c1ede3e221e1873a192b50fcbf07234f33c183787.png)

  

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=3$ for $0\le y\le 2$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=3$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨4x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨12{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =12{y}^{2}{z}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}12{y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}12{y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}12{y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[4{y}^{3}{z}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}32{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[8{z}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for $0\le y\le 2$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨4x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =8+0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8118e8d0-ad36-5eed-a94c-c49d91624022"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087431 :question/problem "Given that $f(x) = x^2,$ what is $f'(x)$ according to the definition of the derivative?" :question/worked-solution "The derivative $f '(x)$ is given by the limit 

$$
\lim_{h\to 0} \dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} .
$$

Since $f(x) = x^2$,  we have that $f(x+h) = (x+h)^2.$ Hence,  we get

$$
\displaystyle f'(x)=\lim_{h\to 0} \dfrac{(x+h)^2-x^2}{h} .
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087881 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-779ee099-0fc5-5dca-bd3b-ce3793ba0e8c" "question-a35127e9-e5f3-508e-9d5a-b3279aa78b1a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087432 :question/problem "Given $y =x^2,$ calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ using the limit of a difference quotient." :question/worked-solution "We let $y=f(x)$ and apply the formula for the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(x+h)^{2}-{x}^{2}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}+2xh+{h}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{2xh+{h}^{2}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{2xh}{h}+\frac{{h}^{2}}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(2x+h) \\  & =2x+0 \\  & =2x\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-ab9ad28a-3195-5102-ad22-90c2dc511297" :question/id #uuid "ab9ad28a-3195-5102-ad22-90c2dc511297" :question/math-academy-id "q-101957" :question/problem "Given that $f(x)=2x+1$, what is ${f}^{′}(x)$ according to the definition of the derivative?" :question/worked-solution "The derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ is given by the limit 

$$
{lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}).
$$

Since $f(x)=2x+1$,  we have that $f(x+h)=2(x+h)+1.$ Hence,  we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{2(x+h)+1-(2x+1)}{h}).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f4d0ff0d-7860-5a8a-a6e6-4fb8f62ae866"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The definition of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying this to $f(x)=-4{x}^{2}+5x$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{-4(x+h)^{2}+5(x+h)-(-4{x}^{2}+5x)}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{-4({x}^{2}+2xh+{h}^{2})+5x+5h+4{x}^{2}-5x}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{-4{x}^{2}-8xh-4{h}^{2}+5x+5h+4{x}^{2}-5x}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{-8xh-4{h}^{2}+5h}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{h(-8x-4h+5)}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(-8x-4h+5) \\  & =-8x+5.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a93c79b4-53dc-5d15-9856-ca96c8afc783"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a93c79b4-53dc-5d15-9856-ca96c8afc783" :answer-field/id #uuid "a93c79b4-53dc-5d15-9856-ca96c8afc783" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f05b0eb8-1f64-572b-9eb7-f009dba2ee76" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f05b0eb8-1f64-572b-9eb7-f009dba2ee76"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f05b0eb8-1f64-572b-9eb7-f009dba2ee76" :answer/id #uuid "f05b0eb8-1f64-572b-9eb7-f009dba2ee76" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-8x+5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186088899 :tutorial/content "The instantaneous rate of change of a function $f(x)$ at the point $x=a,$ denoted $f'(a),$ is given by the limit

$$
f'(a) = \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}.
$$

This formula works for a specific point $x=a.$ If we want a method that works for a *general* point $x,$ then we substitute $a=x$ in the formula and get

$$
f'(x) = \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}.
$$

The function $f'(x)$ is called the **derivative of $f(x)$ with respect to $x$**. It gives the slope of the tangent line to the curve $y=f(x)$ at a general point with coordinates $(x,f(x)).$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186088900 :tutorial/content "For a given curve $y=f(x),$ the derivative can be represented using several different notations. They are

$$
f'(x),\qquad y'(x), \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

In words, the term $y'(x)$  is said like

- "$y$ prime of $x$," or

- "$y$ prime," or sometimes

- "$y$ dash."

The term $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ is said like "dee $y$ by dee $x$."

The important thing to remember is that they all represent the same thing, the derivative." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087898 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133882 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-40abd682-d4fa-55d0-8dea-db00bcc211a6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-40abd682-d4fa-55d0-8dea-db00bcc211a6" :question/id #uuid "40abd682-d4fa-55d0-8dea-db00bcc211a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-109131" :question/problem "Consider the triangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(0,0),(1,1)$ and $(0,1),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ According to Green's theorem, 

$$
{∮}_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+(xy+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,dy={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

Calculate the function $f(x,y).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/56/5673a3eadfa3c01dbb9e2c8bf497b17f34a834d950621afa7d480af625ce1e18.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=xy+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+(xy+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}[y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)]\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=y.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a172fe47-3553-5b48-9c9c-d02e78168ac3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/6d/6d4f13abad5cc193dccedee3114fbd9cbd9fb8e6b5b3ddb0d07f0ed2ed51f4ff.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le y+1,\,-1\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{y+1}(1+x)\operatorname{sin}⁡y\text{ }dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186244254 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{y}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=2x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Therefore,

$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):y\le x\le 4y-{y}^{2},\,0\le y\le 3\}

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{y}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,dx+(2x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2{e}^{y}+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-{e}^{y}-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{y}^{4y-{y}^{2}}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134068 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

We have that $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4xy.\end{aligned}

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+2{x}^{2}y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4xy-2xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2x}2xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186386397 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/c2/c2e08c233cb31124234ab6e5179998a3bdc148024632c7770bdea46cd37dff83.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx+(xy-2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)={y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $Q(x,y)=xy-2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y+2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,x-1\le y\le -2x+2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx+(xy-2y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y+2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x-1}^{-2x+2}y\text{ }dy\,dx\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{x-k}+2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={e}^{y-k}+2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={e}^{y-k}+2 \\ {e}^{y-k} & =x-2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y-k}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2) \\ y-k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)+k\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) = \ln{(x-2)} + k.$

Comparing our answer with the given expression, we conclude that $k=4.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110701 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-fcede9b9-3aa7-543c-ba0b-831f64ff8671" "question-9d666229-2a75-553e-ab1a-3470df672efe" "question-e0086fad-533f-5e80-a92f-0ac75b17640c" "question-34bef420-975f-5d0f-9f81-67d4bd446432" "question-2340627e-913d-5c02-af0a-4af27f0e0758"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110289 :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x) = \dfrac12 e^{x+8}-2.$" :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x+8}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{y+8}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{y+8}-2 \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{y+8} & =x+2 \\ {e}^{y+8} & =2x+4 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y+8}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4) \\ y+8 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4)-8\end{aligned}
$$

     

Therefore, the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) = \ln{(2x+4)} - 8.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110702 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f4092e37-c259-56c3-8698-e5c1a205391f" "question-bc418213-398e-54af-8583-a0bcd69d268b" "question-9b1ff915-f7df-590e-9573-48667059c317" "question-bf8490ce-55f6-59c1-8771-a458611eb22b" "question-6267302e-96c5-5885-be5f-0252c2b87de1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110500 :question/problem "What is the inverse of $f(x) =\ln(x+3)+6?$" :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
y = \ln(x+3)+6
$$

Then, we swap $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+3)+6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+3)+6 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(y+3) & =x-6 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+3)} & ={e}^{x-6} \\ y+3 & ={e}^{x-6} \\ y & ={e}^{x-6}-3\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) = e^{x-6}-3.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110703 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-199584af-715c-57d8-b77d-cfea8258f652" "question-02054798-e30b-5bba-b50a-1ea23b8ac8ca" "question-04376890-0a44-56a8-b428-8110db81b255" "question-3b5ffb6f-7067-559d-aec0-81e9ef0a06b7"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110502 :question/problem "What is the inverse of $f(x) = 2\log_4(3x)-1?$" :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2{log}_{4}⁡(3x)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we swap $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2{log}_{4}⁡(3y)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2{log}_{4}⁡(3y)-1 \\ 2{log}_{4}⁡(3y) & =x+1 \\ {log}_{4}⁡(3y) & =\frac{x+1}{2} \\ {4}^{{log}_{4}⁡(3y)} & ={4}^{(x+1)/2} \\ 3y & ={4}^{(x+1)/2} \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}{4}^{(x+1)/2}\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is $f^{-1}(x) =\dfrac13 4^{(x+1)/2}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-b31f5c4b-dccc-5d6d-b26c-76fe9889b868" :question/id #uuid "b31f5c4b-dccc-5d6d-b26c-76fe9889b868" :question/math-academy-id "q-250404" :question/problem "The inverse of the function $f(x)={e}^{2-x}$ is ${f}^{-1}(x)=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2-x}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={e}^{2-y}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=5\cdot {2}^{x-3}+1,
$$

what is the value of $k?$

$k=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={log}_{2}⁡(\frac{x-1}{5})-k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{2}⁡(\frac{y-1}{5})-k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{2}⁡(\frac{y-1}{5})-k \\ {log}_{2}⁡(\frac{y-1}{5}) & =x+k \\ {2}^{{log}_{2}⁡((y-1)/5)} & ={2}^{x+k} \\ \frac{y-1}{5} & ={2}^{x+k} \\ y-1 & =5\cdot {2}^{x+k} \\ y & =5\cdot {2}^{x+k}+1\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is ${f}^{-1}(x)=5\cdot {2}^{x+k}+1.$ 

Comparing our answer with the given expression, we conclude that $k=-3.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-075d7fee-b2d5-5957-a28d-a7eec528b93a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-075d7fee-b2d5-5957-a28d-a7eec528b93a" :answer-field/id #uuid "075d7fee-b2d5-5957-a28d-a7eec528b93a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f374302c-dbd0-5652-afd7-79c66b75d75d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f374302c-dbd0-5652-afd7-79c66b75d75d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f374302c-dbd0-5652-afd7-79c66b75d75d" :answer/id #uuid "f374302c-dbd0-5652-afd7-79c66b75d75d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186111905 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the transformed exponential function 

$$
f(x)=2^{5x}+1
$$

and we wish to find the inverse function $f^{-1}(x).$ We can do this using the following three steps.

**Step 1:** We start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={2}^{5x}+1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Then, we interchange $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={2}^{5y}+1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={2}^{5y}+1 \\ x-1 & ={2}^{5y} \\ {log}_{2}⁡(x-1) & ={log}_{2}⁡({2}^{5y}) \\ {log}_{2}⁡(x-1) & =5y \\ 5y & ={log}_{2}⁡(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{5}{log}_{2}⁡(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{5}\log_2{(x-1)}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186111881 :tutorial/content "Now suppose we wish to find the inverse of the logarithmic function 

$$
f(x)=3\log_{2}(x-1)+1.
$$

We can find $f^{-1}(x)$ using the same three steps as before.

**Step 1:** We start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = 3\log_{2}(x-1)+1
$$

**Step 2:** Then, we interchange $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
x = 3\log_{2}(y-1)+1
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{log}_{2}⁡(y-1)+1 & =x \\ 3{log}_{2}⁡(y-1) & =x-1 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(y-1) & =\frac{x-1}{3} \\ {2}^{{log}_{2}⁡(y-1)} & ={2}^{(x-1)/3} \\ y-1 & ={2}^{(x-1)/3} \\ y & ={2}^{(x-1)/3}+1\end{aligned}
$$

    

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
f^{-1}(x) = {2}^{(x-1)/3}+1.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110841 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110607 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c0394c3f-264a-5afa-ba91-982051eae5c0" "question-062c010f-c635-5129-83e7-3b14e937de12" "question-e999e0ab-2ba5-58ed-8052-a9586c979824"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-c0394c3f-264a-5afa-ba91-982051eae5c0" :question/id #uuid "c0394c3f-264a-5afa-ba91-982051eae5c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-19176" :question/problem "Find the exact solution to $5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)=15.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x) & =15 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2x) & =\frac{15}{5} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2x) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is $e.$ So, we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x) & =3 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)} & ={e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}=2x.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & ={e}^{3} \\ x & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e95ab9e0-e927-517c-a06b-b2eb56a8f8a5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id
