the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=2+ax+\frac{1}{4}y-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{2}+bxy+c{y}^{2}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y+4}}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y+4}} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =\frac{1}{4}, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32} \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32} \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈2+\frac{1}{4}\cdot x+\frac{1}{4}\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{32}\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-\frac{1}{32})\cdot xy+(-\frac{1}{32})\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =2+\frac{1}{4}x+\frac{1}{4}y-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{2}+(-\frac{1}{32})xy+(-\frac{1}{64}){y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=\frac{1}{4}+(-\frac{1}{32})+(-\frac{1}{64})=\frac{13}{64}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ab8b3d07-995c-53ab-94ae-6bf1bafbde24" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520545}} {:db/id 17592186520603 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284523 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f8a1f57-6edf-5d51-9b7c-2d9bbd429811" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{(1-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186281829} {:answer/id #uuid "13106fba-e2d8-590f-9a50-2b1d63582d06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\pi }{4}{(1-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186281872} {:answer/id #uuid "1abdb628-18f3-5897-af88-0cc7b944c171" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{(1-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186281934} {:answer/id #uuid "2a19cffe-821c-5512-84e1-9848e5f50a0d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(1-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186282054} {:answer/id #uuid "fcf50d5a-a34b-5ce3-bd0f-8c170f17a78a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}{(1-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186283907}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186281829} :answer-field/id #uuid "3d02b8fb-22de-53d2-a4aa-1c9d236c7ce2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284036}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "af702ba5-d262-51dd-8530-cde831134efb" :question/math-academy-id "q-164830" :question/problem "For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}) & =0, & \,{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\end{bmatrix}, & \,{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\pi }{4} \\ \frac{\pi }{4}\end{bmatrix}$ to approximate the value of $f(1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\pi }{4} \\ \frac{\pi }{4}\end{bmatrix},$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =0, & \,\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(a) & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\end{bmatrix}, & \,\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(a) & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈0+\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-\frac{\pi }{4} \\ y-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}x-\frac{\pi }{4} \\ y-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-\frac{\pi }{4} \\ y-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we obtain

Find the sum of the six missing expressions." :question/worked-solution "Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defened by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-y) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-y)\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}-9\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-y) & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-y) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-y) & -\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-y)\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈1+[\begin{aligned}0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-9 & 3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
1+0+x+x+(-9)+3=2x-5.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "92a16d7f-ef9b-52e3-b0ea-6bfb381ddffb" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520603}} {:db/id 17592186520603 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284523 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f8a1f57-6edf-5d51-9b7c-2d9bbd429811" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{(1-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186281829} {:answer/id #uuid "13106fba-e2d8-590f-9a50-2b1d63582d06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\pi }{4}{(1-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186281872} {:answer/id #uuid "1abdb628-18f3-5897-af88-0cc7b944c171" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{(1-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186281934} {:answer/id #uuid "2a19cffe-821c-5512-84e1-9848e5f50a0d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(1-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186282054} {:answer/id #uuid "fcf50d5a-a34b-5ce3-bd0f-8c170f17a78a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}{(1-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186283907}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186281829} :answer-field/id #uuid "3d02b8fb-22de-53d2-a4aa-1c9d236c7ce2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284036}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "af702ba5-d262-51dd-8530-cde831134efb" :question/math-academy-id "q-164830" :question/problem "For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$\dfrac{x+2}{x} = \dfrac{x-4}{x} + 2.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $x = 0$ is an excluded solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

Now, let's multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator. Both denominators in the equation are $x,$ so the least common denominator is $x.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation by $x$ and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+2}{x} & =\frac{x-4}{x}+2 \\ x\cdot (\frac{x+2}{x}) & =x\cdot (\frac{x-4}{x}+2) \\ x\cdot \frac{x+2}{x} & =x\cdot \frac{x-4}{x}+x\cdot 2 \\ \cancel{x}\cdot \frac{x+2}{\cancel{x}} & =\cancel{x}\cdot \frac{x-4}{\cancel{x}}+2x \\ x+2 & =x-4+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =x-4+2x \\ x+2 & =3x-4 \\ 3x-x & =2+4 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. Since $x=3$ is different from $x=0,$ we accept it as a solution.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}24x-(10x+7) & =4\cdot (6x-3) \\ 14x-7 & =24x-12 \\ 24x-14x & =-7+12 \\ 10x & =5 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

= 0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

Now, let's multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator. The equation has the denominators $x, 6x,$ and $3x,$ so the the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators is

$$
\textrm{LCM}(x, 6x, 3x) = 6x.
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation by $6x$ and simplifying, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1+x}{x}+\frac{5+x}{6x} & =\frac{1-x}{3x} \\ 6x\cdot (\frac{1+x}{x}+\frac{5+x}{6x}) & =6x\cdot \frac{1-x}{3x} \\ 6x\cdot (\frac{1+x}{x})+6x\cdot (\frac{5+x}{6x}) & =6x\cdot (\frac{1-x}{3x}) \\ 6x\cdot (\frac{1+x}{x})+6x\cdot (\frac{5+x}{6x}) & =2\cdot 3x\cdot (\frac{1-x}{3x}) \\ 6\cancel{x}\cdot (\frac{1+x}{\cancel{x}})+\cancel{6x}\cdot (\frac{5+x}{\cancel{6x}}) & =2\cdot \cancel{3x}\cdot (\frac{1-x}{\cancel{3x}}) \\ 6(1+x)+(5+x) & =2(1-x).\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6(1+x)+(5+x) & =2(1-x) \\ 6+6x+5+x & =2-2x \\ 7x+11 & =2-2x \\ 7x+2x & =2-11 \\ 9x & =-9 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

The equation has the denominators $f,\,2f,$ and $5f.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(f,2f,5f)=10f.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $10f,$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f+6}{f}-\frac{3f+9}{5f} & =\frac{f+2}{2f} \\ 10f(\frac{f+6}{f}-\frac{3f+9}{5f}) & =10f(\frac{f+2}{2f}) \\ 10f\cdot \frac{f+6}{f}-10f\cdot \frac{3f+9}{5f} & =10f\cdot \frac{f+2}{2f} \\ 10\cdot f\cdot \frac{f+6}{f}-2\cdot 5f\cdot \frac{3f+9}{5f} & =5\cdot 2f\cdot \frac{f+2}{2f} \\ 10\cdot \cancel{f}\cdot \frac{f+6}{\cancel{f}}-2\cdot \cancel{5f}\cdot \frac{3f+9}{\cancel{5f}} & =5\cdot \cancel{2f}\cdot \frac{f+2}{\cancel{2f}} \\ 10(f+6)-2(3f+9) & =5(f+2)\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $f,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}10(f+6)-2(3f+9) & =5(f+2) \\ 10f+60-6f-18 & =5f+10 \\ 4f+42 & =5f+10 \\ -f & =-32 \\ f & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $f=0$ as a solution. Now, let's multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator. The equation has the denominators $3a^2,$ $a,$ and $2a^2,$ so the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators is

$$
\textrm{LCM}(3a^2, a, 2a^2) = 6a^2.
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation by $6a^2$ and simplifying, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2a-5}{3{a}^{2}}+\frac{1}{a} & =\frac{a-1}{2{a}^{2}} \\ 6{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2a-5}{3{a}^{2}}+\frac{1}{a}) & =6{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{a-1}{2{a}^{2}}) \\ 6{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2a-5}{3{a}^{2}})+6{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{a}) & =6{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{a-1}{2{a}^{2}}) \\ 2\cdot 3{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2a-5}{3{a}^{2}})+6a\cdot a\cdot (\frac{1}{a}) & =3\cdot 2{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{a-1}{2{a}^{2}}) \\ 2\cdot \cancel{3{a}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{2a-5}{\cancel{3{a}^{2}}})+6a\cdot \cancel{a}\cdot (\frac{1}{\cancel{a}}) & =3\cdot \cancel{2{a}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{a-1}{\cancel{2{a}^{2}}}) \\ 2\cdot (2a-5)+6a\cdot (1) & =3\cdot (a-1) \\ 2(2a-5)+6a & =3(a-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $a,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2a-5)+6a & =3(a-1) \\ 4a-10+6a & =3a-3 \\ 10a-10 & =3a-3 \\ 10a-3a & =-3+10 \\ 7a & =7 \\ a & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, recall that we cannot allow $a=0$ as a solution. Since $a=1$ is different from $a=0,$ we can accept it as a solution.

Therefore, the solution is $a=1.$"} {:db/id 17592186069067 :question/id #uuid "ac7b9466-2afa-5255-82a9-e6f595901136" :question/math-academy-id "q-14744"} {:db/id 17592186069280 :question/id #uuid :tutorial/content "To solve an equation that contains multiple rational terms, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator. 

For example, consider the equation

$$
\dfrac{1}{2x^2}= \dfrac{1}{2x}-\dfrac{1}{x}.
$$

First, note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution because it would make the denominators equal zero.

Now, let's multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator. The equation has the denominators $2x^2,$ $2x,$ and $x,$ so the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators is 

$$
\textrm{LCM}(2x^2, 2x, x) = {\color{black}2x^2}.
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation by ${\color{black}2x^2}$ and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2{x}^{2}} & =2{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{2x}-\frac{1}{x}) \\ \cancel{2{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{\cancel{2{x}^{2}}} & =\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2x}-\frac{2{x}^{2}}{x} \\ 1 & =\frac{\cancel{2x}\cdot x}{\cancel{2x}}-\frac{\cancel{x}\cdot 2x}{\cancel{x}} \\ 1 & =x-2x \\ 1 & =-x \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. Since $x = -1$ is different from $x=0,$ we can accept it as the solution. 

Therefore, the solution is $x=-1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "71bfcc96-f9ce-5b5f-868d-60177e6790d8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3762 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186068969} {:db/id 17592186069845 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069977 :tutorial/content "To solve an equation that contains multiple rational terms, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator. 

For example, consider the equation

$$
\dfrac{1}{2x^2}= \dfrac{1}{2x}-\dfrac{1}{x}.
$$

First, note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution because it would make the denominators equal zero.

Now, let's multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator. The equation has the denominators $2x^2,$ $2x,$ and $x,$ so the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators is 

$$
\textrm{LCM}(2x^2, 2x, x) = {\color{black}2x^2}.
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation by ${\color{black}2x^2}$ and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2{x}^{2}} & =2{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{2x}-\frac{1}{x}) \\ \cancel{2{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{\cancel{2{x}^{2}}} & =\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2x}-\frac{2{x}^{2}}{x} \\ 1 & =\frac{\cancel{2x}\cdot x}{\cancel{2x}}-\frac{\cancel{x}\cdot 2x}{\cancel{x}} \\ 1 & =x-2x \\ 1 & =-x \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. Since $x = -1$ is different from $x=0,$ we can accept it as the solution. 

Therefore, the solution is $x=-1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "71bfcc96-f9ce-5b5f-868d-60177e6790d8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3762 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "cccb1623-1f88-5a91-a725-a9297c4a42bd" :step/math-academy-id 465010 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069846}} {:db/id 17592186069977 :tutorial/content "To solve an equation that contains multiple rational terms, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator.

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find the vector in the subspace spanned by $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}12 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}24 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{12} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{6}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}24 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}6 & 2 \\ 2 & 9\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{50}\begin{bmatrix}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186381153 :question/id #uuid "679bef56-95dc-516b-b915-5eac172b1256" :question/math-academy-id "q-158298"} {:db/id 17592186382518 :question/id #uuid "e3585dd8-8fa2-556f-ac24-bf117ff60918" :question/math-academy-id "q-83588"} {:db/id 17592186388716 :question/id #uuid "6d9b6de3-4396-5c82-b41c-2429c7a1964b" :question/math-academy-id "q-140472"} {:db/id 17592186389002 :question/id #uuid "51493b5e-5437-5dda-a56f-ba4f747b7597" :question/math-academy-id "q-158362"} {:db/id 17592186394511 :question/id #uuid "d0bf1f01-07c1-5bc9-90e8-13db8dd459d6" :question/math-academy-id "q-83563" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "44b61f5d-9f26-5dfb-88a2-5bd1553444cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186394513} {:answer/id #uuid "313cef30-0e40-5e19-a20c-d67946ddd914" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186394514} {:answer/id #uuid "fea696ab-d539-5029-98a9-afe7403faef2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186394515} {:answer/id #uuid "2bdc7bae-9c94-54c4-9dd8-3c37a0fc36ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186394516} {:answer/id #uuid "5f6ab00e-9bd5-5a22-b9a4-3b4ae167be95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186394517}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186394517} :answer-field/id #uuid "b4acddf6-0263-54d3-b64b-9a44d6523c1e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186394512}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 0 & \,\,\,-1\,\,\,\,\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 0 & \,\,\,-1\,\,\,\,\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 0 & \,\,\,-1\,\,\,\,\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 0 \\ 12\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 0 & \,\,\,-1\,\,\,\,\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & \,\,-1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & \,\,-1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

17592186049970 :topic/id #uuid "22979210-8cd9-5db4-861d-faf167d0a850" :topic/math-academy-id 2124} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134674 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135049 :tutorial/content "We've already seen how to find the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace in the case when the subspace is defined using an orthogonal basis. In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.

For example, consider the following vectors:
![](images/28/28ce7470231775d8889555d0dd9f37ee9215044762a40335bd43578b121486a3.svg)
How can we find the orthogonal projection $\mathbf{x}_S$ of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}?$ Notice that since $\mathbf a_1\cdot \mathbf a_2 \neq 0,$ the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are not orthogonal.

As usual, we would like to write $\mathbf{x}$ as 

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_S + \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp},
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \in S$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \!\in S^\perp.$

![](images/3a/3a5576fcaf9e0be6fc14978eb91dcbaceee75cbfddaa537fdb05d34b8e31e2e0.png)

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\  & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\  & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp,$ that is, $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \perp S,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{1} \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{2}\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{1} &=0 \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the expression for $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ into the system to get
![](images/f1/f1e3c7ae9e966ebcab88901c9e44a5449cb98716f43fc526d306e0af5186923b.svg)

We can write this system in an equivalent matrix form as follows:
![](images/47/472c41e1e509d2db9c41dfa95127382eeba7ab5fbaa4172d680c39335694ef2e.svg)

If we denote 
![](images/26/2650c1020d413a7c988279cc698ab4b7c4caff427615d49b35ef4e9a42651ff0.svg)
and ![](images/9b/9b50884bd0af404e71f9d7734e9bc054fc9439aba02780cf2beb5fa0a6ac1f32.svg) then we obtain

$$
A^TA\mathbf{k} = A^T\mathbf{x}
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	\mathbf{k}=(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{x}.
$$

Also, we note that  $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2$ can be expressed as $\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x}	= A\mathbf{k}.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =Ak \\  & =A({A}^{T}A)^{-1}{A}^{T}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a formula for the orthogonal projection!

Now, we return to our example. Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}6 & 8 \\ 8 & 11\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 14\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -8 \\ -8 & 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 14\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note**: Pay attention to the order in which we carried out the multiplication. If the vectors are linearly dependent, we need to find the basis of the span before applying the formula." :tutorial/id #uuid "3274de58-5861-55c3-9614-08540ad4231e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3627 :tutorial/title "The General Formula for the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace"} :step/id #uuid "c20a2e38-a98a-579e-9564-09d78a7f10c9" :step/math-academy-id 20248 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134677}} {:db/id 17592186134677 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133789 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133598 :question/id #uuid "ac8363a8-fc77-52e0-b060-5e3a45c5171a" :question/math-academy-id "e-5576"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c07721dd-4b97-5d57-8de1-5098117e3071" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049548} {:db/id 17592186050009} {:db/id 17592186050308} {:db/id 17592186050727}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134240} {:db/id 17592186134243} {:db/id 17592186275463} {:db/id 17592186326855} {:db/id 17592186351518} {:db/id 17592186354508} {:db/id 17592186365003} {:db/id 17592186365171} {:db/id 17592186381153} {:db/id 17592186382518} {:db/id 17592186388716} {:db/id 17592186389002} {:db/id 17592186394511} {:db/id 17592186394518} {:db/id 17592186394738}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane"} :step/id #uuid "184ad4b9-e662-5d0f-9c92-14f6b77fcc1f" :step/math-academy-id 20249 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134675}} {:db/id 17592186134678 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135051 :tutorial/content "As we've already seen, the orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the one-dimensional subspace $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ is given by 

$$
\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}} \, \mathbf{x} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}} \: \mathbf{a}.
$$

If we suppose that $\mathbf{a}$ denotes the column-vector ![](images/c2/c23a26d5ce1137e222e28a4bc872f9bcffda2cd6430f2d5532618ccf0ed95fa5.svg) then the dot product $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}$ is simply $\mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{a},$ and we can write the formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{(a\cdot x)}{(a\cdot a)}\,a \\  & =[\frac{({a}^{T}x)}{({a}^{T}a)}]a \\  & =a[\frac{({a}^{T}x)}{({a}^{T}a)}] \\  & =a[({a}^{T}a)^{-1}{a}^{T}x] \\  & =a\,({a}^{T}a)^{-1}{a}^{T}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's compare the above with the formula that we use when we want to project onto an arbitrary subspace:

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}
$$

 
As we can see, they are basically the same thing!" :tutorial/id #uuid "491ffb4a-98e5-59b5-8c01-3d23f872cc3f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3628 :tutorial/title "Some Intuition Behind the Formula"} :step/id #uuid "5b14c806-2358-52c9-aabe-db4086c3d1ef" :step/math-academy-id 20250}] :activity/title "Projecting Vectors Onto Subspaces in Euclidean Spaces (Arbitrary Bases)" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134003} {:db/id 17592186134674 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135049 :tutorial/content "We've already seen how to find the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace in the case when the subspace is defined using an orthogonal basis. In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.

For example, consider the following vectors:
![](images/28/28ce7470231775d8889555d0dd9f37ee9215044762a40335bd43578b121486a3.svg)
How can we find the orthogonal projection $\mathbf{x}_S$ of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}?$ Notice that since $\mathbf a_1\cdot \mathbf a_2 \neq 0,$ the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are not orthogonal.

As usual, we would like to write $\mathbf{x}$ as 

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_S + \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp},
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \in S$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \!\in S^\perp.$

![](images/3a/3a5576fcaf9e0be6fc14978eb91dcbaceee75cbfddaa537fdb05d34b8e31e2e0.png)

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\  & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\  & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp,$ that is, $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \perp S,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{1} \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{2}\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{1} &=0 \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the expression for $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ into the system to get
![](images/f1/f1e3c7ae9e966ebcab88901c9e44a5449cb98716f43fc526d306e0af5186923b.svg)

We can write this system in an equivalent matrix form as follows:
![](images/47/472c41e1e509d2db9c41dfa95127382eeba7ab5fbaa4172d680c39335694ef2e.svg)

If we denote 
![](images/26/2650c1020d413a7c988279cc698ab4b7c4caff427615d49b35ef4e9a42651ff0.svg)
and ![](images/9b/9b50884bd0af404e71f9d7734e9bc054fc9439aba02780cf2beb5fa0a6ac1f32.svg) then we obtain

$$
A^TA\mathbf{k} = A^T\mathbf{x}
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	\mathbf{k}=(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{x}.
$$

Also, we note that  $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2$ can be expressed as $\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x}	= A\mathbf{k}.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =Ak \\  & =A({A}^{T}A)^{-1}{A}^{T}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a formula for the orthogonal projection!

Now, we return to our example. Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}6 & 8 \\ 8 & 11\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 14\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -8 \\ -8 & 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 14\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note**: Pay attention to the order in which we carried out the multiplication. Carrying out the operations in the order shown above can save us a lot of work!" :tutorial/id #uuid "0a9a954f-9338-5c3f-a9db-9b39a1a60c0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3626 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f3cce71c-fd0d-5040-949b-813f3fdcbdd7" :step/math-academy-id 20246 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134676}} {:db/id 17592186135049 :tutorial/content "We've already seen how to find the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace in the case when the subspace is defined using an orthogonal basis. {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d0bf1f01-07c1-5bc9-90e8-13db8dd459d6" :question/math-academy-id "q-83563" :question/problem "Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,w=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 0 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 0 & \,\,\,-1\,\,\,\,\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 0 & \,\,\,-1\,\,\,\,\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 0 & \,\,\,-1\,\,\,\,\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 0 \\ 12\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 1 & \text{ }1\,\, \\ 0 & \,\,\,-1\,\,\,\,\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & \,\,-1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & \,\,-1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "29aa6d02-91fd-5979-90db-6f86dd498b05" :step/next {:db/id 17592186504725}} {:db/id 17592186504725 :step/content {:db/id 17592186351518 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "073d74ff-585a-5211-ab42-9064581e88f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186348509} {:answer/id #uuid "59fc5c2f-0341-50bd-bee7-ed31a5e540a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186349275} {:answer/id #uuid "7a8587e9-698e-5aac-bff3-351d87f2a068" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186349573} {:answer/id #uuid "f8595241-4221-55b2-ab69-0bdadd3f1407" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186350624} {:answer/id #uuid "fec525da-79fa-5e81-8939-908fa7601311" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186350687}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186348509} :answer-field/id #uuid "19097d36-8180-55c4-bb9a-01abbd6396f2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350750}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "be7ed026-22ac-5b61-bb76-23314f742216" :question/math-academy-id "q-83574" :question/problem "Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 14\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 12\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{12}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 12\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5d35991b-d925-5bca-a777-1935eac2dc98" :step/next {:db/id 17592186504730}} {:db/id 17592186504727 :step/content {:db/id 17592186388974 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26b1ea4a-8431-5e9b-892f-bca7c95f80b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388976} {:answer/id #uuid "a5c9edc5-9c1a-5e2a-b1fe-0d7188e07e9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388977} {:answer/id #uuid "a1d236a8-2a2f-599a-b81e-073c9d88e925" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 7 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388978} {:answer/id #uuid "e60312e7-b230-5a43-aa7d-233414826603" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 7 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388979} {:answer/id #uuid "82820516-f5de-5854-9a60-bb231ec12fc9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388980}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186388977} :answer-field/id #uuid "c310404e-e4a9-55ab-a9ab-4c596d9b583c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186388975}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7f3f0d39-46aa-5c30-a041-815de875f218" :question/math-academy-id "q-158129" :question/problem "Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -2 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -4\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & -3 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot {(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -2 \\ 10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot {\begin{bmatrix}6 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{18}\begin{bmatrix}9 & -6 \\ -6 & 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "71bec694-ee30-53a5-a601-06a5e14ae2ed"} {:db/id 17592186504730 :step/content {:db/id 17592186388960 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "466a14af-419f-527e-b9f3-45ccda2c256a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388962} {:answer/id #uuid "49467b16-c66d-5981-95f1-f41a27d0f189" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ -2 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388963} {:answer/id #uuid "33ffe7a1-67d2-5481-b344-193572a6847f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388964} {:answer/id #uuid "a2ab1c71-6000-5675-98fd-db1405a57c38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -11 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388965} {:answer/id #uuid "162444cd-a8a6-5f12-b11d-5f7dc0e0ed43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -10 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186388966}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186388964} :answer-field/id #uuid "d9b778d9-2ec0-5436-ace6-68397064b26b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186388961}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "bd91585f-60ab-5f83-868d-d63a69da0526" :question/math-academy-id "q-158122" :question/problem "Find the vector in the subspace spanned by $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the Pythagorean identity

$$
\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x= 1
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic Pythagorean identity

$$
\cosh^2x -\sinh^2x=1
$$

which we can write as

$$
1+\sinh^2x=\cosh^2x
$$

Additionally, we have

$$
\sech x = \dfrac{1}{\cosh x}
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int\frac{1}{1 + \sinh^{2} x}dx &= \int\frac{1}{\cosh^{2} x}dx \\
&= \int(\frac{1}{\cosh x})^{2}dx \\
&= \intsech^{2} xdx \\
&= \tanh x + C
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048717} {:db/id 17592186048878} {:db/id 17592186167408 :question/id #uuid "73150534-b7bb-5cf7-bc82-812c547a0e7e" :question/math-academy-id "q-95837" :knowledge-point/_questions \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the secant-tangent identity

$$
1 + \tan^2 x= \sec^2{x}
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic secant-tangent identity

$$
1-\tanh^2x=\sech^2{x}
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the integral and evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{0}^{\ln 2}\frac{\tanh x - \tanh^{3} x}{sech x}dx &= \int_{0}^{\ln 2}((1 - \tanh^{2} x)\tanh x)/(sech x)dx \\
&= \int_{0}^{\ln 2}\frac{sech^{2} x\tanh x}{sech x}dx \\
&= \int_{0}^{\ln 2}sech x\tanh xdx \\
&= \left.- sech x\right|_{0}^{\ln 2} \\
&=-sech (\ln 2) + sech 0 \\
&=-\frac{2}{e^{\ln 2} + e^{-\ln 2}} + \frac{2}{e^{0} + e^{0}} \\
&= - (2)/((2 + \frac{1}{2})) + 1 \\
&= - (2)/((\frac{5}{2})) + 1 \\
&=-\frac{4}{5} + 1 \\
&= \frac{1}{5}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167410 :question/id #uuid "56c8df0d-1de4-5ce0-8410-0a86f9263d39" :question/math-academy-id "q-95839"} {:db/id 17592186167411 :question/id #uuid "0b743b6c-82de-526e-bf7a-2e5e628e262a" :question/math-academy-id "q-95840"} {:db/id 17592186166797 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166635 :question/id #uuid "7af9f5f6-1e14-55ea-8a09-25d211cb40d8" :question/math-academy-id "e-8435"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a5f377f3-700a-57a9-96e5-954aed678e62" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167412 :question/id #uuid "1dc61873-d9b3-5c3b-88b3-295cdcb5e13e" :question/math-academy-id "q-95842"} {:db/id 17592186167413 :question/id #uuid "65cce72e-e753-5997-9c02-b796ef4d2df3" :question/math-academy-id "q-95843"}] :knowledge-point/title "Integrating a Function Using the Hyperbolic Cosecant-Cotangent Identity"} {:db/id 17592186166635 :question/id #uuid "7af9f5f6-1e14-55ea-8a09-25d211cb40d8" :question/math-academy-id "e-8435" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186166797 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a5f377f3-700a-57a9-96e5-954aed678e62" :knowledge-point/title "Integrating a Function Using the Hyperbolic Cosecant-Cotangent Identity"}] :question/problem "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\ln 5} \dfrac{\csch{x}}{\coth^2x - 1} \, \textrm{d}x$." :question/worked-solution "$$
\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the cosecant-cotangent identity

$$
1 + \cot^2 x= \csc^2{x}
$$

Using Osbourn's rule, we get the hyperbolic cosecant-cotangent identity

$$
\coth^2x - 1=\csch^2{x}
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the integral and evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} \int_{0}^{\ln 5} \dfrac{\csch{x}}{\coth^2x - 1} \, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{0}^{\ln 5} \dfrac{\csch{x}}{\csch^2x} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\ln 5} \dfrac{1}{\csch{x}} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\ln 5} \sinh{x} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left.\cosh{x} \, \Big\right|_{0}^{\ln 5} \\[5pt] &= \cosh(\ln{5}) - \cosh{0} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{\ln{5}}+e^{-\ln{5}}}{2} - \dfrac{e^0+e^0}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left(5+\dfrac 1 5\right)}{2} - \dfrac{1+1}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{13}{5} - 1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8}{5} \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167412 :question/id #uuid "1dc61873-d9b3-5c3b-88b3-295cdcb5e13e" :question/math-academy-id "q-95842"} {:db/id 17592186167413 :question/id #uuid "65cce72e-e753-5997-9c02-b796ef4d2df3" :question/math-academy-id "q-95843"} {:db/id 17592186166798 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166636 :question/id #uuid "14733493-2ad9-5fc2-9afe-26384f6ce9ed" :question/math-academy-id "e-8436"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a95e37c6-66f4-5a70-87e8-31f3694a20a4" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167414 :question/id #uuid "9e79c8a7-9968-551a-a93c-f88a6b928eaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-95844"} {:db/id 17592186167415 :question/id #uuid "a912deae-3900-593b-9411-e0dd5aafca72" :question/math-academy-id "q-95845"} {:db/id 17592186527994 :question/id #uuid "cef928b3-a5b9-5b14-83bc-17bf537996f2" :question/math-academy-id "q-96454"}] :knowledge-point/title "Integrating Hyperbolic Functions With Linear Arguments"} {:db/id 17592186166636 :question/id #uuid "14733493-2ad9-5fc2-9afe-26384f6ce9ed" :question/math-academy-id "e-8436" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186166798 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a95e37c6-66f4-5a70-87e8-31f3694a20a4" :knowledge-point/title "Integrating Hyperbolic Functions With Linear Arguments"}] :question/problem "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$Calculate $\displaystyle{\displaystyle \int \dfrac{2}{\cosh^2(2x+1)-1} \, \textrm{d}x}$." :question/worked-solution "$$
\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the Pythagorean identity

$$
\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = 1
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the hyperbolic Pythagorean identity

$$
\cosh^2 \theta - \sinh^2 \theta = 1
$$

Setting

$$
\theta = 2x + 1
$$

we get

$$
\cosh^2 (2x+1) - \sinh^2(2x+1) = 1
$$

which can be written as

$$
\cosh^2 (2x+1) -1 = \sinh^2(2x+1)
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int(2)/(\cosh^{2} (2x + 1) - 1)dx &= 2\int(1)/(\sinh^{2} (2x + 1))dx \\
&= 2\intcsch^{2} (2x + 1)dx \\
&=-\coth (2x + 1) + C
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167414 :question/id #uuid "9e79c8a7-9968-551a-a93c-f88a6b928eaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-95844"} {:db/id 17592186167415 :question/id #uuid "35e1d4ff-896a-599d-bb79-ecb5cec36df6" :step/math-academy-id 31417} {:db/id 17592186167733 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168118 :tutorial/content "We can compute integrals containing hyperbolic functions using the hyperbolic counterparts of the Pythagorean identity. We use Osborn's rule to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity.

Osborn's rule states that to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity, we

- replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function, and
- for any product of two trigonometric sines, change the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

$$
\displaystyle \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

For example, suppose we want to calculate the following integral:

$$
\int \cosh^2{x} - \sinh^2{x} \: \textrm{d}x
$$

First, we recall the Pythagorean identity

$$
\cos^2{x} + \sin^2{x} = 1
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the corresponding hyperbolic identity

$$
\cosh^2{x} - \sinh^2{x} = 1
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our integral as follows:

$$
\int\cosh^{2} x - \sinh^{2} x_(⏟)_(1)dx = \int1dx = x + C
$$

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "250a3423-70a4-5d38-9b0f-6f801a0479d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5553 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1283c2a5-d791-5099-bd72-546a74c8f4b8" :step/math-academy-id 34427 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167630}} {:db/id 17592186167734 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168119 :tutorial/content "$$

$$

We can use Osborn's rule to write down the hyperbolic equivalents of the sectant-tangent and cotangent-cosecant identities.

From the secant-tangent identity

$$
1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x
$$

we have the equivalent hyperbolic identity

$$
1 - \tanh^2 x = \sech^2 x
$$

Similarly, from the cotangent-cosecant identity

$$
1+\cot^2 x = \csc^2 x
$$

we have the equivalent hyperbolic identity

$$
1-\coth^2 x = -\csch^2 x
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\coth^2 x - 1 = \csch^2 x
$$

These identities can be used to solve certain integrals involving the expressions $\tanh^2{x}$, $\coth^2 x$, $\sech^2 x$, or $\csch^2{x}$." :tutorial/id #uuid "525b90c4-f6ea-5c55-8602-49547e261df1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5554 :tutorial/title "Calculating Integrals Using Related Hyperbolic Identities"} :step/id #uuid "ec6b416a-7645-5f7b-b41d-c553c9f1a62b" :step/math-academy-id 34428 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167631}}] :activity/title "Integration Using the Hyperbolic Pythagorean Identities" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186167027} {:db/id 17592186167733 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168118 :tutorial/content "We can compute integrals containing hyperbolic functions using the hyperbolic counterparts of the Pythagorean identity. "Integrating Hyperbolic Functions With Linear Arguments"} :step/id #uuid "35e1d4ff-896a-599d-bb79-ecb5cec36df6" :step/math-academy-id 31417} {:db/id 17592186168118 :tutorial/content "We can compute integrals containing hyperbolic functions using the hyperbolic counterparts of the Pythagorean identity. We use Osborn's rule to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity.

Osborn's rule states that to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity, we

- replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function, and
- for any product of two trigonometric sines, change the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

$$
\displaystyle \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

For example, suppose we want to calculate the following integral:

$$
\int \cosh^2{x} - \sinh^2{x} \: \textrm{d}x
$$

First, we recall the Pythagorean identity

$$
\cos^2{x} + \sin^2{x} = 1
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the corresponding hyperbolic identity

$$
\cosh^2{x} - \sinh^2{x} = 1
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our integral as follows:

$$
\int\cosh^{2} x - \sinh^{2} x_(⏟)_(1)dx = \int1dx = x + C
$$

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "250a3423-70a4-5d38-9b0f-6f801a0479d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5553 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186168119 :tutorial/content "$$
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

We can use Osborn's rule to write down the hyperbolic equivalents of the sectant-tangent and cotangent-cosecant identities.

From the secant-tangent identity

$$
1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x
$$

we have the equivalent hyperbolic identity

$$
1 - \tanh^2 x = \sech^2 x
$$

Similarly, from the cotangent-cosecant identity

$$
1+\cot^2 x = \csc^2 x
$$

we have the equivalent hyperbolic identity

$$
1-\coth^2 x = -\csch^2 x
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
\coth^2 x - 1 = \csch^2 x
$$

These identities can be used to solve certain integrals involving the expressions $\tanh^2{x}$, $\coth^2 x$, $\sech^2 x$, or $\csch^2{x}$." :tutorial/id #uuid "525b90c4-f6ea-5c55-8602-49547e261df1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5554 :tutorial/title "Calculating Integrals Using Related Hyperbolic Identities"} {:course/id #uuid "4965f9cc-fd21-5d50-b441-6e80983b17dd" :course/math-academy-id 106 :db/id 17592186046645} {:db/id 17592186050910 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186429391 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. If ![](images/88/888a6e0af4cb0ad21e91c823ce01e3b7b44005650d8abb33b7e7cd15f5c8b1d0.svg) and ![](images/15/155d90bc4b1df2a185aed86db995a16762338cda30417ecb5a459b131e171dd8.svg), find

I. $\Vert \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \Vert.$

II. $\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{y}).$" :question/worked-solution "Since $\mathbf{Q}$ is orthogonal, we have that $\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y}$ for any vectors $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}.$

The linear transformation $\mathbf{Q}$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $\mathbf{Q}$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is orthogonal.

- $|| \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) || = || \mathbf{x} ||.$

- If $\mathbf{x} \perp \mathbf{y}$ then $\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \perp \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{y})$ for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$ In general, $\mathbf{Q}$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $\mathbf{Q}$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

In this case, since $\mathbf{Q}$ is orthogonal, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q(x)‖ & =‖x‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y}.$ As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x)\cdot Q(y) & =x\cdot y \\  & =(-1)\cdot 3+(-2)\cdot 0+2\cdot 5 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048849} {:db/id 17592186049045} {:db/id 17592186049606} {:db/id 17592186198978 :question/id #uuid "5b4e4425-10cb-5811-9da8-6b08b3f0fd92" :question/math-academy-id "q-40489" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198448 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "455b3713-34a3-535d-8baf-d279a0341e9f" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Angle Preserving Property of Orthogonal Linear Transformations"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c5739013-0ec3-5054-9df2-0416169aee06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186197739} {:answer/id #uuid "cb80e9c9-9a83-5c04-a3ab-b7735d5f125a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186197740} {:answer/id #uuid "cc77a078-56f6-5c64-a1d0-37853dbff1ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186197741} {:answer/id #uuid "e099e132-6017-54bd-af9b-dabda71bcfb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186197742} {:answer/id #uuid "2c36f56b-9a3f-5112-a631-00ca6bd5658b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186197743}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "e099e132-6017-54bd-af9b-dabda71bcfb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186197742} :answer-field/id #uuid "ec57d5bb-fbdf-5711-9938-796ddd4e592a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186197738}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Find $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)$, where $x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $y=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

In this case, since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have

"![](images/20/20b1f07891dd26e4839258d3c2232368b3aebbf527a2b0f31bcdde2369fc66d4.svg)

Consider the vectors above, and let $\mathbf{Q}$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0$

II. $\{\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{u}_1),\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{u}_2)\}$ is orthogonal

III. $\{\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{u}_1),\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{u}_2)\}$ is orthonormal" :question/worked-solution "Since $\mathbf{Q}$ is orthogonal, we have that $\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y}$ for any vectors $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}.$

The linear transformation $\mathbf{Q}$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $\mathbf{Q}$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is orthogonal.

- $|| \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) || = || \mathbf{x} ||.$

- If $\mathbf{x} \perp \mathbf{y}$ then $\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \perp \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{y})$ for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$ In general, $\mathbf{Q}$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $\mathbf{Q}$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

$$

$$

$$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following are orthogonal sets?
- **U.** $U={Q(\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$
- **W.** $W={Q(\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix})}$
- **V.** $V={Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

Let's denote the elements of $U,W,$ and $V$ respectively as 

$\,$ ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})},\,$ ${Q({w}_{1}),Q({w}_{2})},\,$ and $\,{Q({v}_{1}),Q({v}_{2}),Q({v}_{3})}.$ 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- $Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2})=0,\,Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0,\,Q({v}_{2})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2}) & ={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}=18-18=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthogonal.

- For the set $W,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2}) & ={w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=1-1=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $W$ is orthogonal.

- For the Set $V,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2}) & ={v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=2+12-5=9\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthogonal set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$U$ and $W$ only"."} {:db/id 17592186411865 :question/id #uuid "8d807e12-6960-57f6-b74d-aa3fe66f0f76" :question/math-academy-id "q-178271"} {:db/id 17592186415156 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
{u}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -6\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$
- **II.** ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthogonal
- **III.** ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=12-12=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that, for example, $Q({u}_{1})$ is not a unit vector since

$$
‖Q({u}_{1})‖=‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-6)^{2}}\ne 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} {:db/id 17592186446168 :question/id #uuid "ac6fbe63-89e3-55f0-b383-00653c46559a" :question/math-academy-id "q-178025" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "85bffa49-25ed-5277-8eb0-2bf0d83a3acf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186446158} {:answer/id #uuid "acfdb839-bbb9-5d75-a684-8e0ba2f1180c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "None of the statements are true." :db/id 17592186446161} {:answer/id #uuid "e4112fbf-91d8-5bb1-acad-1777ebe798bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186446162} {:answer/id #uuid "eb713c79-d5f4-5d03-8da7-db12deacf3d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186446164} {:answer/id #uuid "f04b535e-e446-5693-b598-2a2ae8017998" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186446165}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186446162} :answer-field/id #uuid "5243b6a3-407c-5377-9662-ad587ee4e1e3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186446167}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
{u}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$

II. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthogonal

III. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthonormal" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{5}=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, both $Q({u}_{1})$ and $Q({u}_{2})$ are unit vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q({u}_{1})‖ & =‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}+(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}}=1 \\ ‖Q({u}_{2})‖ & =‖{u}_{2}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}+(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} {:db/id 17592186485518 :question/id #uuid "3a3b6415-46fa-5ac6-8f1e-cce0985c5f71" :question/math-academy-id "q-40515" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198449 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b4a5d6b1-e76a-5b33-8973-04d1d9062dc6" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Orthogonality of a Two-Vector Set"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c21b706-ee61-5347-b1e9-163e20da045d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$V$ only" :db/id 17592186484840} {:answer/id #uuid "511d2e30-3a63-5d27-8065-e177abbd52b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$V$ and $W$ only" :db/id 17592186484993} {:answer/id #uuid "64b5d7dc-d5a7-536d-952d-7f23ec21eaea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$W$ only" :db/id 17592186485035} {:answer/id #uuid "a8a7e5ba-e12b-5de2-9808-9ac0af0c0ae8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$U$ only" :db/id 17592186485183} {:answer/id #uuid "dcfa56ff-89e4-5c4c-b084-fe9d0a2df44d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$U$ and $W$ only" :db/id 17592186485281}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "64b5d7dc-d5a7-536d-952d-7f23ec21eaea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$W$ only" :db/id 17592186485035} :answer-field/id #uuid "3a79a8e6-4bbb-52fc-b050-7b31066c3423" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186485393}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following are orthogonal sets?

I. $U=\{Q(\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix})\}$

II. $V=\{Q(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2 \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 6\end{bmatrix})\}$

III. $W=\{Q(\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -5\end{bmatrix})\}$" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

Let's denote the elements of $U,W,$ and $V$ respectively as 

$\,$ $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\},\,$ $\{Q({v}_{1}),Q({v}_{2}),Q({v}_{3})\},\,$ and $\,\{Q({w}_{1}),Q({w}_{2})\}.$

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- $Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2})=0,\,Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0,\,Q({v}_{2})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0.$

- $Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2}) & ={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=20-3=17\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $U$ is not and orthogonal set.

- For the Set $V,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2}) & ={v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2 \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}=3-4+1=0,\,✓ \\ Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{3}) & ={v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}=2+8+18=28\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthogonal set.

- For the set $W,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2}) & ={w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}=-15+15=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $W$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$W$ only"."} {:db/id 17592186485595 :question/id #uuid "fd59782d-c853-5fe4-812d-f8b2814488a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-140567" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198449 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b4a5d6b1-e76a-5b33-8973-04d1d9062dc6" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Orthogonality of a Two-Vector Set"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8ec03f18-13be-55eb-92af-32d5b84aa90d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$U$ and $W$ only" :db/id 17592186485126} {:answer/id #uuid "9902057c-da91-5c74-b86e-dd54d2418d30" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$V$ and $W$ only" :db/id 17592186485146} {:answer/id #uuid "ae328ea7-ac34-5c69-a500-80ec39d884b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$U,V,$ and $W$" :db/id 17592186485193} {:answer/id #uuid "b8fa2677-4376-5029-b220-a56e49c627ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$W$ only" :db/id 17592186485216} {:answer/id #uuid "e17db08c-8042-5528-9797-e2d47b07097c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$V$ only" :db/id 17592186485294}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "b8fa2677-4376-5029-b220-a56e49c627ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$W$ only" :db/id 17592186485216} :answer-field/id #uuid "bbd54c08-5bbd-5945-9a88-65da2698583c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186485448}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. transformation** if for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we have that

$$
\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y}.
$$

In this case, we say that $\mathbf{Q}$ *preserves the dot product*.

The linear transformation $\mathbf{Q}$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $\mathbf{Q}$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is orthogonal.

- $\| \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \| = \| \mathbf{x} \|$. In other words, $\mathbf{Q}$ preserves vector norms.

- If $\mathbf{x} \perp \mathbf{y}$ then $\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \perp \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{y})$ for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$ In general, $\mathbf{Q}$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $\mathbf{Q}$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set." :tutorial/id #uuid "fed8f501-fcb5-5852-bf23-1e999e4c9e1e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8098 :tutorial/title
