Find $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)$, where $x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}$ and $y=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

In this case, since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x)\cdot Q(y) & =x\cdot y \\  & =1\cdot (-3)+3\cdot 4+(-2)\cdot 1 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0bda9774-6623-5015-9c4f-2876bc204742" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406658}} {:db/id 17592186406658 :step/content {:db/id 17592186406655 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "047c19ef-c76a-57b3-b13e-81cac8438947" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186473112} {:answer/id #uuid "0f411e21-0bfc-5e60-be10-aa9385c60d56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186473113}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186473113} :answer-field/id #uuid "41b5e6b2-6fa4-5699-91d3-98491ea01274" :answer-field/key "U" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186473951} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3b5e99f8-6d7b-5605-8eeb-768c689a1a11" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186473114} {:answer/id #uuid "d3e8b7c2-03e8-52a8-8c30-1f1597b0a406" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186473115}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186473114} :answer-field/id #uuid "2909a2f7-876c-5e10-a289-6837f83679fc" :answer-field/key "V" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186473952} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "829a1b56-ccd5-5381-aeca-6ba71098f21a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186473116} {:answer/id #uuid "adcc7d05-7e81-525a-b650-a03adf317913" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186473117}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186473117} :answer-field/id #uuid "51b28bdf-55b7-5470-b1f6-bd8182431d5f" :answer-field/key "W" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186473953}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9892c6c7-24de-57f2-a3e8-0b32de0c1349" :question/math-academy-id "q-40491" :question/problem "Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following are orthogonal sets?
- **U.** $U={Q(\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$
- **W.** $W={Q(\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix})}$
- **V.** $V={Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

Let's denote the elements of $U,W,$ and $V$ respectively as 

$\,$ ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})},\,$ ${Q({w}_{1}),Q({w}_{2})},\,$ and $\,{Q({v}_{1}),Q({v}_{2}),Q({v}_{3})}.$ 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- $Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2})=0,\,Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0,\,Q({v}_{2})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2}) & ={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}=18-18=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthogonal.

- For the set $W,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2}) & ={w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=1-1=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $W$ is orthogonal.

- For the Set $V,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2}) & ={v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=2+12-5=9\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9892c6c7-24de-57f2-a3e8-0b32de0c1349" :question/math-academy-id "q-40491" :question/problem "Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. - **U.** $U={Q(\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$
- **W.** $W={Q(\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix})}$
- **V.** $V={Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

Let's denote the elements of $U,W,$ and $V$ respectively as 

$\,$ ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})},\,$ ${Q({w}_{1}),Q({w}_{2})},\,$ and $\,{Q({v}_{1}),Q({v}_{2}),Q({v}_{3})}.$ 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- $Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2})=0,\,Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0,\,Q({v}_{2})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2}) & ={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}=18-18=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthogonal.

- For the set $W,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2}) & ={w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=1-1=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $W$ is orthogonal.

- For the Set $V,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2}) & ={v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=2+12-5=9\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthogonal set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$U$ and $W$ only"."} :step/id #uuid "5c0620be-2d88-50a9-b295-5b90712b0a8b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406659}} {:db/id 17592186406659 :step/content {:db/id 17592186406654 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24e42699-a0f0-5e81-a194-c91514b7e8ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186406638} {:answer/id #uuid "46c27bd0-b639-51d1-a04d-8098da45991e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186406642} {:answer/id #uuid "b3565871-fc75-5a3f-bb6e-506cbb0458f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186406644} {:answer/id #uuid "bfd57b0f-3965-5b70-833f-7fa36e06ae4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186406646} {:answer/id #uuid "e14e0ad1-a7b2-5023-b79c-bff39fbd35df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186406649}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406644} :answer-field/id #uuid "491c6e1c-81dd-5170-b618-833ce2679d93" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186406651}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8a69da2c-f673-5e64-a265-9fe904a3c9ad" :question/math-academy-id "q-40514" :question/problem "Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. - $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

$$

$$

$$

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{5}=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, both $Q({u}_{1})$ and $Q({u}_{2})$ are unit vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q({u}_{1})‖ & =‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}+(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}}=1 \\ ‖Q({u}_{2})‖ & =‖{u}_{2}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}+(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q({u}_{1})‖ & =‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{4}{5})^{2}+(\frac{3}{5})^{2}}=1 \\ ‖Q({u}_{2})‖ & =‖{u}_{2}‖=\sqrt{(-\frac{3}{5})^{2}+(\frac{4}{5})^{2}}=1\end{aligned}

"$$
{u}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

II. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthogonal

III. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthonormal" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=2+2\ne 0.
$$

- Statement II is false. Notice that, $Q({u}_{1})⊥̸Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}\ne 0.
$$

- Statement III is false since the set is not even orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} :step/id #uuid "eef50253-8c08-55c7-bab7-bc37bdee6bfe" :step/next {:db/id 17592186526149}} {:db/id 17592186526149 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284764 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e1f6862c-27fd-5c39-8eb2-3cbbffed6df8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465669} {:answer/id #uuid "786a7ab2-a3ec-5b80-8a00-e9e1753b87d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465670}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465669} :answer-field/id #uuid "55fa8074-b199-52f0-b9ec-a64e6d2e74dd" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466678} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "14cbd69a-f982-5d8b-a7b5-faa1d54ef043" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465671} {:answer/id #uuid "a3dbd501-b3c0-564f-92ea-a9a572fb9e89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465672}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465671} :answer-field/id #uuid "77082866-697e-5473-bb08-593811756def" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466679} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "270b69ea-ae43-51a2-bc71-ac5760e7b855" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465673} {:answer/id #uuid "f89e42f6-9f2a-5d60-9603-c8642f276749" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465674}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465673} :answer-field/id #uuid "07d18537-0a6d-59ae-9629-b8bdfac0f081" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466680}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e16f6fa7-ae80-51bb-bdf3-1add916dcb13" :question/math-academy-id "q-178269" :question/problem "$$

:topic/math-academy-id 3946} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186193748 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193806 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ be an $n \times m$ observation matrix with standardized data, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature.

Suppose we have the following **singular value decomposition** (SVD) of $X{:}$ 

$$
X = U \Sigma V^T
$$

Note that in the SVD, the columns of $U$ are orthonormal, which implies that $U^T U = I$ (the identity matrix). 

Using this decomposition, the sample covariance matrix of $X$ can be derived as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}(V{Σ}^{T}{U}^{T})(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =\frac{1}{n-1}V{Σ}^{T}{{({U}^{T}U)}_{⏟}}_{I}Σ{V}^{T} \\  & =V(\frac{1}{n-1}{Σ}^{T}Σ){V}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression $\dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma$ represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix $C.$ 

Now, notice the following:

- The matrix $\dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma$ is a diagonal $m \times m$ matrix with the eigenvalues of $C$ (in descending order) on the main diagonal.

- The matrix $V$ is an $m \times m$ matrix whose columns are the unit eigenvectors of $C.$

To summarize, if we write down the singular value decomposition of the standardized observation matrix $X,$ the columns of the matrix $V$ in the SVD are the **principal components** of the data." :tutorial/id #uuid "fec0f21a-271c-5558-9427-a50d62b4e629" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14786 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4fcc5fda-8a47-5812-b960-71863e23d4e9" :step/math-academy-id 610887 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193749}} {:db/id 17592186193749 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192832 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192612 :question/id #uuid "b0a1a305-4617-50f6-a0d9-2b573277f68f" :question/math-academy-id "e-21883"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a5228a68-1e0a-5761-ac90-40fcab271214" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048143} {:db/id 17592186049975}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186193314} {:db/id 17592186193315} {:db/id 17592186526003} {:db/id 17592186526041} {:db/id 17592186526056} {:db/id 17592186526064}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Principal Component from SVD"} :step/id #uuid "15ca33ca-5d01-5308-bba1-0c17a2514826" :step/math-academy-id 610888 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193750}} {:db/id 17592186193750 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193807 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a sample of $n$ observations, where each observation has $m$ features. We store this data in the $n \times m$ observation matrix $X,$ where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature.

![](images/fe/fe9bd930e502d38eccc99f9c9a7a4b994bfa6caed26dd0b2a2675128ef18252a.svg)

We assume the data has been mean-centered. Let $\mathbf{x}_j$ denote the $j$th column of $X.$ The sample covariance matrix, $C_X,$ is given by

![](images/12/126db3a0c2d3fde367318bab5f59bccae7dd2cab8342435e7faf7de24e690997.svg)

The **total variance** of the observed data equals the sum of the entries on the leading diagonal of $C_X$ (the trace of the matrix). That is,

$$
\textrm{Total Variance}  = \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_1] + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_2] + \cdots + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_m].
$$

How is the total variance related to the singular values of $X?$

We recall that using the singular value decomposition $X = U \Sigma V^T,$ the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_m$ of $C_X$ are related to the singular values $\sigma_1,\ldots, \sigma_m$ of $X$ by:

$$
\lambda_i = \dfrac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1} \quad \text{for } i=1,\ldots,m.
$$

 

Next, we will use this relationship to compute the total variance." :tutorial/id #uuid "b4ae7cae-c19f-5ca8-9b4f-42f746d53a9c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14787 :tutorial/title "Total Variance of the Observation Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "9f54348f-13f4-5af1-8c13-0e7909839edf" :step/math-academy-id 610891 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193753}} {:db/id 17592186193751 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193808 :tutorial/content "A nutritionist measured $3$ features among a group of clients:

- body mass index ($x_1$)

- height ($x_2$)

- weight ($x_3$)

The collected data was stored in the mean-centered observation matrix $X,$ where each row contains measurements for a particular client. The nutritionist finds that the singular values of $X$ are 

$$
\sigma_1=12, \qquad \sigma_2=5, \qquad \sigma_3=4.
$$

The nutritionist then decides to reduce the dimensionality of the data set. To do this, they convert the original observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ using the equation 

$$
Y = X V_1,
$$

where $V_1$ is the $3 \times 1$ matrix containing the first principal component of the data only. As a result, $Y$ is an $n \times 1$ matrix that gives a single feature associated with each client.

What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix $Y$ compared to the initial observation matrix $X?$

The total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(12)^{2}+(5)^{2}+(4)^{2} \\  & =185.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the nutritionist used only the first principal component, the preserved variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Preserved} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{1}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(12)^{2} \\  & =144.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{Preserved}}{\text{Total}} & =\frac{144}{185} \\  & ≈0.778 \\  & =77.8%.\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize:

- The nutritionist reduced the dimensionality of the data from $3$ (initially, each client had three features) to just $1$ (only one feature characterizes each client after the transformation).

- In doing so, $77.8\%$ of the variance is preserved in the transformed data." :tutorial/id #uuid "bde3e2b4-d644-5955-bbda-5e4e79c40df2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14788 :tutorial/title "Computing the Remaining Variance After Dimensionality Reduction"} :step/id #uuid "c2cc97eb-c337-5109-9c6d-41adae21e68d" :step/math-academy-id 610892 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193752}} {:db/id 17592186193752 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192833 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192613 :question/id #uuid "ad59f3c2-8ca8-5d05-b626-501682800f01" :question/math-academy-id "e-21884"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9dbfeaac-fc49-543d-b2b0-673b7dbb05d7" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186193316} {:db/id 17592186193317} {:db/id 17592186525991} {:db/id 17592186526020} {:db/id 17592186526045} {:db/id 17592186526092}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Variance from SVD"} :step/id #uuid "eca9251a-22f4-5c77-b3b2-ef3bbb2d347c" :step/math-academy-id 610893} {:db/id 17592186193753 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193809 :tutorial/content "To find the total variance in terms of singular values, define the change of variables $Y = XV.$ The covariance of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{Y}=\frac{1}{n-1}{Y}^{T}Y=\frac{1}{n-1}(XV)^{T}(XV)={V}^{T}{{(\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X)}_{⏟}}_{{C}_{X}}V.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $V$ contains the eigenvectors of $C_X,$ the matrix $C_Y$ is diagonal and contains the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of $C_X{:}$

![](images/c3/c344eb83c1e16eba7fbb71c00ce28dc72875826b5c487a33cd2235499c94d4f3.svg)

The total variance is defined as the trace (sum of diagonal elements) of the covariance matrix. A key property of the trace is that it is invariant under orthogonal transformations like $Y=XV.$ Therefore, the total variance of $Y$ is the same as the total variance of $X{:}$

$$
\textrm{Total Variance} = \text{Tr}(C_X) = \text{Tr}(C_Y) = \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i.
$$

Substituting $\lambda_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1},$ we conclude that the total variance is *proportional to* the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\textrm{Total Variance} \:\propto\: \sum_{i=1}^m \sigma^2_i.}
$$

![](images/fe/fe9bd930e502d38eccc99f9c9a7a4b994bfa6caed26dd0b2a2675128ef18252a.svg)

We assume the data has been mean-centered. Let $\mathbf{x}_j$ denote the $j$th column of $X.$ The sample covariance matrix, $C_X,$ is given by

![](images/12/126db3a0c2d3fde367318bab5f59bccae7dd2cab8342435e7faf7de24e690997.svg)

The **total variance** of the observed data equals the sum of the entries on the leading diagonal of $C_X$ (the trace of the matrix). That is,

$$
\textrm{Total Variance}  = \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_1] + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_2] + \cdots + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_m].
$$

How is the total variance related to the singular values of $X?$

We recall that using the singular value decomposition $X = U \Sigma V^T,$ the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_m$ of $C_X$ are related to the singular values $\sigma_1,\ldots, \sigma_m$ of $X$ by:

$$
\lambda_i = \dfrac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1} \quad \text{for } i=1,\ldots,m.
$$

 

Next, we will use this relationship to compute the total variance." :tutorial/id #uuid "b4ae7cae-c19f-5ca8-9b4f-42f746d53a9c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14787 :tutorial/title "Total Variance of the Observation Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "9f54348f-13f4-5af1-8c13-0e7909839edf" :step/math-academy-id 610891 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193753}} {:db/id 17592186193807 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a sample of $n$ observations, where each observation has $m$ features. We store this data in the $n \times m$ observation matrix $X,$ where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature.

![](images/fe/fe9bd930e502d38eccc99f9c9a7a4b994bfa6caed26dd0b2a2675128ef18252a.svg)

We assume the data has been mean-centered. Let $\mathbf{x}_j$ denote the $j$th column of $X.$ The sample covariance matrix, $C_X,$ is given by

![](images/12/126db3a0c2d3fde367318bab5f59bccae7dd2cab8342435e7faf7de24e690997.svg)

The **total variance** of the observed data equals the sum of the entries on the leading diagonal of $C_X$ (the trace of the matrix). That is,

$$
\textrm{Total Variance}  = \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_1] + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_2] + \cdots + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_m].
$$

How is the total variance related to the singular values of $X?$

We recall that using the singular value decomposition $X = U \Sigma V^T,$ the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_m$ of $C_X$ are related to the singular values $\sigma_1,\ldots, \sigma_m$ of $X$ by:

$$
\lambda_i = \dfrac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1} \quad \text{for } i=1,\ldots,m.
$$

 

Next, we will use this relationship to compute the total variance." :tutorial/id #uuid "b4ae7cae-c19f-5ca8-9b4f-42f746d53a9c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14787 :tutorial/title "Total Variance of the Observation Matrix"} {:db/id 17592186193753 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193809 :tutorial/content "To find the total variance in terms of singular values, define the change of variables $Y = XV.$ The covariance of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{Y}=\frac{1}{n-1}{Y}^{T}Y=\frac{1}{n-1}(XV)^{T}(XV)={V}^{T}{{(\frac{1}{n-1}{X}^{T}X)}_{⏟}}_{{C}_{X}}V.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $V$ contains the eigenvectors of $C_X,$ the matrix $C_Y$ is diagonal and contains the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of $C_X{:}$

![](images/c3/c344eb83c1e16eba7fbb71c00ce28dc72875826b5c487a33cd2235499c94d4f3.svg)

The total variance is defined as the trace (sum of diagonal elements) of the covariance matrix. A key property of the trace is that it is invariant under orthogonal transformations like $Y=XV.$ Therefore, the total variance of $Y$ is the same as the total variance of $X{:}$

$$
\textrm{Total Variance} = \text{Tr}(C_X) = \text{Tr}(C_Y) = \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i.
$$

Substituting $\lambda_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1},$ we conclude that the total variance is *proportional to* the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\textrm{Total Variance} \:\propto\: \sum_{i=1}^m \sigma^2_i.}
$$

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "9ab13b86-9d0f-53e4-b7b1-bee88604c031" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14956 :tutorial/title "Finding the Total Variance"} :step/id #uuid "aecacf05-e50b-52b9-85aa-b28cf5b31b8c" :step/math-academy-id 611564 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193751}} {:db/id 17592186193751 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193808 :tutorial/content "A nutritionist measured $3$ features among a group of clients:

- body mass index ($x_1$)

- height ($x_2$)

- weight ($x_3$)

The collected data was stored in the mean-centered observation matrix $X,$ where each row contains measurements for a particular client. The nutritionist finds that the singular values of $X$ are 

$$
\sigma_1=12, \qquad \sigma_2=5, \qquad \sigma_3=4.
$$

The nutritionist then decides to reduce the dimensionality of the data set. To do this, they convert the original observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ using the equation 

$$
Y = X V_1,
$$

where $V_1$ is the $3 \times 1$ matrix containing the first principal component of the data only. As a result, $Y$ is an $n \times 1$ matrix that gives a single feature associated with each client.

What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix $Y$ compared to the initial observation matrix $X?$

The total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(12)^{2}+(5)^{2}+(4)^{2} \\  & =185.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the nutritionist used only the first principal component, the preserved variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Preserved} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{1}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(12)^{2} \\  & =144.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{Preserved}}{\text{Total}} & =\frac{144}{185} \\  & ≈0.778 \\  & =77.8%.\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize:

- The nutritionist reduced the dimensionality of the data from $3$ (initially, each client had three features) to just $1$ (only one feature characterizes each client after the transformation).

- In doing so, $77.8\%$ of the variance is preserved in the transformed data." :tutorial/id #uuid "bde3e2b4-d644-5955-bbda-5e4e79c40df2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14788 :tutorial/title "Computing the Remaining Variance After Dimensionality Reduction"} :step/id #uuid "c2cc97eb-c337-5109-9c6d-41adae21e68d" :step/math-academy-id 610892 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193752}} {:db/id 17592186193808 :tutorial/content "A nutritionist measured $3$ features among a group of clients:

We can express Green's theorem in flux form as a single picture, shown below.

17592186134936 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135164 :tutorial/content "Consider the vector field 

$$
\mathbf{F} = \langle 2x+1,\: 3z,\: xy \rangle
$$

and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown below. 

![](images/cf/cf90197ac99a066db75154200de4cbee2494fef15deed6be7b7c4cd501ae8f26.png)

 

Let's find the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

To find the total flux directly, we would need to find the flux through each of the six surfaces of our rectangular solid and then add the results. However, using the divergence theorem

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}
= \iiint\limits_R \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} \: \textrm{d}V,
$$

we can reduce this computation to a single triple integral.

Computing the divergence of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3z)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy) \\  & =2+0+0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux through $S$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}2\,\text{d}V \\  & =2{∭}_{R}\,\text{d}V \\  & =2\cdot \text{Volume}(R) \\  & =2\cdot (3\cdot 2\cdot 1) \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e318cc2d-81e3-5cbd-b0ce-2f076bfd06b8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7732 :tutorial/title "Calculating the Flux Across a Surface"} :step/id #uuid "f13db816-3a2c-5bc5-86bb-261c0c695783" :step/math-academy-id 44794 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134933}} {:db/id 17592186134939 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135170 :tutorial/content "The **divergence theorem** is a higher-dimensional analog of Green's theorem in flux form. It states the following:

*Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then*

$$
\iiint\limits_R \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} \: \textrm{d}V
=
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{n}\:\mathrm{d}S
$$

*where $\mathbf{n}$ is the outward-pointing unit normal to $S.$*

In other words, the sum of the microscopic "fluxes" (divergences) of $\mathbf{F}$ inside $R$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\mathbf{F}$ through the boundary of $R.$ 

The divergence theorem can be summarized in a single diagram.

![](images/ff/ffabcceb5f4fd520a57f909c476b267f584ac4dc3fb948a5c1996b71dbc74e6f.png)

The divergence theorem can be used to simplify flux calculations. Calculating the flux of $\mathbf F$ across a surface can be time-consuming because we often need to consider the flux of $\mathbf F$ across multiple faces that make up $S.$ The divergence theorem often allows us to reduce a complicated flux calculation to a single triple integral." :tutorial/id #uuid "ca1c4682-71c7-5950-950a-a33ad1e84c23" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7773 :tutorial/title "The Divergence Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "91aeb514-1bab-5aae-a601-fdf72405bbbf" :step/math-academy-id 45010 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134936}}] :activity/title "The Divergence Theorem" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134012} {:db/id 17592186134922 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135160 :tutorial/content "Consider a two-dimensional vector field $\mathbf{F}$ on $\mathbb R^2$ with component functions $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ defined over a region $D.$

32} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186055532 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055965 :tutorial/content "Let's remind ourselves of the first few powers of $\textrm{i}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{i}}^{1} & =\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{2} & =-1 \\ {\text{i}}^{3} & =-\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{4} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

At the fourth power, we return to the value of $1,$ which can also be written as $\textrm{i}^0 = 1.$ This means that if we continue to increase the powers, we would cycle through the same four values once again, as shown below.

![](images/5e/5e3f3a42dd591daf109e474eec99e446706e0d8e46f1252540839cd50d957463.png)

So, for $\textrm{i}^5$ through $\textrm{i}^8,$ the exact same pattern repeats. Remembering that $\textrm{i}^4 = 1,$ we have

$$
\eqalign{
		\textrm{i}^5&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i}\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^6&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^7&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^8&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1 .
	}
$$

Similarly, for $\textrm{i}^9$ through to $\textrm{i}^{12},$ the pattern repeats again:

$$
\eqalign{
		\textrm{i}^9&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i}\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^{10}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^{11}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^{12}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1 
	}
$$

Therefore, to simplify a higher integer power of $\textrm{i},$ we *divide the power by $4$ and raise $\textrm{i}$ to the remainder*.

[{:db/id 17592186088567 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088995 :tutorial/content "So, we know that the polynomial $p(x) = x^3-2x^2-x+2$ can be factored as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2 & =(x-2)({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

By dividing both sides by $(x-2),$ we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\dfrac{x^3-2x^2-x+2}{x-2} = x^2-1.
$$

Since the result of dividing the polynomial $p(x)$ by the factor $({x-{\color{black}2}})$ gives *another* polynomial, namely $x^2-1,$ we say that $({x-{\color{black}2}})$ divides $p(x)$ *with no remainder*. 

We can confirm that we get a remainder of zero when $p(x)$ is divided by $({x-{\color{blue}2}})$ using synthetic division:

|  | $x^3$ | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{blue}2$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $2$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $2$ | $0$ | $-2$ |
|  | $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $0$ |" :tutorial/id #uuid "1471f79a-59cb-50b0-b82f-f640e329bb7c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9720 :tutorial/title "Connection With Polynomial Division"} :step/id #uuid "f91395f3-3117-5229-a814-b5ebada7f90c" :step/math-academy-id 191472 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088617}} {:db/id 17592186088616 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088933 :tutorial/content "If we know a *root* of a polynomial, we can immediately determine a *factor* of the polynomial using the **factor theorem**. 

The factor theorem states that if $p(x)$ is a polynomial and $x={\color{blue}{r}}$ is a *root* of $p(x),$ meaning that 

$$
p({\color{blue}{r}})=0
$$

then $(x-{\color{blue}{r}})$ is a *factor* of $p(x).$

The converse of the factor theorem is also true. In other words, if $(x-{\color{blue}{r}})$ is a factor of $p(x),$ then $x={\color{blue}{r}}$ is a root of the polynomial.

For example, consider the polynomial $p(x),$ defined as

$$
p(x)=x^3-2x^2-x+2.
$$

Note that $x = {\color{blue}2}$ is a root of this polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(2) & ={2}^{3}-2(2)^{2}-2+2 \\  & =8-8-2+2 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, according to the factor theorem, $(x-{\color{blue}2})$ is a *factor* of the polynomial. Indeed, it can be shown that this polynomial can be factored as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2 & =(x-2)({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

We'll learn more about factoring polynomials using the factor theorem in future lessons. But for now, we can check that this is correct by multiplying the parentheses." :tutorial/id #uuid "6ffefc48-3af9-5767-83c4-bf215db91563" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3719 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "848515fd-f525-5e59-ac3a-e5f8bb64943f" :step/math-academy-id 20941 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088567}} {:db/id 17592186088617 :step/content {:db/id 17592186087755 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186087571 :question/id #uuid "01993d51-8a9f-5156-b5cc-2784e93da5aa" :question/math-academy-id "e-5753"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "23c4516d-ba9c-5b55-b971-ceeb575d50c3" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048369} {:db/id 17592186051061}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186088153} {:db/id 17592186088297} {:db/id 17592186522713} {:db/id 17592186522746}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Factor Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "cd1ba65e-8d34-5dd7-89fc-a3588ee3811c" :step/math-academy-id 20942 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088618}} {:db/id 17592186088618 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088934 :tutorial/content "We can also apply the factor theorem to factors of the form $(ax-b).$

For example, suppose that $(2x-3)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x).$ Then, we can immediately obtain a root of $p(x)$ by setting the factor equal to $0$ and solving for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-3 & =0 \\ 2x & =3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the factor theorem, it follows that 

$$
p\left(\dfrac32\right) = 0.
$$

We can summarize this more general form of the factor theorem as follows:

- If $({\color{red}a}x-{\color{blue}b})$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x),$ then $x=\dfrac{{\color{blue}b}}{{\color{red}a}}$ is a root of $p(x).$

- Conversely, if $x=\dfrac{{\color{blue}b}}{{\color{red}a}}$ is a root of $p(x),$ then $({\color{red}a}x-{\color{blue}b})$ is a factor of $p(x).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cd34f044-e27c-5559-bb43-7d385325b69e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3720 :tutorial/title "The Factor Theorem for General Linear Factors"} :step/id #uuid "4e0fd1fd-b17d-5ee1-99f9-799218de5423" :step/math-academy-id 20943 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088619}} {:db/id 17592186088619 :step/content {:db/id 17592186087756 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186087572 :question/id #uuid "da4e2c42-894b-5f2a-917b-a5df22f41019" :question/math-academy-id "e-5754"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dd5d3a7d-ef95-5d7d-a92a-ce76d6b400bb" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048673}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186088157} {:db/id 17592186088298} {:db/id 17592186522720} {:db/id 17592186522791}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Factor Theorem to Factors With Leading Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "b6addca5-a5ce-5e5a-ba37-b179ad6bd1f6" :step/math-academy-id 20944}] :activity/title "The Factor Theorem" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186087917} {:db/id 17592186088616 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088933 :tutorial/content "If we know a *root* of a polynomial, we can immediately determine a *factor* of the polynomial using the **factor theorem**.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2 & =(x-2)({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

By dividing both sides by $(x-2),$ we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\dfrac{x^3-2x^2-x+2}{x-2} = x^2-1.
$$

Since the result of dividing the polynomial $p(x)$ by the factor $({x-{\color{black}2}})$ gives *another* polynomial, namely $x^2-1,$ we say that $({x-{\color{black}2}})$ divides $p(x)$ *with no remainder*.

The factor theorem states that if $p(x)$ is a polynomial and $x={\color{blue}{r}}$ is a *root* of $p(x),$ meaning that 

$$
p({\color{blue}{r}})=0
$$

then $(x-{\color{blue}{r}})$ is a *factor* of $p(x).$

The converse of the factor theorem is also true. In other words, if $(x-{\color{blue}{r}})$ is a factor of $p(x),$ then $x={\color{blue}{r}}$ is a root of the polynomial.

For example, consider the polynomial $p(x),$ defined as

$$
p(x)=x^3-2x^2-x+2.
$$

Note that $x = {\color{blue}2}$ is a root of this polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(2) & ={2}^{3}-2(2)^{2}-2+2 \\  & =8-8-2+2 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, according to the factor theorem, $(x-{\color{blue}2})$ is a *factor* of the polynomial. Indeed, it can be shown that this polynomial can be factored as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2 & =(x-2)({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

We'll learn more about factoring polynomials using the factor theorem in future lessons. But for now, we can check that this is correct by multiplying the parentheses." :tutorial/id #uuid "6ffefc48-3af9-5767-83c4-bf215db91563" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3719 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186088618 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088934 :tutorial/content "We can also apply the factor theorem to factors of the form $(ax-b).$

For example, suppose that $(2x-3)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x).$ Then, we can immediately obtain a root of $p(x)$ by setting the factor equal to $0$ and solving for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-3 & =0 \\ 2x & =3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the factor theorem, it follows that 

$$
p\left(\dfrac32\right) = 0.
$$

We can summarize this more general form of the factor theorem as follows:

- If $({\color{red}a}x-{\color{blue}b})$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x),$ then $x=\dfrac{{\color{blue}b}}{{\color{red}a}}$ is a root of $p(x).$

- Conversely, if $x=\dfrac{{\color{blue}b}}{{\color{red}a}}$ is a root of $p(x),$ then $({\color{red}a}x-{\color{blue}b})$ is a factor of $p(x).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cd34f044-e27c-5559-bb43-7d385325b69e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3720 :tutorial/title "The Factor Theorem for General Linear Factors"} :step/id #uuid "4e0fd1fd-b17d-5ee1-99f9-799218de5423" :step/math-academy-id 20943 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088619}} {:db/id 17592186088934 :tutorial/content "We can also apply the factor theorem to factors of the form $(ax-b).$

:question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=1\cdot 2=2.
$$

Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{ave}} & =\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{D}(2x+3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[2xy+{y}^{3}]_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4x+8)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[2{x}^{2}+8x]_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot {1}^{2}+8\cdot 1) \\  & =\frac{10}{2} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281652 :question/id #uuid "1ba106c5-525d-577c-b0dd-66ad242d632a" :question/math-academy-id "q-163255"} {:db/id 17592186374220 :question/id #uuid $f(x,y)=2x+y$ on the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $y\ge 0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region $D:$ 

![](images/b5/b5ba69ab02aa13e201b7b9113f6a36e705ad19e6412499504afc4f239459a8f3.png)

Notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {2}^{2}=2\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,{[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}[2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{8}{3}((2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{2\pi }\cdot \frac{16}{3}=\frac{8}{3\pi }.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281588 :question/id #uuid "636e23a3-a873-5229-81ee-5d1161e02dcd" :question/math-academy-id "q-163070"} {:db/id 17592186281653 :question/id #uuid Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ on the semicircle shown above." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(-1,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $y=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-2x}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-2x} \\ {y}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}-2x \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-2x \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{4}-{0}^{4})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{4}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{[-\frac{{cos}^{5}⁡\theta }{5}]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}({cos}^{5}⁡\pi -{cos}^{5}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}\cdot \frac{4}{5}=\frac{8}{5\pi }.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281663 :question/id #uuid "128ce1a7-9b5d-51fb-9a3d-78ee6a5214c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163279"} {:db/id 17592186374241 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {2}^{2}=4\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (4-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{[\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2[(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)] \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{4\pi }\cdot 4\pi =1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481407 :question/id #uuid "b0a81f04-6f59-512d-aa20-c54e3b26a51d" :question/math-academy-id "q-163277"} {:db/id 17592186481408 :question/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Recall that the average value of a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $D = [a,b]$ is given by

$$
f_\textrm{ave} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Length}(D)}\int_a^b f(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

There is an analogous definition for functions of two variables, stated below:

*Suppose $D$ is a closed and bounded region in $\mathbb{R}^2$ which has non-zero finite area $\textrm{Area}(D).$ If $f (x, y)$ is a continuous function on $D,$ then **the average value of $\boldsymbol f$ on $\boldsymbol D$** is given by*

$$
f_{\textrm{ave}} =\dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c862ff42-4e5b-5bbb-aed6-3d9760d339b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7770 :tutorial/title "The Average Value of a Function"} :step/id #uuid "c77b7ad4-9d8d-58f4-bd79-4c0b0b47cfea" :step/content {:db/id 17592186168150 :tutorial/content "Given a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $[a, b],$ the mean value theorem for integrals guarantees that there exists a number $c \in [a,b]$ such that

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a),
$$

which can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/0a/0afb9b15787eb89f73f322290bdbe2288027c54924d274c438773ce151a17291.png)

 

We have a similar theorem for functions with two variables. The so-called **mean value theorem for double integrals** states:

*If the function $f(x,y)$ is continuous on a closed and bounded region $D,$ then there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that*

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

This has a nice geometrical interpretation when $f$ is non-negative on $D.$ In this case, the theorem tells us that there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ 

The diagram below shows the case when $D$ is rectangular, and the corresponding cylinder is a rectangular solid.

"Suppose that we want to solve the quadratic equation

$$
x^2 -2x +2=0.
$$

This quadratic is written in standard form with $a=1,$ $b=-2,$ and $c=2.$ However, its discriminant is negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}^{2}-4ac & =(-2)^{2}-4(1)(2) \\  & =4-8 \\  & =-4 \\  & <0\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the quadratic equation has no real solutions. However, if we allow complex solutions, we may solve the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(2)}}{2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{-4}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 2\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $x^2 -2x +2=0$ has two solutions, $x=1+\textrm{i}$ and $x=1-\textrm{i}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "275a04ea-da37-527f-9ade-d57aa888110b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2827 :tutorial/content "We can also solve a quadratic equation with complex solutions using the square root method.

To demonstrate, let's find the solutions of the equation $(x-2)^2=-16.$

The left-hand side is a perfect square. Therefore, we can solve the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2} & =-16 \\ x-2 & =\pm \sqrt{-16} \\ x-2 & =\pm 4\text{i} \\ x & =2\pm 4\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Sometimes, we need to complete the square first before applying the square root method. $$

This quadratic is written in standard form with $a=1,$ $b=-2,$ and $c=2.$ However, its discriminant is negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}^{2}-4ac & =(-2)^{2}-4(1)(2) \\  & =4-8 \\  & =-4 \\  & <0\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the quadratic equation has no real solutions. However, if we allow complex solutions, we may solve the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(2)}}{2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{-4}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 2\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

- Revenue: This is the total amount of money (in dollars) that a company gains after selling $x$ units of product.

- Cost: This is the total amount of money (in dollars) that a company spends to create $x$ units of product.

- Profit. The difference between revenue and cost. It represents the amount of *additional* money that the business has earned after paying its costs.

The revenue function $R(x)$ associated with a price function $p(x)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & =(\text{number of units})\cdot (\text{price per unit}) \\  & =x\cdot p(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Also, recall that the cost function $C(x)$ associated with producing $x$ units of a good can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}C(x) & =(\text{fixed cost})+(\text{number of units})\cdot (\text{cost per unit}) \\  & =(\text{fixed cost})+x\cdot (\text{cost per unit})\end{aligned}
$$

The quantity $x\cdot (\textrm{cost per unit})$ is sometimes called the **variable cost** since it is the part of the cost function $C(x)$ that is dependent on the number of units $x$ produced by the company. 

Finally, if we know the revenue function $R(x)$ and the cost function $C(x),$ then the profit function $P(x)$ is given by

$$
P(x) = R(x) - C(x).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fb6a794d-d60c-5d16-8912-b69af938c892" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4663 :tutorial/title "A Review of Price and Cost Functions"} :step/id #uuid Let's start by adding multiples of $360^\circ$ to $240^\circ$:

$$
240^{∘} + 360^{∘} = 600^{∘}✓
$$

There are no answer choices larger than $600^\circ$, so we can stop here.

Now, let's subtract multiples of $360^\circ$ from $240^\circ$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
240^{∘} - 360^{∘} &= -120^{∘} \\
240^{∘} - 2 \cdot (360^{∘}) &= -480^{∘}✓
\end{aligned}
$$

There are no answer choices smaller than $-480^\circ$, so we can stop here.

So, of the given angles, the coterminal angles are $600^\circ$ and $-480^\circ$."} {:db/id 17592186060097 :question/id #uuid "4460855f-5c1d-50f3-afe3-835edc64570b" :question/math-academy-id "q-1677"} Let's start by adding multiples of $2\pi$ to

$$
\dfrac {3 \pi} {5}
$$

$$
\frac{3π}{5} + 2π = \frac{13π}{5}
$$

There are no answer choices larger than

$$
\dfrac {13 \pi} {5}
$$

Now, let's subtract multiples of $2\pi$ from

$$
\dfrac {3 \pi} {5}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{3π}{5} - 2π &= -\frac{7π}{5}✓ \\
\frac{3π}{5} - 2 \cdot (2π) &= -\frac{17π}{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

There are no answer choices smaller than

$$
-\dfrac {17 \pi} {5}
$$

so we can stop here.

So, of the given angles, the only coterminal angle is

$$
-\dfrac{7\pi}{5}

"80b57f6b-0f3a-58c6-a53f-22f4b5c50a44" :step/math-academy-id 13174 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060550}} {:db/id 17592186060548 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060901 :tutorial/content "All the angles we have constructed so far have been inside the range $(-360^\circ, 360^\circ)$. However, we can also construct angles outside this range.

The way we do this involves **coterminal angles**. Coterminal angles are different angles that appear as the same angle in the coordinate plane. For example, the angles $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$ are coterminal because a rotation of $360^\circ$ is the same as the rotation of $0^\circ$. In general, whenever we add or subtract a multiple of $360^\circ$, we get a coterminal angle.

The standard way in which we draw a **positive** angle $\theta$ in the coordinate plane is as follows:

- Subtract integer multiples of $360^\circ$ until we get a coterminal angle that lies in the range $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$.
- Draw the resulting angle in the coordinate plane.

For example, to represent the angle $405^\circ$ in the coordinate plane, we first subtract $360^\circ$:

$$
405^{∘} - 360^{∘} = 45^{∘}✓
$$

The result, $45^\circ$, is a coterminal angle that lies in the range $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$. So, to draw the angle $405^\circ$, we draw the coterminal angle $45^\circ$ in the coordinate plane.

![](images/6c/6c96b1f8b34764c0d1a8ffb2362349d3ac3f4f99eaaf5c8e4c249fab1f29ceb3.png)

**Note:** For every multiple of $\color{blue}360^\circ$ we subtract, we make one complete rotation counter-clockwise around the origin. A rotation of ${\color{blue}360^\circ}$ is the same as the rotation of ${\color{blue}0^\circ}$, so it doesn't contribute to our final angle.

Here, we subtracted ${\color{blue}360^\circ}$ a single time, so we make a single rotation.

![](images/dd/dd44ea334cc1cf709685a71a5a88025955e5cc1fb96cd9d938272b8024b99acc.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "4c50e7f7-6a06-51b1-8970-2f34f25890c7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2709 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "36e80ef2-d5c8-59b3-8dde-d93df12c37e0" :step/math-academy-id 13181 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060547}} {:db/id 17592186060549 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060902 :tutorial/content "To find a coterminal angle of a given angle $\theta$, we rotate $360^\circ$ clockwise or counter-clockwise from $\theta$. We could do this again and again, each time looping by $360^\circ$ to find an infinite number of coterminal angles:
$\theta \pm 360^\circ n,\quad \text{where} n \text{is any integer.}$

For instance, the angles $-240^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $480^\circ$, and $840^\circ$ are all coterminal.

![](images/16/1684bdb452645ca612d0e0b08321b688f8d3e4a7a6de005a3afd620707eae9ee.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "a87549c4-ee2e-552b-95ea-50727cc87fbe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2710 :tutorial/title "Finding Multiple Coterminal Angles"} :step/id #uuid "a1c2e014-ae34-535b-8a47-0683fdb921ab" :step/math-academy-id 13182 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060544}} {:db/id 17592186060550 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060903 :tutorial/content "The method for constructing a *negative* angle $\theta$ outside the range $(-360^\circ, 360^\circ)$ is similar to the method for positive angles, but with one main difference: we *add* multiples of $360^\circ$, instead of subtracting. So the steps are:

- Add integer multiples of $360^\circ$ until we get a coterminal angle that lies in the range $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$.
- Draw the resulting angle in the coordinate plane.

For example, we can represent the angle $-660^\circ$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-660^{∘} + 360^{∘} &= -300^{∘} \\
- 300^{∘} + 360^{∘} &= 60^{∘}✓
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we draw the angle $60^\circ$ in the coordinate plane.

![](images/e7/e76aff5a8e7bc805be56a61db114f111a9ab15f54b01eb3dd5542c1023224b85.png)

Again, for every multiple of $360^\circ$ that we add, we make one complete rotation around the origin clockwise. A rotation of ${\color{blue}360^\circ}$ is the same as the rotation of ${\color{blue}0^\circ}$, so it doesn't contribute to our final angle." :tutorial/id #uuid "b9973405-ead1-5dfa-92ff-238e697e4ad2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2712 :tutorial/title "Constructing Negative Angles that Contain More Than One Full Rotation"} :step/id #uuid "2b4977be-02bb-5aef-85fd-9b94974a8ea1" :step/math-academy-id 13195 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060546}} {:db/id 17592186060901 :tutorial/content "All the angles we have constructed so far have been inside the range $(-360^\circ, 360^\circ)$. However, we can also construct angles outside this range.

The way we do this involves **coterminal angles**. Coterminal angles are different angles that appear as the same angle in the coordinate plane. For example, the angles $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$ are coterminal because a rotation of $360^\circ$ is the same as the rotation of $0^\circ$. In general, whenever we add or subtract a multiple of $360^\circ$, we get a coterminal angle.

The standard way in which we draw a **positive** angle $\theta$ in the coordinate plane is as follows:

- Subtract integer multiples of $360^\circ$ until we get a coterminal angle that lies in the range $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$.
- Draw the resulting angle in the coordinate plane.

For example, to represent the angle $405^\circ$ in the coordinate plane, we first subtract $360^\circ$:

$$
405^{∘} - 360^{∘} = 45^{∘}✓
$$

The result, $45^\circ$, is a coterminal angle that lies in the range $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$. So, to draw the angle $405^\circ$, we draw the coterminal angle $45^\circ$ in the coordinate plane.

![](images/6c/6c96b1f8b34764c0d1a8ffb2362349d3ac3f4f99eaaf5c8e4c249fab1f29ceb3.png)

**Note:** For every multiple of $\color{blue}360^\circ$ we subtract, we make one complete rotation counter-clockwise around the origin. A rotation of ${\color{blue}360^\circ}$ is the same as the rotation of ${\color{blue}0^\circ}$, so it doesn't contribute to our final angle.

Here, we subtracted ${\color{blue}360^\circ}$ a single time, so we make a single rotation.

![](images/dd/dd44ea334cc1cf709685a71a5a88025955e5cc1fb96cd9d938272b8024b99acc.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "4c50e7f7-6a06-51b1-8970-2f34f25890c7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2709 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186060902 :tutorial/content "To find a coterminal angle of a given angle $\theta$, we rotate $360^\circ$ clockwise or counter-clockwise from $\theta$. We could do this again and again, each time looping by $360^\circ$ to find an infinite number of coterminal angles:
$\theta \pm 360^\circ n,\quad \text{where} n \text{is any integer.}$

For instance, the angles $-240^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $480^\circ$, and $840^\circ$ are all coterminal.

![](images/16/1684bdb452645ca612d0e0b08321b688f8d3e4a7a6de005a3afd620707eae9ee.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "a87549c4-ee2e-552b-95ea-50727cc87fbe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2710 :tutorial/title "Finding Multiple Coterminal Angles"} {:db/id 17592186060903 :tutorial/content "The method for constructing a *negative* angle $\theta$ outside the range $(-360^\circ, 360^\circ)$ is similar to the method for positive angles, but with one main difference: we *add* multiples of $360^\circ$, instead of subtracting. So the steps are:

- Add integer multiples of $360^\circ$ until we get a coterminal angle that lies in the range $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$.
- Draw the resulting angle in the coordinate plane.

For example, we can represent the angle $-660^\circ$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-660^{∘} + 360^{∘} &= -300^{∘} \\
- 300^{∘} + 360^{∘} &= 60^{∘}✓
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we draw the angle $60^\circ$ in the coordinate plane.

![](images/e7/e76aff5a8e7bc805be56a61db114f111a9ab15f54b01eb3dd5542c1023224b85.png)

Again, for every multiple of $360^\circ$ that we add, we make one complete rotation around the origin clockwise. A rotation of ${\color{blue}360^\circ}$ is the same as the rotation of ${\color{blue}0^\circ}$, so it doesn't contribute to our final angle." :tutorial/id #uuid "b9973405-ead1-5dfa-92ff-238e697e4ad2" :db/id 17592186277796}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/89/8901e7155a476f0019b6d66e3b62b579b91daf99a448e497c93efce1d94415b0.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,2x+yz⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,2x+yz⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/8f/8fa71e16d84eb92506e9b10269182f907cb4f2437d0a9bdd3822da48c4cbba4a.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+yz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+2y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =2x+2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}{S}_{1} & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2x+2y\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x+2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x+2y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}+2xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+2y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[y+{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+yz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}{S}_{2} & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-2x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}-2x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-1\cdot {[{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-1\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =2+(-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198628 :question/id #uuid "094e7fc2-0489-524c-9276-17e9e447e5af" :question/math-academy-id "q-162564"} {:db/id 17592186278431 :question/id #uuid "df8892a4-0ff3-5c81-818d-9a1c55b02265" :question/math-academy-id "q-161219" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e9c78dc-55fa-58d4-a093-f9544e5dfbd9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{28}{3}" :db/id 17592186275601} {:answer/id #uuid "78632b46-36da-5697-b93d-bc2adc1c9045" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186276568} {:answer/id #uuid "79740243-a948-508f-ad95-f7961fb345fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{19}{3}" :db/id 17592186276581} {:answer/id #uuid "7c58ab40-2a38-5ea8-a5ef-7548298d0ad5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186276612} {:answer/id #uuid "7c6fd983-c520-5566-9c80-71e44ea0a60f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186276613}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186276612} :answer-field/id #uuid "6e7ff9e2-fb54-58a9-9896-204ca397e982" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277922}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/9a/9afc7f79f4612ce579e82a6b3c5086922d14051978907bfeb5c133a3f99791c7.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/fa/fa4986b1de44fa4ccc75114e64abfd93d0de16618f2f1b29695d9115019b6e3e.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=4$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=4$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+4⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =x{y}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}x{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4x]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+8\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}+8y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{26}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-x{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{2}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{26}{3}+(-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278432 :question/id #uuid "8c3f4c19-765d-5833-904a-bf7538da3049" :question/math-academy-id "q-161222" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "71b4b278-b65f-5406-9647-519faf867137" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186276501} {:answer/id #uuid "7305c0b2-d8c2-5e47-bbb3-3425beae0e64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{12}" :db/id 17592186276519} {:answer/id #uuid "9eb283a3-ac7c-5ffa-9921-e523b36374a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{12}" :db/id 17592186276903} {:answer/id #uuid "bca4ccd7-be58-541f-ae27-b6666d1303c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186277157} {:answer/id #uuid "be2e5824-d10f-5cc6-81d8-eaf9f7d77d64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186277175}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186276501} :answer-field/id #uuid "d99b0f37-11a6-51ae-b457-b0354976d304" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186278108}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/01/01902836fd1e91ac829f67a279103a9b3d5732d7b058f03c695b6733a42e673d.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](images/c0/c058465d6ca7855446711ebc44f6b23913ee786d2fd9bb32ae6c671964e1ad32.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & ={x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+x{y}^{2}+x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}+\frac{5}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{5}{4}y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{19}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-({x}^{3}+{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-({x}^{3}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{7}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "![](images/80/804976bf326ed561ff8e7b4f5a6c65361039a686a4449edfdf8e6f497ee5cbda.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the right and left sides. 

![](images/de/de9eb8381df05d2d5e6222a51b0ccbc5729e522df94a4aace570881d1226a1ca.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =x-z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x-z\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x-z\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}x-z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-xz]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}-z\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}z-\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}z\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}z\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{2}z\,\text{d}z \\  & =[x]_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1\cdot 2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =(-1)+2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198391 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198033 :question/id #uuid "06cccfa3-4b70-5e67-9e9f-9f5c83b319bf" :question/math-academy-id "e-12386"} :knowledge-point/id Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$
n=\frac{⟨x,y,z⟩}{r}.
$$

In our case, we have $r=3.$ Therefore,

$$
n=\frac{1}{3}⟨x,y,z⟩.
$$

Using the fact that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x-y,\,y+x,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x-y,\,y+x,\,z⟩\cdot ⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(x(x-y)+y(y+x)+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({x}^{2}-xy+{y}^{2}+xy+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 9 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}3\,\text{d}S \\  & =3{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =3\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =3\cdot 4\pi \cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =108\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278437 :question/id #uuid "b6a9b04d-4452-53ab-bc15-c881e40cd0e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-161235"} {:db/id 17592186278438 :question/id #uuid
