"The function $f(x) = e^{x-k}+2$ has an inverse function given by $f^{-1}(x) = \ln{(x-2)}+4$. What is the value of $k$?" :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= e^{x - k} + 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= e^{y - k} + 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= e^{y - k} + 2 \\
e^{y - k} &= x - 2 \\
\ln (e^{y - k}) &= \ln (x - 2) \\
y - k &= \ln (x - 2) \\
y &= \ln (x - 2) + k
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \ln{(x-2)} + k
$$

Comparing our answer with the given expression, we conclude that $k=4$."} {:db/id 17592186049053} {:db/id 17592186050322} {:db/id 17592186050649} {:db/id 17592186110917 :question/id #uuid "d8e1513c-ddca-5cb5-ae10-96061624f027" :question/math-academy-id "q-148276"} {:db/id 17592186110983 :question/id #uuid "002518fb-44a2-5882-a8cc-6a4a012ecbe5" :question/math-academy-id "q-228737"} {:db/id 17592186110701 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110289 :question/id #uuid "09634460-21c4-5389-92f4-15339282b7ff" :question/math-academy-id "e-10455"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bfadce43-b527-59fc-b6c7-ec963bb543b4" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186110918 :question/id #uuid "2ee49026-9916-5580-8e7a-6bc7d6034caa" :question/math-academy-id "q-148286"} {:db/id 17592186110919 :question/id #uuid "f3d3c000-853d-56b8-8379-349b72e8e0ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-148353"} {:db/id 17592186110984 :question/id #uuid "14688cac-c8b6-51f6-a150-a4fce8b53f8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-228738"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Inverses of Exponential Functions With More Than Two Transformations"} {:db/id 17592186110289 :question/id #uuid "09634460-21c4-5389-92f4-15339282b7ff" :question/math-academy-id "e-10455" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186110701 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bfadce43-b527-59fc-b6c7-ec963bb543b4" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Inverses of Exponential Functions With More Than Two Transformations"}] :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x) = \dfrac12 e^{x+8}-2$." :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= \frac{1}{2}e^{x + 8} - 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{1}{2}e^{y + 8} - 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{1}{2}e^{y + 8} - 2 \\
\frac{1}{2}e^{y + 8} &= x + 2 \\
e^{y + 8} &= 2x + 4 \\
\ln (e^{y + 8}) &= \ln (2x + 4) \\
y + 8 &= \ln (2x + 4) \\
y &= \ln (2x + 4) - 8
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \ln{(2x+4)} - 8
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110918 :question/id #uuid "2ee49026-9916-5580-8e7a-6bc7d6034caa" :question/math-academy-id "q-148286"} {:db/id 17592186110919 :question/id #uuid "f3d3c000-853d-56b8-8379-349b72e8e0ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-148353"} {:db/id 17592186110984 :question/id #uuid "14688cac-c8b6-51f6-a150-a4fce8b53f8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-228738"} {:db/id 17592186110702 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110500 :question/id #uuid "fc54368a-099e-5b85-a6c4-15db9be3ee8f" :question/math-academy-id "e-4127"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2efb7d6d-25e9-5bf3-b2b3-5085221b0e76" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048741} {:db/id 17592186049944}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111045 :question/id #uuid "5ef680fd-12ef-5d85-be42-1fc022ab628e" :question/math-academy-id "q-250496"} {:db/id 17592186111209 :question/id #uuid "ffbd93fd-b692-5745-8d6f-d17ae1780b7d" :question/math-academy-id "q-46620"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Inverses of Logarithmic Functions With Up to Two Transformations"} {:db/id 17592186110500 :question/id #uuid "fc54368a-099e-5b85-a6c4-15db9be3ee8f" :question/math-academy-id "e-4127" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186110702 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2efb7d6d-25e9-5bf3-b2b3-5085221b0e76" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Inverses of Logarithmic Functions With Up to Two Transformations"}] :question/problem "What is the inverse of $f(x) =\ln(x+3)+6$?" :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y$:

$$
y = \ln(x+3)+6
$$

Then, we swap $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \ln (y + 3) + 6
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \ln (y + 3) + 6 \\
\ln (y + 3) &= x - 6 \\
e^{\ln (y + 3)} &= e^{x - 6} \\
y + 3 &= e^{x - 6} \\
y &= e^{x - 6} - 3
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = e^{x-6}-3
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048741 :topic/id #uuid "ba61133e-2980-52f4-ab73-d0df517adbd4" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186110606 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110503 :knowledge-point/title "Finding Inverses of Logarithmic Functions With More Than Two Transformations"}] :question/problem "What is the inverse of $f(x) = 2\log_4(3x)-1$?" :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= 2\log_{4} (3x) - 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we swap $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= 2\log_{4} (3y) - 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= 2\log_{4} (3y) - 1 \\
2\log_{4} (3y) &= x + 1 \\
\log_{4} (3y) &= \frac{x + 1}{2} \\
4^{\log_{4} (3y)} &= 4^{(x + 1)/2} \\
3y &= 4^{(x + 1)/2} \\
y &= \frac{1}{3}4^{(x + 1)/2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) =\dfrac13 4^{(x+1)/2}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186110985 :question/id #uuid "9ae8277e-37c6-59e9-af56-0d7eccfa6c61" :question/math-academy-id "q-228842" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186110703 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a220ac5f-7b5c-59ef-82d5-aa84654f9fc2" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Inverses of Logarithmic Functions With More Than Two Transformations"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "d7396d89-4bc9-5ba9-b9b1-12012d5351ed" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186107628}] :question/problem "The inverse of the function $f(x) = 5\log_{4} (10x - 1)$ is $f^{-1}(x) =$ {{field-1}}."} {:db/id 17592186111404 :question/id #uuid "563c3061-82c3-5460-a8aa-2540c795762a" :question/math-academy-id "q-81648"} {:db/id 17592186048675} {:db/id 17592186048724} {:answer-field/id #uuid "d7396d89-4bc9-5ba9-b9b1-12012d5351ed" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186107628} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186111649} :activity/id #uuid "f0ccfa97-349a-51e7-8c3e-2b151be71120" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048787 :topic/id #uuid "bee6b4ad-7bf3-5c2d-82dc-c00a53e573bb" :topic/math-academy-id 1472} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186111649 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111905 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the transformed exponential function

$$
f(x)=2^{5x}+1
$$

and we wish to find the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$. We can do this using the following three steps.

**Step 1:** We start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= 2^{5x} + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Then, we interchange $x$ and $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= 2^{5y} + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= 2^{5y} + 1 \\
x - 1 &= 2^{5y} \\
\log_{2} (x - 1) &= \log_{2} (2^{5y}) \\
\log_{2} (x - 1) &= 5y \\
5y &= \log_{2} (x - 1) \\
y &= \frac{1}{5}\log_{2} (x - 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{5}\log_2{(x-1)}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dc5609e8-50a8-59fe-af6c-4cfc16ccc454" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6516 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "27fb8a99-b935-578a-a9a7-3c26c121777d" :step/math-academy-id 458787 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111650}} {:db/id 17592186111650 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110700 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110501 :question/id #uuid "2b08436f-c561-59c5-bb79-621a1780b470" :question/math-academy-id "e-4128"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c01b24c5-c253-5a11-8055-9be0d60da592" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049053} {:db/id 17592186050322} {:db/id 17592186050649}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186110917} {:db/id 17592186110983}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Inverses of Exponential Functions With Up to Two Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "91aff0b1-b90e-5801-8592-dc12106afede" :step/math-academy-id 458788 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111651}} {:db/id 17592186111651 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110701 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110289 :question/id #uuid "09634460-21c4-5389-92f4-15339282b7ff" :question/math-academy-id "e-10455"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bfadce43-b527-59fc-b6c7-ec963bb543b4" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186110918} {:db/id 17592186110919} {:db/id 17592186110984}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Inverses of Exponential Functions With More Than Two Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "027efb8b-b7f4-57c3-9b47-e73dfdc14471" :step/math-academy-id 458791 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111652}} {:db/id 17592186111652 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111881 :tutorial/content "Now suppose we wish to find the inverse of the logarithmic function

$$
f(x)=3\log_{2}(x-1)+1
$$

We can find $f^{-1}(x)$ using the same three steps as before.

**Step 1:** We start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = 3\log_{2}(x-1)+1
$$

**Step 2:** Then, we interchange $x$ and $y$:

$$
x = 3\log_{2}(y-1)+1
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, we make $y$ the subject of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3\log_{2} (y - 1) + 1 &= x \\
3\log_{2} (y - 1) &= x - 1 \\
\log_{2} (y - 1) &= \frac{x - 1}{3} \\
2^{\log_{2} (y - 1)} &= 2^{(x - 1)/3} \\
y - 1 &= 2^{(x - 1)/3} \\
y &= 2^{(x - 1)/3} + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = {2}^{(x-1)/3}+1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cf6e7706-d6b7-5b75-ac3f-184a71b3330a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2818 :tutorial/title "Finding the Inverse of a Transformed Logarithmic Function"} :step/id #uuid "2d5c352f-41f8-5a6a-bb13-3c7b0d3b54e8" :step/math-academy-id 458795 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111653}} {:db/id 17592186111653 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110702 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110500 :question/id #uuid "fc54368a-099e-5b85-a6c4-15db9be3ee8f" :question/math-academy-id "e-4127"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2efb7d6d-25e9-5bf3-b2b3-5085221b0e76" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048741} {:db/id 17592186049944}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111045} {:db/id 17592186111209}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Inverses of Logarithmic Functions With Up to Two Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "54971f0b-36de-5930-a669-5c88c032a9cb" :step/math-academy-id 458796 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111654}} {:db/id 17592186111654 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110703 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110502 :question/id #uuid "c6d0d3ad-111a-5db1-b521-0c9416dfb6b8" :question/math-academy-id "e-4140"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a220ac5f-7b5c-59ef-82d5-aa84654f9fc2" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186110985} {:db/id 17592186111404}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Inverses of Logarithmic Functions With More Than Two Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "3b1ca6f9-7082-5953-a9d6-ea4f7272ccd1" :step/math-academy-id 458799}] :activity/title "Inverses of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186110841} {:db/id 17592186111649 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111905 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the transformed exponential function

solve logarithmic equations containing the natural logarithm $(\ln),$ we can use the same method as usual: first isolate the logarithm, and then exponentiate both sides of the equation using the same base as the logarithm.

The key is to remember that the base of the natural logarithm is $e.$

To demonstrate, let's solve for $x$ in the equation $\ln x = 2.$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is $e.$ So, we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡x & =2 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} & ={e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $e^{\ln x} = x.$ 

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution is $x=e^2.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7e032551-9488-5bc5-858a-2197849a42cf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2821 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{9+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{9\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/9)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{9+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (3\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186250166 :question/id #uuid "c6b1e250-deab-5051-9d86-76fdce192937" :question/math-academy-id "q-114033" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10b46bc9-97cb-5bce-918b-8b92646973b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{6})+C" :db/id 17592186247570} {:answer/id #uuid "1b1e75f2-49eb-5a5d-9cee-c6ed60930c7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(6x)+C" :db/id 17592186247668} {:answer/id #uuid "3de5bd43-5bd8-5d01-8064-06ac8fdb185f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C" :db/id 17592186247970} {:answer/id #uuid "c07e9314-0212-563d-818b-d17717a081be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{6})+C" :db/id 17592186249137} {:answer/id #uuid "c7202512-7634-5743-96f4-8104d0655a3a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(6x)+C" :db/id 17592186249191}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186249191} :answer-field/id #uuid "c3dd683c-9379-5f34-9cdb-095ffd9b03f3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186250005}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Calculate $\int \frac{3}{1+36{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

${\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{6}{\sqrt{100-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{6}{\sqrt{100-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =6{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{100\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/100)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{10}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/100}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{5}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/10)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{10})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{10}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{10}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=10\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $5$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{6}{\sqrt{100-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{5}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/10)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 10\,\text{d}u \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =6\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =6\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-6\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =6\cdot \frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186320815 :question/id #uuid "b439af01-6063-5a0d-8dfc-d235cf8c0346" :question/math-academy-id "q-351291"} {:db/id 17592186320915 :question/id #uuid "b0098fa7-60fc-5090-aeb3-d82239a596c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-351827"} {:db/id 17592186320917 :question/id #uuid "88256796-f1d7-5511-b30e-ef033cdfdfae" :question/math-academy-id "q-351834" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186064220 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f2f9806d-3a72-5f0a-a6f4-db8dad8871f6" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Trigonometric Functions"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c4d6374a-a8f4-5012-ba14-79979bb09a1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186319994}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "c4d6374a-a8f4-5012-ba14-79979bb09a1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186319994} :answer-field/id #uuid "d0e46496-0573-5f7f-b6a6-15d10b4e8306" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186320599}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{3}{\sqrt{3-75{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3\cdot (1-25{x}^{2})}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-25{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(5x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

  

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(5x)}^{2}.$   

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-0.2$ | $0.2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-1$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{3}{\sqrt{3-75{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-0.2}^{0.2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(5x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}\,\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(1)-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-1)) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}(\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\,\pi }{5}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186320918 :question/id #uuid "8a43d62d-e653-5802-9217-17e3b89ace8c" :question/math-academy-id "q-351835"} {:db/id 17592186320919 :question/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$\int \frac{2}{|x|\sqrt{4{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{2\,\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{4{x}^{2}-1}}=4\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|2x|\sqrt{(2x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $2x.$

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|x|\sqrt{4{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =4\int \frac{1}{|2x|\sqrt{(2x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =2\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =2\,\text{arcsec}\,u+C \\  & =2\,\text{arcsec}(2x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186250173 :question/id #uuid "721577ab-4fa8-5463-8c74-5d6cebd1decf" :question/math-academy-id "q-114051"} {:db/id 17592186250174 :question/id #uuid $$

:step/content {:db/id 17592186065433 :tutorial/content "Consider the integral

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-4x^2}} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

This integral, apart from the coefficient of $4$ in the denominator, resembles the basic integral

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\textrm{d}u = \arcsin(u)+C.
$$

In fact, they look almost the same, but instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $4x^2 = (2x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \textrm d x.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can often use this trick whenever we see an integral that closely resembles an integral for an inverse trigonometric function.

**Note:** As always, after solving an integral using substitution, we should always double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)+C] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53af5e98-4580-5243-a97c-de9e0d5f8fab" :tutorial/math-academy-id 863 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d3e15f90-13b8-5437-b44e-fcdec07ad48c" :step/math-academy-id :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we learned how to use substitution to evaluate integrals that give rise to inverse trigonometric functions.

Although you can always solve these integrals by going through the substitution process, it is convenient to remember the following key results:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(ax)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(ax)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{a}^{2}-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{a})+C \\ \int \frac{1}{1+(ax)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(ax)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{{a}^{2}+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{a})+C \\ \int \frac{1}{|ax|\sqrt{(ax)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\text{arcsec}(ax)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To remember the results above, note the following:

- Whenever the integrand has an $ax$ term, the argument of the resulting inverse trigonometric function is $ax.$

- Otherwise, if the $a$ and $x$ are separated, then the argument of the resulting inverse trigonometric function is $\dfrac{x}{a}.$

- All the results are multiplied by $\dfrac{1}{a},$ except for $\arcsin \left( \dfrac{x}{a} \right) + C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "02539765-4345-5409-87f9-9901a59b7ebf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4800 :tutorial/title "Summary of Key Results"} :step/id #uuid "b420ebdd-a5d6-5ce1-8cde-23990b2968f7" :step/math-academy-id 641177}] :activity/title "Integration by Substitution With Inverse Trigonometric Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064411} {:db/id 17592186065076 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065433 :tutorial/content "Consider the integral

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-4x^2}} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

This integral, apart from the coefficient of $4$ in the denominator, resembles the basic integral

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\textrm{d}u = \arcsin(u)+C.
$$

In fact, they look almost the same, but instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $4x^2 = (2x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \textrm d x.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can often use this trick whenever we see an integral that closely resembles an integral for an inverse trigonometric function.

**Note:** As always, after solving an integral using substitution, we should always double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)+C] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53af5e98-4580-5243-a97c-de9e0d5f8fab" :tutorial/math-academy-id 863 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d3e15f90-13b8-5437-b44e-fcdec07ad48c" :step/math-academy-id 641164 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065077}} {:db/id 17592186065433 :tutorial/content "Consider the integral

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-4x^2}} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

This integral, apart from the coefficient of $4$ in the denominator, resembles the basic integral

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\textrm{d}u = \arcsin(u)+C.
$$

In fact, they look almost the same, but instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $4x^2 = (2x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \textrm d x.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can often use this trick whenever we see an integral that closely resembles an integral for an inverse trigonometric function.

**Note:** As always, after solving an integral using substitution, we should always double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)+C] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53af5e98-4580-5243-a97c-de9e0d5f8fab" :tutorial/math-academy-id 863 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065077 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064218 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065381 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we learned how to use substitution to evaluate integrals that give rise to inverse trigonometric functions.

Although you can always solve these integrals by going through the substitution process, it is convenient to remember the following key results:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(ax)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(ax)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{a}^{2}-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{a})+C \\ \int \frac{1}{1+(ax)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(ax)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{{a}^{2}+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{a})+C \\ \int \frac{1}{|ax|\sqrt{(ax)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\text{arcsec}(ax)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To remember the results above, note the following:

- Whenever the integrand has an $ax$ term, the argument of the resulting inverse trigonometric function is $ax.$

- Otherwise, if the $a$ and $x$ are separated, then the argument of the resulting inverse trigonometric function is $\dfrac{x}{a}.$

- All the results are multiplied by $\dfrac{1}{a},$ except for $\arcsin \left( \dfrac{x}{a} \right) + C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "02539765-4345-5409-87f9-9901a59b7ebf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4800 :tutorial/title "Summary of Key Results"} :step/id #uuid "b420ebdd-a5d6-5ce1-8cde-23990b2968f7" :step/math-academy-id 641177} {:db/id 17592186065381 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we learned how to use substitution to evaluate integrals that give rise to inverse trigonometric functions.

Although you can always solve these integrals by going through the substitution process, it is convenient to remember the following key results:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(ax)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(ax)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{a}^{2}-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{a})+C \\ \int \frac{1}{1+(ax)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(ax)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{{a}^{2}+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{a})+C \\ \int \frac{1}{|ax|\sqrt{(ax)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\text{arcsec}(ax)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To remember the results above, note the following:

- Whenever the integrand has an $ax$ term, the argument of the resulting inverse trigonometric function is $ax.$

- Otherwise, if the $a$ and $x$ are separated, then the argument of the resulting inverse trigonometric function is $\dfrac{x}{a}.$

- All the results are multiplied by $\dfrac{1}{a},$ except for $\arcsin \left( \dfrac{x}{a} \right) + C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "02539765-4345-5409-87f9-9901a59b7ebf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4800 :tutorial/title "Summary of Key Results"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046658} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186528030} :activity/id #uuid "5f0e245e-59f9-5be1-a308-bb06116b8f87" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048189 :topic/id #uuid "86b8f7ea-5908-5137-a377-052e6fc4f731" :topic/math-academy-id 315} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186528017 :step/content {:db/id 17592186319105 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a18383d3-63cd-5639-931d-a7a1c504ecad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186318118} {:answer/id #uuid "eef5da2c-2eb9-5619-b5fc-8c0b83845f3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi" :db/id 17592186527772}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186527772} :answer-field/id #uuid "d4db02f7-5977-595a-8560-ebd6520e3bc1" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186318876}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "684a7fc3-f685-5be8-90e1-52ef15ddd822" :question/math-academy-id "q-346458" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{6}{\sqrt{100-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{6}{\sqrt{100-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =6{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{100\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/100)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{10}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/100}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{5}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/10)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{10})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{10}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{10}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=10\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $5$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{6}{\sqrt{100-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{5}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/10)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 10\,\text{d}u \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =6\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =6\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-6\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =6\cdot \frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2c3f1281-e85c-5d9a-bc26-8e73de6690dd"} {:db/id 17592186528030 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064876 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0edb1c73-87ee-58c2-a730-43e7f693d596" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{9})+C" :db/id 17592186330078} {:answer/id #uuid "26074d64-e780-5986-be16-fa82ceeb0164" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C" :db/id 17592186330281} {:answer/id #uuid "3ec2d31d-3894-565f-9b91-3bc180c6d541" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C" :db/id 17592186330506} {:answer/id #uuid "581c2751-ecf3-5021-a41f-a828e408e3cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{9})+C" :db/id 17592186330735} {:answer/id #uuid "59dbc6dd-87a6-5e93-99fe-8c88f23299aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{9})+C" :db/id 17592186330753}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186330506} :answer-field/id #uuid "ef0aa3c5-1f7e-5feb-b2ae-0f439aa2181d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186332622}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ea76ea1f-1600-5c9d-b198-b9fb197580ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-49548" :question/problem "$\int \frac{1}{9+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{9+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{9\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/9)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{9+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (3\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "70dd22f2-9869-50f8-94c8-d430f170fc72" :step/next {:db/id 17592186528046}} {:db/id 17592186528032 :step/content {:db/id 17592186335976 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4c842fc6-bdb7-5fd1-95ec-a8a6c5c213af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{arcsec}(7x)+C" :db/id 17592186333694} {:answer/id #uuid "8817bce9-1d12-59f6-a5d1-e12cf7bf9ea0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{arcsec}(7x)}{7}+C" :db/id 17592186334193} {:answer/id #uuid "d4994be2-56ea-5429-8d7d-0f2980d19115" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{arcsec}(49x)}{7}+C" :db/id 17592186334851} {:answer/id #uuid "d5ef86d7-cffa-55cc-8343-9157ea5e011e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\text{arcsec}(7x)}{49}+C" :db/id 17592186334864} {:answer/id #uuid "eff32ea7-4fa2-5bab-91d2-777e88bff4bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{arcsec}(49x)+C" :db/id 17592186335089}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186333694} :answer-field/id #uuid "ebde86f4-5f82-5ab1-8866-0726b82f2be1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335652}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1090f68a-a5e7-5187-bfa4-8579cbfba1e4" :question/math-academy-id "q-69475" :question/problem "$\int \frac{7\,\text{d}x}{|7x|\sqrt{(7x)^{2}-1}}=$" :question/worked-solution "Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{7\,\text{d}x}{|7x|\sqrt{(7x)^{2}-1}}=7\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|7x|\sqrt{(7x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $7x.$

So, let's substitute $u=7x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=7\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{7}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}7\int \frac{1}{|7x|\sqrt{(7x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x & =7\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{7}\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(7x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7383fea3-7641-5ed4-9a63-ebf82d877776" :step/next {:db/id 17592186528036}} {:db/id 17592186528036 :step/content {:db/id 17592186250166 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10b46bc9-97cb-5bce-918b-8b92646973b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{6})+C" :db/id 17592186247570} {:answer/id #uuid "1b1e75f2-49eb-5a5d-9cee-c6ed60930c7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(6x)+C" :db/id 17592186247668} {:answer/id #uuid "3de5bd43-5bd8-5d01-8064-06ac8fdb185f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C" :db/id 17592186247970} {:answer/id #uuid "c07e9314-0212-563d-818b-d17717a081be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{6})+C" :db/id 17592186249137} {:answer/id #uuid "c7202512-7634-5743-96f4-8104d0655a3a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(6x)+C" :db/id 17592186249191}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186249191} :answer-field/id #uuid "c3dd683c-9379-5f34-9cdb-095ffd9b03f3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186250005}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c6b1e250-deab-5051-9d86-76fdce192937" :question/math-academy-id "q-114033" :question/problem "Calculate $\int \frac{3}{1+36{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $36{x}^{2}=(6x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=6x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{9+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{9\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/9)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{9+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (3\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "70dd22f2-9869-50f8-94c8-d430f170fc72" :step/next {:db/id 17592186528046}} {:db/id 17592186528017 :step/content {:db/id 17592186319105 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a18383d3-63cd-5639-931d-a7a1c504ecad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186318118} {:answer/id #uuid "eef5da2c-2eb9-5619-b5fc-8c0b83845f3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi" :db/id 17592186527772}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186527772} :answer-field/id #uuid "d4db02f7-5977-595a-8560-ebd6520e3bc1" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186318876}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "684a7fc3-f685-5be8-90e1-52ef15ddd822" :question/math-academy-id "q-346458" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{6}{\sqrt{100-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =6{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{100\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/100)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{10}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/100}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{5}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/10)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{10})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{10}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{10}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=10\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $5$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{6}{\sqrt{100-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{5}{\int }_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/10)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{5}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 10\,\text{d}u \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =6\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =6\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-6\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =6\cdot \frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2c3f1281-e85c-5d9a-bc26-8e73de6690dd"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a18383d3-63cd-5639-931d-a7a1c504ecad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :question/math-academy-id "q-114033" :question/problem "Calculate $\int \frac{3}{1+36{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $36{x}^{2}=(6x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=6x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{1+36{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{1+(6x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(6x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8908a2eb-eec4-5e4f-a375-5d012b4873f3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186528017}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10b46bc9-97cb-5bce-918b-8b92646973b1" :answer/type {:db/id {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}\cdot {7}^{2x}-50\cdot {7}^{2x} & =0 \\ (2{x}^{2}-50)\cdot {7}^{2x} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
2{x}^{2}-50=0\,\text{and}\,{7}^{2x}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation $2{x}^{2}-50=0$ can be factored as

$$
\begin{aligned}2({x}^{2}-25) & =0 \\ 2(x-5)(x+5) & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-5,5.$

- The equation $2=0$ is not a possible solution because it's a false statement.

- The equation ${7}^{2x}=0$ has no solutions because ${7}^{2x}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

Therefore, in ascending order, the original equation has the solutions

"![](images/ff/ffaf242238a8d32ce0f134cff6e0cf4256b2888b0a71f65e3c5ec470cbce284a.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above and the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle 2y + \ln{(\sqrt{x+5})}, \: e^{y/3} + 3x \right\rangle.$ 
Find a repeated integral in plane polar coordinates that's equivalent to $\displaystyle \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \, .$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}
=
\oint\limits_{C} (2y + \ln{(\sqrt{x+5})}) \: \mathrm{d}x + \left( e^{y/3} + 3x \right) \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/e4/e4c7913793a4b08916a832e575c5b2c167d5dfeec244eea23857731df1e514e7.png)

Since $P(x,y)= 2y + \ln{(\sqrt{x+5})}$ and $Q(x,y)=e^{y/3} + 3x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(2y+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x+5}))\,dx+({e}^{y/3}+3x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3-2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 3, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \right\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}r\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186519842} {:db/id 17592186176223 :question/id #uuid "e6e3c388-6148-5c9d-8b7f-1f6ea60657b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-108544" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186175987 Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}(3y-{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\,dx+(7x+\sqrt{y+5})\,dy\,?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/de/deeb5648e328ecc93cf6c1de620e103da0f7677705d1e89e4654deff8d411f66.png)

Since $P(x,y)=3y-{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ and $Q(x,y)=7x+\sqrt{y+5},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=7.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(3y-{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\,dx+(7x+\sqrt{y+5})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(7-3)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{2}4r\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186176313 :question/id #uuid "20585d4c-063f-50c6-8591-a785c62137ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-125719"} {:db/id 17592186262635 :question/id #uuid Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨{y}^{2}+{x}^{2},\,xy+y{e}^{y}⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})\,dx+(xy+y{e}^{y})\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/23/232ced663dcac27ce2775af66dd2ef215ed937e0f4eb5e3e6fb008a3d82dc069.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}+{x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=xy+y{e}^{y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})\,dx+(xy+y{e}^{y})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,-\pi \le \theta \le 0}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{0}\,{\int }_{0}^{1}-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362542 :question/id #uuid "8131655d-848c-5eb2-a4f8-11a5d73df386" :question/math-academy-id "q-169204"} {:db/id 17592186387685 :question/id #uuid Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨x+y,\,-xy⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(-xy)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/e1/e1c053e1cc4b4304c1302da2c57278200931b84e4ba687269d0ea89a99b523b8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=x+y$ and $Q(x,y)=-xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(-xy)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y-1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y-1)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 6,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

 

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(-y-1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{6}(-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186416112 :question/id #uuid "fdb21538-b802-59ae-83c3-94940f8f1068" :question/math-academy-id "q-126516" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186175987 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "![](images/bc/bc0660c37a6658635311a9a973ae3f4802740622a0b35ade22d6050ce648efa6.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}({y}^{3}-x)\,dx+({x}^{3}+{e}^{1/y})\,dy\,?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/77/7724df0035511419dcb5117ba8aa337380325af22ee235d206a954aa12c62fe9.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{3}-x$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{3}+{e}^{1/y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{3}-x)\,dx+({x}^{3}+{e}^{1/y})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}3({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}3{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186459208 :question/id #uuid "10fd1bae-a694-5bc5-b3cf-fcf342c64799" :question/math-academy-id "q-126677" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e66697d-f4a8-5190-9c92-04e431212fa0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458684} {:answer/id #uuid "21c3618c-e307-593c-be1d-ae62e518df4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}r(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458696} {:answer/id #uuid "5f8d4fbc-5dde-5631-9343-463c2c790561" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{2}r(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458790} {:answer/id #uuid "7378996c-e490-54ee-8ec3-96c3c35dfd15" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458831} {:answer/id #uuid "876615df-473a-5e4a-9661-1a6b746a5404" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458865}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458831} :answer-field/id #uuid "e3be5c97-a9dc-5eec-ad89-fde98181ed37" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459190}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "![](images/eb/eb2da6fbb22b19d027212685ca521f5186a831502617c2089766c5e9fe739696.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x))\,dx+({x}^{2}+3xy)\,dy\,?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/48/4822bfa926feccb0a12c14580ac325f4f10a0e4f815d0247b2231bf08b8c2326.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x)$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+3xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x+3y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x))\,dx+({x}^{2}+3xy)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+3y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186459263 :question/id #uuid "a150df94-0dd2-516e-ab2f-283c22ad4f30" :question/math-academy-id "q-126707" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "14eb9fcd-7abf-50ea-acb9-8e896cb286b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458663} {:answer/id #uuid "4752d255-6d05-5b8c-9bc7-d3d564d74fbb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )r\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458759} {:answer/id #uuid "4d3491ea-d8ce-5605-97f6-fd42cbc08809" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )r\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458767} {:answer/id #uuid "62d8034f-3c24-592c-b26b-73464d3851ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}({r}^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458798} {:answer/id #uuid "778250fc-a408-537b-8277-d49912ff9021" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458840}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458767} :answer-field/id #uuid "294a80e3-eaa7-5f33-b4a3-69d8d31c5ae7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459103}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "![](images/18/184b50ce54b01453d5b645eef7edc186823e8ae34afaefa2527e34122c1722cc.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3})\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/93/93a1c20377ddd0731c6190712d9d6d77551124fa33001334e84f52049bb6b800.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1+2{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3})\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-(1+2{y}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 9,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-2\cdot {r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )r\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186519776 :question/id #uuid "0ba10e69-e889-58f2-81da-5e14a75e9ef5"} {:db/id 17592186519789 :question/id #uuid "442c0b16-fa87-5944-8279-ae2d47c10e31"} {:db/id 17592186519796 Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y)dx+({y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above." :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/f3/f393d0facc98fe365e2c622e24223d6045b48b490937ba6e2f25d86d7eb4810f.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)={y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2},
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-8{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=8{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y)dx+({y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(8{y}^{2}-(-8{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}8({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}8{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}8{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}[2{r}^{4}]_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}32\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32[\theta ]_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =32\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =16\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186459266 :question/id #uuid "a7d3359f-1209-53f1-b438-cca94d3b404c" :question/math-academy-id "q-126737" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24f7045b-5228-59f7-a899-69db8a29caed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186458702} {:answer/id #uuid "64eeeb99-1d14-5f8d-8274-71cc4b59f7db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi " :db/id 17592186458803} {:answer/id #uuid "8f089fd7-57f0-5309-8b86-329b4b579d58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186458877} {:answer/id #uuid "b143a56b-f222-5495-aa7a-9092c0670a7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186458946} {:answer/id #uuid "bbe1ae9b-b60a-5838-a56d-dad4b77ce8e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186458967}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458967} :answer-field/id #uuid "f3e4c3bc-9dab-52ff-8019-5399ade463a4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459196}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "![](images/fb/fb6a49b2172b3a60676ef74a244298eff05ffc65be6feca089c4a953757f2e59.png)

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above." :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/d8/d816d9153e22dd109e20e3e387f6a0028e3f6a9eaf1d284dfae8b5fdf54cfc6e.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2},\,Q(x,y)=\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y,
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186176024 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175879 :question/id #uuid "40a301b7-9eaa-59e1-bcb0-4a35fecbff69" :question/math-academy-id "e-9551"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "695a4336-df48-56c9-8472-c2f51a496819" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049084} {:db/id 17592186051070}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176311 :question/id #uuid "e77d34a7-9f25-5206-895c-5f4fa0d1f689" :question/math-academy-id "q-125716"} {:db/id 17592186176485 :question/id #uuid "bdd86cce-9e5b-5a18-9af7-54a7f6efd03e" :question/math-academy-id "q-41469"} {:db/id 17592186262625 :question/id #uuid "d73aed01-512e-5f02-83f5-67f605d164e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-126526"} {:db/id 17592186262628 :question/id #uuid "5ee4972b-d705-5cec-8dc7-f572de324a82" :question/math-academy-id "q-126542"} {:db/id 17592186262632 :question/id #uuid "db4bf9cd-fbd1-5e73-9e78-d4f96b20828d" :question/math-academy-id "q-126567"} {:db/id 17592186405036 :question/id #uuid "a9b65d2f-1d10-5cc6-91ba-5ed12d5b8509" :question/math-academy-id "q-126539"} {:db/id 17592186405043 :question/id #uuid "88dc642a-08f7-5754-86d1-6d7942af6e8c" :question/math-academy-id "q-126564"} {:db/id 17592186416111 :question/id #uuid "d616e0c6-f6b2-5a83-83cf-32e007120166" :question/math-academy-id "q-126569"} {:db/id 17592186459234 :question/id #uuid "48fe30a0-5320-52ad-9ed5-45000abef204" :question/math-academy-id "q-126532"}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem"} {:db/id 17592186175879 :question/id #uuid "40a301b7-9eaa-59e1-bcb0-4a35fecbff69" :question/math-academy-id "e-9551" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186176024 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "695a4336-df48-56c9-8472-c2f51a496819" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem"}] :question/problem "Given that
![](images/1e/1e78bf74df5607a1d80b3bd51b3222505e3bb201817448a7a5ebe5b0a73cffa9.svg)
where $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle y^2+\sin x, \: 3xy-\cos y  \right\rangle$ and $C$ is the circle $x^2+y^2=4$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}
=
\oint\limits_{C} (y^2+\sin x) \: \mathrm{d}x + (3xy-\cos y) \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/79/798665574b8f0e11d991bb0d934efd01bdeb65840c2e86498be4edbc59578439.png)

Since $P(x,y)= y^2+\sin x$ and $Q(x,y)= 3xy-\cos y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,dx+(xy-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0\leq r \leq 2,\: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi  \big\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is $r^2\sin\theta.$"} {:db/id 17592186176311 :question/id #uuid "e77d34a7-9f25-5206-895c-5f4fa0d1f689" :question/math-academy-id "q-125716" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186176024 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "695a4336-df48-56c9-8472-c2f51a496819" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9211e1af-2c66-5f2d-9047-11aa8e63b870" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "r - r^{3}\sin 2θ" :db/id 17592186174125} {:answer/id #uuid "e4d2e78d-20ab-5f92-81f4-4061dc11ec75" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "e^{\cos θ} - \sin^{2} θ" :db/id 17592186174126} {:answer/id #uuid "029cc37d-1300-55e1-a1eb-c0396c774c9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "r - r^{2}\sin θ" :db/id 17592186174127} {:answer/id #uuid "1f508d93-fe49-5796-a8ee-e2f2e93f9e63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "r + r^{2}\sin θ" :db/id 17592186174128} {:answer/id #uuid "63a45ad0-78f6-598a-9b00-e8310310981b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "re^{\cos θ} - r\sin^{2} θ" :db/id 17592186174129}] :answer-field/id #uuid "9608a74f-b086-5f31-b192-ae95683f2fa5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186174124}] :question/problem "Given that

"Suppose we want to evaluate the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_{C}\left( e^{-x^2}- x^2y \right) \: \mathrm{d}x + \left(y+xy^2\right) \mathrm{d}y,
$$

where $C$ is the unit circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1,$ oriented counterclockwise. 

Direct evaluation of this integral is likely to be a difficult task. However, we can make light work of this tricky integral using Green's theorem.

Recall that Green's theorem states the following:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ (shown below) satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem.

![](images/dd/dd859c753a8a5445eafab5db4f1e796b48997e1abb1728accd03fe3825e595d6.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y) = e^{-x^2}- x^2y, \qquad Q(x,y) = y+xy^2,
$$

we obtain the partial derivatives   

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{-{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(y+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

This double integral will be easier to evaluate if we switch to plane polar coordinates. 

The region $D$ in $xy$-coordinates can be represented as the region $\Delta$ in polar coordinates, given by

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral by applying the change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0b5a23c7-4ccf-5122-8b5f-98fbabb0e367" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5838 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0b3de726-ead0-5369-a1fe-3dcc61b38bbc" :step/math-academy-id 35776 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176808}} {:db/id 17592186176808 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176024 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175879 :question/id #uuid "40a301b7-9eaa-59e1-bcb0-4a35fecbff69" :question/math-academy-id "e-9551"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "695a4336-df48-56c9-8472-c2f51a496819" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049084} {:db/id 17592186051070}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176311} {:db/id 17592186176485} {:db/id 17592186262625} {:db/id 17592186262628} {:db/id 17592186262632} {:db/id 17592186405036} {:db/id 17592186405043} {:db/id 17592186416111} {:db/id 17592186459234}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "f69ccccf-5d34-5f08-95d0-7af5d0c7628b" :step/math-academy-id 35777 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176735}}] :activity/title "Green's Theorem in Polar Coordinates" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186176145} {:db/id 17592186176807 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177037 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate the line integral

"![](images/eb/eb2da6fbb22b19d027212685ca521f5186a831502617c2089766c5e9fe739696.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x))\,dx+({x}^{2}+3xy)\,dy\,?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/48/4822bfa926feccb0a12c14580ac325f4f10a0e4f815d0247b2231bf08b8c2326.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x)$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+3xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x+3y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x))\,dx+({x}^{2}+3xy)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+3y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "33aa2c01-ef8c-530d-9a87-558d09200d7c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186459337}} {:db/id 17592186459332 :step/content {:db/id 17592186459223 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "76e9497e-95ac-551f-b7f9-a976c2b420b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi " :db/id 17592186458839} {:answer/id #uuid "8daee35f-46c8-5466-b3b4-c225766c4214" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\pi " :db/id 17592186458874} {:answer/id #uuid "9f77bfdf-543d-55d9-98f8-52a2f2343148" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16\pi " :db/id 17592186458910} {:answer/id #uuid "a61402b4-43f9-5d6a-b293-8db1d57747f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32\pi " :db/id 17592186458925} {:answer/id #uuid "e782fbf2-3eee-5d13-a745-b3e38c6a490e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi " :db/id 17592186459031}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458910} :answer-field/id #uuid "16ca1c58-b325-53c7-b363-8ad3f071412f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459095}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3227ab6b-7873-5e0c-8df6-f96bbac69dd6" :question/math-academy-id "q-126735" :question/problem "![](images/1f/1f56006dd06fab3bbc736c45ac6e9d65a401b88e0a9eb8a5db404fb67b89977e.png)
