$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/f3/f393d0facc98fe365e2c622e24223d6045b48b490937ba6e2f25d86d7eb4810f.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)={y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2},
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-8{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=8{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y)dx+({y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(8{y}^{2}-(-8{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}8({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}8{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}8{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}[2{r}^{4}]_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}32\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32[\theta ]_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =32\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =16\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b39e3053-19ff-54d9-8a03-cabe47ece267" :step/next {:db/id 17592186459334}} {:db/id 17592186459334 :step/content {:db/id 17592186459266 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24f7045b-5228-59f7-a899-69db8a29caed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186458702} {:answer/id #uuid "64eeeb99-1d14-5f8d-8274-71cc4b59f7db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi " :db/id 17592186458803} {:answer/id #uuid "8f089fd7-57f0-5309-8b86-329b4b579d58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186458877} {:answer/id #uuid "b143a56b-f222-5495-aa7a-9092c0670a7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186458946} {:answer/id #uuid "bbe1ae9b-b60a-5838-a56d-dad4b77ce8e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186458967}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458967} :answer-field/id #uuid "f3e4c3bc-9dab-52ff-8019-5399ade463a4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459196}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "a7d3359f-1209-53f1-b438-cca94d3b404c" :question/math-academy-id "q-126737" :question/problem "![](images/fb/fb6a49b2172b3a60676ef74a244298eff05ffc65be6feca089c4a953757f2e59.png)

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above." :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/d8/d816d9153e22dd109e20e3e387f6a0028e3f6a9eaf1d284dfae8b5fdf54cfc6e.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2},\,Q(x,y)=\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y,
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cb7edd78-bd6a-5d85-baab-eeb17426674d"} {:db/id 17592186459335 :step/content {:db/id 17592186459234 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1f21bd52-4aa7-5ea8-a034-d3560d1d5b01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r" :db/id 17592186458686} {:answer/id #uuid "648aec14-e325-59f4-a6ad-4fe7fed0f4d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186458801} {:answer/id #uuid "6c53cfdb-2fdd-546b-ab1b-dc3144c77b6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r" :db/id 17592186458818} {:answer/id #uuid "76be6580-ecd9-54fd-be34-2e6d6eb3bf26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r" :db/id 17592186458837} {:answer/id #uuid "867e3063-71a8-5b3f-ba08-0e4184738773" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-1" :db/id 17592186458863}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458818} :answer-field/id #uuid "7bb86058-0e7f-5528-b79d-a77b82e246b7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459138}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "48fe30a0-5320-52ad-9ed5-45000abef204" :question/math-academy-id "q-126532" :question/problem "Given that 

$$
{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx-{x}^{2}y\,dy={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{5}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?" :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that 

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/04/0470588a034222b183694b087d417e8ead0d2fd72357e796373794d00523708f.png)

Since $P(x,y)=x+y$ and $Q(x,y)=-{x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx-{x}^{2}y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2xy-1)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 5,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(-2xy-1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(-2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}(-2{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{5}-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d286d5c7-a12c-594f-9ccb-48543ab9d3ae" :step/next {:db/id 17592186459319}} {:db/id 17592186459337 :step/content {:db/id 17592186459263 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "14eb9fcd-7abf-50ea-acb9-8e896cb286b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458663} {:answer/id #uuid "4752d255-6d05-5b8c-9bc7-d3d564d74fbb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )r\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458759} {:answer/id #uuid "4d3491ea-d8ce-5605-97f6-fd42cbc08809" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )r\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458767} {:answer/id #uuid "62d8034f-3c24-592c-b26b-73464d3851ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}({r}^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458798} {:answer/id #uuid "778250fc-a408-537b-8277-d49912ff9021" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458840}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458767} :answer-field/id #uuid "294a80e3-eaa7-5f33-b4a3-69d8d31c5ae7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459103}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a150df94-0dd2-516e-ab2f-283c22ad4f30" :question/math-academy-id "q-126707" :question/problem "![](images/18/184b50ce54b01453d5b645eef7edc186823e8ae34afaefa2527e34122c1722cc.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3})\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/93/93a1c20377ddd0731c6190712d9d6d77551124fa33001334e84f52049bb6b800.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1+2{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3})\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-(1+2{y}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 9,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above." :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/d8/d816d9153e22dd109e20e3e387f6a0028e3f6a9eaf1d284dfae8b5fdf54cfc6e.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2},\,Q(x,y)=\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y,
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cb7edd78-bd6a-5d85-baab-eeb17426674d"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24f7045b-5228-59f7-a899-69db8a29caed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :question/problem "Given $f(x)=x+2$ and $g(x)=x-5$, find $(fg)(-1).$" :question/worked-solution "The notation $(fg)(x)$ means  the product of the functions  $f(x)$ and $g(x).$

**Method 1**

To evaluate $(fg)(-1),$ we find $f(-1)$ and $g(-1),$ and then multiply the results.

First, we find $f(-1)$ and $g(-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1) & =(-1)+2=1 \\ g(-1) & =(-1)-5=-6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we multiply the results:

$$
(fg)(-1)=f(-1)g(-1)=1\cdot (-6)=-6

$$

$$

$$

$$

**Method 1**

To evaluate $(f+g)(4),$ we find $f(4)$ and $g(4),$ and then add the results.

First, we find $f(4)$ and $g(4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4) & =2(4)+1=9 \\ g(4) & =-3(4)+5=-7\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we add the results:

$$
(f+g)(4)=f(4)+g(4)=9+(-7)=2
$$

**Method 2**

First, we find $(f+g)(x)$ by adding the two functions:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f+g)(x) & =(2x+1)+(-3x+5) \\  & =-x+6 \\  & =6-x\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(f+g)(4) & =6-4=2\end{aligned}

[{:db/id 17592186055528 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055964 :tutorial/content "It's possible to perform arithmetic with functions, just like with numbers. Shown below are the four arithmetic operations, addition $(+)$, subtraction $(-)$, multiplication $(\cdot)$, and division $(/)$, applied to the functions

$$
f(x) = 4x + 1
$$

and

$$
g(x) = x - 2
$$

- **Addition**
$\begin{aligned} (f + g)(x) &= f(x) + g(x) \\ &= (4x + 1) + (x - 2) \\ &= 4x + 1 + x - 2 \\ &= 5x - 1 \end{aligned}$
- **Subtraction**
$(f - g)(x)|= f(x) - g(x); = (4x + 1) - (x - 2); = 4x + 1 - x + 2; = 3x + 3$
- **Multiplication**
$(fg)(x)|= f(x)g(x); = (4x + 1)(x - 2); = 4x^{2} - 8x + x - 2; = 4x^{2} - 7x - 2$
- **Division**
$(f/g)(x)|= (f(x))/(g(x)); = \frac{4x + 1}{x - 2}$

**Note:** In the case of division, we must have that

$$
g(x)\neq 0
$$

so that we avoid dividing by zero." :tutorial/id #uuid "c656d962-19ad-5e04-b117-fa8d0c9034b8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2751 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186055552 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055971 :tutorial/content "When we're asked to evaluate the sum of two functions at a particular point, there are two methods that we can use. We could either evaluate both functions at the point and sum the results. Or, we could sum the two functions and then evaluate the result at the point.

To demonstrate, let's find the $(f+g)(1)$ for

$$
f(x) = x^2 -1
$$

and

$$
g(x) = 2x-3
$$

The notation $(f+g)(x)$ means the sum of the functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$.

**Method 1**

To evaluate $(f + g)(1)$, we find $f(1)$ and $g(1)$, and then add the results:

First, we find $f(1)$ and $g(1)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(1) &= (1)^{2} - 1 = 0 \\
g(1) &= 2(1) - 3 =-1
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we add the results:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(f + g)(1) &= f(1) + g(1) \\
&= 0 + (-1) \\
&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

First, we find $(f+g)(x)$ by adding the two functions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(f + g)(x) &= (x^{2} - 1) + (2x - 3) \\
&= x^{2} + 2x - 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate $(f + g)(1)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(f + g)(1) &= (1)^{2} + 2(1) - 4 =-1
\end{aligned}
$$

Both these methods work fine, but method $1$ is usually faster.

Finally, note that we can evaluate the difference between two functions using the same methods." :tutorial/id #uuid "74671b66-6f9b-59a5-96e2-aeb7ca503afe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2834 :tutorial/title "Evaluating the Sum or Difference of Two Functions"} :step/id #uuid "c0ba47b0-a276-56f7-965d-acc1c060fc97" :step/math-academy-id 15088 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055551}}] :activity/title "The Arithmetic of Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186054889} {:db/id 17592186055528 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055964 :tutorial/content "It's possible to perform arithmetic with functions, just like with numbers. $$

and

$$

$$

- **Addition**
$\begin{aligned} (f + g)(x) &= f(x) + g(x) \\ &= (4x + 1) + (x - 2) \\ &= 4x + 1 + x - 2 \\ &= 5x - 1 \end{aligned}$
- **Subtraction**
$(f - g)(x)|= f(x) - g(x); = (4x + 1) - (x - 2); = 4x + 1 - x + 2; = 3x + 3$
- **Multiplication**
$(fg)(x)|= f(x)g(x); = (4x + 1)(x - 2); = 4x^{2} - 8x + x - 2; = 4x^{2} - 7x - 2$
- **Division**

at a particular point, there are two methods that we can use. We could either evaluate both functions at the point and sum the results. Or, we could sum the two functions and then evaluate the result at the point.

To demonstrate, let's find the $(f+g)(1)$ for

$$
f(x) = x^2 -1
$$

and

$$
g(x) = 2x-3
$$

The notation $(f+g)(x)$ means the sum of the functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$.

**Method 1**

To evaluate $(f + g)(1)$, we find $f(1)$ and $g(1)$, and then add the results:

First, we find $f(1)$ and $g(1)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(1) &= (1)^{2} - 1 = 0 \\
g(1) &= 2(1) - 3 =-1
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we add the results:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(f + g)(1) &= f(1) + g(1) \\
&= 0 + (-1) \\
&=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

First, we find $(f+g)(x)$ by adding the two functions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(f + g)(x) &= (x^{2} - 1) + (2x - 3) \\
&= x^{2} + 2x - 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate $(f + g)(1)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(f + g)(1) &= (1)^{2} + 2(1) - 4 =-1
\end{aligned}
$$

Both these methods work fine, but method $1$ is usually faster.

Finally, note that we can evaluate the difference between two functions using the same methods." :tutorial/id #uuid "74671b66-6f9b-59a5-96e2-aeb7ca503afe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2834 :tutorial/title "Evaluating the Sum or Difference of Two Functions"} :step/id #uuid "c0ba47b0-a276-56f7-965d-acc1c060fc97" :step/math-academy-id 15088 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055551}} {:db/id 17592186055551 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054628 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054544 :question/id #uuid "b6a4d0a8-f579-5d6d-ad74-59b68d2046e6" :question/math-academy-id "e-4162"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0e8b25b3-5cc4-51b7-8ff9-fc1773797ad4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048652}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055450} {:db/id 17592186055458} {:db/id 17592186233434} {:db/id 17592186233435} {:db/id 17592186234197} {:db/id 17592186234260} {:db/id 17592186234261} {:db/id 17592186234407} {:db/id 17592186410421}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating the Sum or Difference of Two Functions"} :step/id #uuid "d9de7d87-ac26-5915-a421-2a3c6f706e14" :step/math-academy-id 15087 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055529}} {:db/id 17592186055971 :tutorial/content "When we're asked to evaluate the sum of two functions at a particular point, there are two methods that we can use. **Method 1**

To evaluate $(fg)(4),$ we find $f(4)$ and $g(4),$ and then multiply the results.

First, we find $f(4)$ and $g(4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4) & =4(4)-6=10 \\ g(4) & =5(4)-10=10\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we multiply the results:

$$
(fg)(4)=f(4)g(4)=10\cdot 10=100
$$

**Method 2**

First, we find $(fg)(x)$ by multiplying the two functions:

$$
\begin{aligned}(fg)(x) & =(4x-6)(5x-10) \\  & =20{x}^{2}-70x+60\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(fg)(4) & =20(4)^{2}-70(4)+60 \\  & =320-280+60 \\  & =100\end{aligned}

17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -3 & -6\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $6a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 1 & -3 \\ 4 & -2 & 2 & -6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -3 & -6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 1 & -3 \\ 4 & -2 & 2 & -6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}15 & 30 \\ 30 & 60\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 20\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}15 & 30 & 10 \\ 30 & 60 & 20\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}15 & 30 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}-2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
6a+\frac{b}{c}=6\cdot \frac{2}{3}+\frac{(-2)}{1}=2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134333 :question/id #uuid "871a1be1-8f4a-5616-a788-c400e98cd9b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-40943" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2563641c-3674-599a-bc9b-6a7ff8dc6db8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186324278} {:answer/id #uuid "3380e44e-eb6f-5319-9afd-04efe1186590" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186324383} {:answer/id #uuid "4a8960b7-70fe-5198-ad4d-9a451b90165c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186324576} {:answer/id #uuid "d91bf06c-7c91-517f-8dda-93fec52181f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186325860} {:answer/id #uuid "f579c837-0e7b-5922-9481-0a119644e5dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186326131}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186325860} :answer-field/id #uuid "a6ad0704-99f4-509f-bb7d-ffd14144c5c5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326518}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a+2b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6 & -8 & 2 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 \\ 2 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -8 & 2 & 0 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 & 2 \\ 6 & -8 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 & 6\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-4(\frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3})+2{x}_{3}=-2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2+{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2+{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+2b+c=1+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+0=4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186269136 :question/id #uuid "ef71613a-c794-54f5-9a74-68efbe48ffea" :question/math-academy-id "q-137034"} {:db/id 17592186326894 :question/id #uuid "d34cdae0-7b23-59fc-a8bc-f0d99444106f" :question/math-academy-id "q-40921" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "027310f9-ee0d-507a-bc28-d9da862bc3bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186323994} {:answer/id #uuid "13cbf72a-775b-5500-b4ce-fd7dee8abc45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186324150} {:answer/id #uuid "6058f5f8-765c-528f-b9e3-77d370e52e5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186324776} {:answer/id #uuid "df18dbbf-d1af-5d62-9ba8-07e3f6047abf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186325920} {:answer/id #uuid "df1f5f2f-9dda-564b-8601-3ba072795d25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186325921}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186323994} :answer-field/id #uuid "58847018-c5c9-5b9a-9650-5b07e75b721b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326372}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of  $3a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 & -3 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 & -3 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 \\ -18 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 & 12 \\ -18 & 6 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{2}{9}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{9}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{9} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
3a+\frac{b}{c}=3\cdot \frac{2}{9}+\frac{(\frac{1}{3})}{1}=1.

A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\,+\,{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $2a-3b-6c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable.  

From the third row, we have

$$
{x}_{3}=1,
$$

and from the first row we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a-3b-6c=2(\frac{1}{2})-3(1)-6(0)=-2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186326913 :question/id #uuid "85d7c223-d931-53ec-98fb-80a06e5b2764" :question/math-academy-id "q-41904" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133801 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9642ac63-6925-5ea3-925d-e697a6222064" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given in Matrix Form with Collinearity"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3c20af83-4b36-5128-89ee-a2b0f277470a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186324458} {:answer/id #uuid "58d3b34f-653e-5908-8110-49345a2e51c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186324708} {:answer/id #uuid "5c3eb528-5cf9-526f-857f-315ec81f0eb3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186324735} {:answer/id #uuid "b0bbe617-b13b-516f-806c-a9356a26279f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186325479} {:answer/id #uuid "c5751e84-51f5-5505-bf51-a2e74963787c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186325674}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "b0bbe617-b13b-516f-806c-a9356a26279f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186325479} :answer-field/id #uuid "ac5ff18b-ee0a-5c8e-a1ac-a863dbac8c0a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186326532}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 & -4 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 & -4 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}40 & -20 \\ -20 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}10 & -5 & 1 \\ -10 & 5 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}10 & -5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have

$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}\,+\,{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R,

what is the value of $a-4b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 & 6 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 6 & -4 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -4 & -1 \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 12 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second row, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-(-\frac{3}{2})+2{x}_{3}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-1-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1-2{x}_{3} \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a-4b+c=-2-4\cdot (-\frac{3}{2})+0=4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186368554 :question/id #uuid "8912c2e3-5605-5590-8ee8-b25e93901622" :question/math-academy-id "q-42245" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1299ade0-03c4-5049-abac-d1b905ea647d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7" :db/id 17592186368556} {:answer/id #uuid "de3e0276-368e-58fc-81ca-2ba8066692a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186368557} {:answer/id #uuid "ce89137e-5a01-54bb-9780-320b4e37ec64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186368558} {:answer/id #uuid "ce900d5f-43f0-5f77-adbc-98050b478ea1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186368559} {:answer/id #uuid "ba8250d4-f373-5760-9fc7-2ed30b0938ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186368560}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186368557} :answer-field/id #uuid "1812231c-b731-57f0-8e96-cc3da0e4fe33" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186368555}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a+b+4c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 \\ 4 & -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 & -1 \\ 4 & -4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.

 From the second row, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=-3.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-(-3)+2{x}_{3}=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-4-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-4-2{x}_{3} \\ -3 \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+4c=(-2)+(-3)+4\cdot 0=-5.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186415140 :question/id #uuid "090045f3-969e-5b87-b1e6-6f48922501d3" :question/math-academy-id "q-136945" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "612c1237-1d75-5779-901e-394b60ae8abc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186415123} {:answer/id #uuid "985ff754-4000-553d-84fd-3adae2a90775" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186415127} {:answer/id #uuid "a0f160c1-cc03-5355-b516-d2d19b494551" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186415129} {:answer/id #uuid "b6774fe7-0b94-51e6-8366-d780b5d12442" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186415130} {:answer/id #uuid "fe32f448-8a3a-522b-9c2c-5ad76f739b65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186415133}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415127} :answer-field/id #uuid "bf2aa749-d040-57c2-b657-f15f0f4f8d98" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415137}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}c \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R

what is the value of $a+3b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6 & -6 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -6 & -4 & 2 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ -4 & 4 & 4 & -4\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 4 & 4 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -4\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{3}=-2,
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+(-2)=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-1+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

:question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2} &=2 \\ {x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} &=2 \\ 2{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2} &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $3a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 1 & -4 \\ 2 & -8\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & -8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 1 & -4 \\ 2 & -8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & -8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6 & -24 \\ -24 & 96\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ -32\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -24 & 8 \\ -24 & 96 & -32\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}6 & -24 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{4}{3}+4{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}+4{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
3a+\frac{b}{c}=3\cdot \frac{4}{3}+\frac{4}{1}=8.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134374 :question/id #uuid "00e4806c-b4ce-579d-8d0e-03b84320da38" :question/math-academy-id "q-41919" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133802 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8bc1e31e-5794-5ae3-8620-6bcaadde6a15" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System With Collinearity"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "195f5438-dbcb-5fdf-b558-bce11648bd92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186324187} {:answer/id #uuid "34da3d3b-8b0d-5731-9512-7880150858c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186324401} {:answer/id #uuid "acc58718-2cff-5c4d-a0a5-bc1a9d33067c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186325439} {:answer/id #uuid "cd585b41-d5de-5636-9761-c198aae3b03f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186325751} {:answer/id #uuid "edef752f-66e7-582a-9d21-188b3b7ac00b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186326067}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "cd585b41-d5de-5636-9761-c198aae3b03f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186325751} :answer-field/id #uuid "2c9ed528-04bf-5ec5-8933-3ee5c01fd349" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186326296}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$

$$

$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 & 2 \\ -1 & -5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 5 & -5 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 & 2 \\ -1 & -5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}30 & -30 \\ -30 & 30\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}30 & -30 & 1 \\ -30 & 30 & -1\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}30 & -30 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{30}+{x}_{2}.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{30}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{30} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.

$$

\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=1\end{aligned}\right.\,\,\begin{bmatrix}20 & 10 & a \\ 10 & 5 & 5 \\ c & 5 & 5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}b \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations and its corresponding normal equation shown above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The normal equation corresponding to $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ \begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}20 & 10 & 10 \\ 10 & 5 & 5 \\ 10 & 5 & 5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=10+4+10=24.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186442296 :question/id #uuid "9375f3f0-3aa6-5a84-b715-8086fa3c68db" :question/math-academy-id "q-136883" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1053e502-fa88-53f4-be0b-479818f8c240" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186442290} {:answer/id #uuid "299f4294-b751-5683-b5f0-226953e8f833" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186442291} {:answer/id #uuid "2b3bc517-738d-5126-88d0-bb939758899a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186442292} {:answer/id #uuid "65d7077d-9a54-50ce-b898-454bc4952add" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186442293} {:answer/id #uuid "95715e13-7ac3-5517-874f-49e84cbcd24f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186442294}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442294} :answer-field/id #uuid "78b40939-3724-59f7-a9d3-46896f75c235" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186442295}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the system of linear equations and its corresponding normal equation shown above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$

$$

2167} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134698 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135060 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following inconsistent system of equations:

![](images/6b/6bcdc34077d88eac5ed89d408a1d2525b617a4f427b13433757df918585d380f.svg)

Since the system is inconsistent, we cannot find an exact solution. However, as we've previously seen, we can attempt to find the so-called least-squares solution, which is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

$$
\|  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \|
$$

is as small as possible. 

As before, the least-squares solution can be found by solving the corresponding normal equation, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\hat{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, note the following: 

- Previously, we solved the normal equation by left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T A)^{-1}.$

- However, in this case, the second column of $A$ is a multiple of the first.

- So, the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent.

- Therefore, $A^T A$ is not invertible.

To solve the normal equation in this case, we proceed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\hat{x} & ={A}^{T}b \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}5 & -20 \\ -20 & 80\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 20\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the last equation by Gaussian elimination, we obtain the general solution

![](images/b9/b93bd5cb988f208eb26115bfaa08e81be989ee79cf3655612c1a0522a5566d95.svg)

Notice that our solution is not unique! The second term of the least-squares solution (highlighted in blue) represents vectors from the null space of $A.$ 

In general, if a matrix $A$ has collinear columns, then the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b$ is not unique." :tutorial/id #uuid "2f2e227a-264e-5e00-8c12-ea534f4b351f" :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following inconsistent system of equations:

![](images/6b/6bcdc34077d88eac5ed89d408a1d2525b617a4f427b13433757df918585d380f.svg)

Since the system is inconsistent, we cannot find an exact solution. However, as we've previously seen, we can attempt to find the so-called least-squares solution, which is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

$$
\|  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \|
$$

is as small as possible. 

As before, the least-squares solution can be found by solving the corresponding normal equation, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\hat{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, note the following: 

- Previously, we solved the normal equation by left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T A)^{-1}.$

- However, in this case, the second column of $A$ is a multiple of the first.

- So, the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent.

- Therefore, $A^T A$ is not invertible.

To solve the normal equation in this case, we proceed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\hat{x} & ={A}^{T}b \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}5 & -20 \\ -20 & 80\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 20\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the last equation by Gaussian elimination, we obtain the general solution

![](images/b9/b93bd5cb988f208eb26115bfaa08e81be989ee79cf3655612c1a0522a5566d95.svg)

Notice that our solution is not unique! The second term of the least-squares solution (highlighted in blue) represents vectors from the null space of $A.$ 

In general, if a matrix $A$ has collinear columns, then the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b$ is not unique." :tutorial/id #uuid "2f2e227a-264e-5e00-8c12-ea534f4b351f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3637 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "73e4890e-8287-5a80-8c3c-2c95ce05512e" :step/math-academy-id 20272 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134733}} {:db/id 17592186135060 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following inconsistent system of equations:

17592186415138}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "01d4a87d-4b65-5a4c-9736-928bedaa6703" :question/math-academy-id "q-137086" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} &=3 \\ -2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2} &=1 \\ {x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} &=-5\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $12a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6 & -18 \\ -18 & 54\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ 30\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -18 & -10 \\ -18 & 54 & 30\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}6 & -18 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{5}{3}+3{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{3}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
12a+\frac{b}{c}=12\cdot (-\frac{5}{3})+\frac{3}{1}=-17.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "40c07ba2-e36f-5f6c-9e19-b8d5be6314d0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415145}} {:db/id 17592186415145 :step/content {:db/id 17592186415141 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29e85101-f9b2-5d74-83c6-aabdd8fc2745" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186415114} {:answer/id #uuid "2baff1db-5ead-50b2-af5a-abe277ae4820" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186415115} {:answer/id #uuid "2ccd28ea-578f-5414-8332-a6408e6df178" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186415116} {:answer/id #uuid "2e8878bb-5944-584d-9b48-2add56ecc5fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186415117} {:answer/id #uuid "8cd78f8e-e662-5c98-aa4d-0c408cd252ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186415126}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415126} :answer-field/id #uuid "a27c023d-32d0-5cf3-ade4-1f1674089f41" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415135}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4a92698e-17e4-57b8-8191-7aa9adc0e63f" :question/math-academy-id "q-137092" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} &=1 \\ 4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} &=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $6a+\frac{4b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}24 & -12 \\ -12 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}24 & -12 & 4 \\ -12 & 6 & -2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}24 & -12 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
6a+\frac{4b}{c}=6\cdot \frac{1}{6}+\frac{4\cdot \frac{1}{2}}{1}=3.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b7f52acc-285e-5a90-8147-1ce492061ed5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415148}} {:db/id 17592186415146 :step/content {:db/id 17592186415143 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0bd7515d-bc8c-5fbf-b8b7-be4ee29a026e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186415110} {:answer/id #uuid "229bfab5-ba1b-52fe-b0f1-2051f81b3eae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186415111} {:answer/id #uuid "383d6df1-6a22-5c04-94da-26eb4b0bd68d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186415120} {:answer/id #uuid "59b52a2f-1933-53c4-9f7d-6b819b9dbb83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186415122} {:answer/id #uuid "7818ba2a-afff-5ecd-8ff6-f5c7aa948efc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186415124}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415124} :answer-field/id #uuid "54a4eb9e-e422-55cf-a2cc-fe7a41adc569" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415134}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d4a26f8e-8621-57f0-b0fb-289f901931d0" :question/math-academy-id "q-136954" :question/problem "$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -18 & -3 \\ -18 & 54 & 9\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}6 & -18 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$

 Hence, the general solution is

$$

$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $14a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -6\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & -6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}14 & -28 \\ -28 & 56\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ -18\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}14 & -28 & 9 \\ -28 & 56 & -18\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}14 & -28 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{9}{14}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{9}{14}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{9}{14} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$

$$

$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}14 & -14 \\ -14 & 14\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ -7\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}14 & -14 & 7 \\ -14 & 14 & -7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}14 & -14 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$

#uuid "8912c2e3-5605-5590-8ee8-b25e93901622" :question/math-academy-id "q-42245" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a+b+4c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 \\ 4 & -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 & -1 \\ 4 & -4 & 8 & -4\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\,\,\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.

 From the second row, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=-3.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-(-3)+2{x}_{3}=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-4-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-4-2{x}_{3} \\ -3 \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+4c=(-2)+(-3)+4\cdot 0=-5.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c604cb99-8f2f-571b-8dc3-8a3b1b413bdf" :step/next {:db/id 17592186491220}} {:db/id 17592186491275 :step/content {:db/id 17592186269139 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7360267e-e517-562f-a7ab-234dea8e16b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186267158} {:answer/id #uuid "8a852bda-8769-55af-b974-271e085d782f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186267380} {:answer/id #uuid "abc3d198-0e91-5133-9e31-d766dcdd7bac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186267694} {:answer/id #uuid "df227e4e-6f3a-5099-aa04-1ab50365aa3d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186268116} {:answer/id #uuid "f0784891-ea63-5109-abfd-c29f5a65f3e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186268282}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186267158} :answer-field/id #uuid "5fef7bda-8cd4-5d78-b705-1883723f2fd4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268579}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7264a872-6f66-52f9-bc5f-7b2565f54aa2" :question/math-academy-id "q-137096" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2} &=3 \\ -2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} &=6 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a-\frac{3b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 \\ 18 & 36\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ -18\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 18 & 36 & -18\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-1-2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a-\frac{3b}{c}=-1-\frac{3(-2)}{1}=5.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f75e5e8e-a87b-5720-97a7-18016502e31b"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1299ade0-03c4-5049-abac-d1b905ea647d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7" "b9b18fd2-40c6-532b-a289-0305c371077f" :question/math-academy-id "q-137090" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=3 \\ 6{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} &=1 \\ 3{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $-4a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 \\ -18 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 & -9 \\ -18 & 6 & 3\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{9}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}6 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{6} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-4a+\frac{b}{c}=-4\cdot (-\frac{1}{6})+\frac{(\frac{1}{3})}{1}=1.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "29f94980-1925-529b-a3fe-5406bc761b87" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500421}} {:db/id 17592186500405 :step/content {:db/id 17592186326897 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06c8cf07-1252-5e91-b5c9-12f38c1f946f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186324034} {:answer/id #uuid "91384dd4-5bcc-5860-814c-f96556460493" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186325204} {:answer/id #uuid "93d14029-007f-54bd-9d2a-0c82c9066807" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186325227} {:answer/id #uuid "a9f7e58b-5b63-5e1f-ae19-6232045969c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186325419} {:answer/id #uuid "b3759c15-e036-5c30-848d-c2b42024912f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186325509}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186324034} :answer-field/id #uuid "6314ea6d-cf55-58df-9abc-6434d47d5c83" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326389}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "db567127-1e8b-50cb-a3d2-dc5e2ea462cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-40950" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\,+\,{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $2a-3b-6c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable.  

From the third row, we have

$$
{x}_{3}=1,
$$

and from the first row we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$

$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 \\ 18 & 36\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ -18\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 18 & 36 & -18\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}_{1}=-1-2{x}_{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$
