#uuid "7264a872-6f66-52f9-bc5f-7b2565f54aa2" :question/math-academy-id "q-137096" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2} &=3 \\ -2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} &=6 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a-\frac{3b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 \\ 18 & 36\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ -18\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 18 & 36 & -18\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}9 & 18 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-1-2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a-\frac{3b}{c}=-1-\frac{3(-2)}{1}=5.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8a36cb6a-17f3-5f3e-b938-a84d2ec531d8"} {:db/id 17592186500405 :step/content {:db/id 17592186326897 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06c8cf07-1252-5e91-b5c9-12f38c1f946f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186324034} {:answer/id #uuid "91384dd4-5bcc-5860-814c-f96556460493" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186325204} {:answer/id #uuid "93d14029-007f-54bd-9d2a-0c82c9066807" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186325227} {:answer/id #uuid "a9f7e58b-5b63-5e1f-ae19-6232045969c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186325419} {:answer/id #uuid "b3759c15-e036-5c30-848d-c2b42024912f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186325509}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186324034} :answer-field/id #uuid "6314ea6d-cf55-58df-9abc-6434d47d5c83" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326389}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "db567127-1e8b-50cb-a3d2-dc5e2ea462cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-40950" :question/problem "$$

$$

$$

what is the value of $2a-3b-6c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable.  

From the third row, we have

$$
{x}_{3}=1,
$$

and from the first row we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a-3b-6c=2(\frac{1}{2})-3(1)-6(0)=-2.

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 & -4 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 & -4 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}40 & -20 \\ -20 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}10 & -5 & 1 \\ -10 & 5 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}10 & -5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{10} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$
15a+\frac{b}{c}=15\cdot \frac{1}{10}+\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{1}=2.

$$

what is the value of $3a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 1 & -4 \\ 2 & -8\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & -8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 1 & -4 \\ 2 & -8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & -8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6 & -24 \\ -24 & 96\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ -32\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -24 & 8 \\ -24 & 96 & -32\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}6 & -24 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{4}{3}+4{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}+4{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
3a+\frac{b}{c}=3\cdot \frac{4}{3}+\frac{4}{1}=8.

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "871a1be1-8f4a-5616-a788-c400e98cd9b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-40943" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a+2b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6 & -8 & 2 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 \\ 2 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -8 & 2 & 0 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 & 2 \\ 6 & -8 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 & 6\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-4(\frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3})+2{x}_{3}=-2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2+{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2+{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+2b+c=1+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+0=4.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7cbcefec-3607-5a27-9d56-de67179c2918" :step/next {:db/id 17592186504740}} {:db/id 17592186504740 :step/content {:db/id 17592186415139 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0aa14c10-e738-56f6-ba1c-e071a121f17f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "13" :db/id 17592186415109} {:answer/id #uuid "3394fe0c-1ef5-5d2a-acd6-6a75d0644ea8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-10" :db/id 17592186415118} {:answer/id #uuid "796589ac-95c1-56f9-b1db-31d0e03ed1d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186415125} {:answer/id #uuid "a0ae1013-f366-5e65-90ff-b5b5ec91675a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-17" :db/id 17592186415128} {:answer/id #uuid "f6952c2b-bc0a-5679-9e51-c3da4a58655d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-19" :db/id 17592186415132}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415128} :answer-field/id #uuid "ed476833-2f74-5fd6-89de-22e15124bc5f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415138}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "01d4a87d-4b65-5a4c-9736-928bedaa6703" :question/math-academy-id "q-137086" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} &=3 \\ -2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2} &=1 \\ {x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} &=-5\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $12a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6 & -18 \\ -18 & 54\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ 30\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -18 & -10 \\ -18 & 54 & 30\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}6 & -18 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{5}{3}+3{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{3}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
12a+\frac{b}{c}=12\cdot (-\frac{5}{3})+\frac{3}{1}=-17.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e6b7a5fc-6d4b-57a2-804b-e4534f859630" :step/next {:db/id 17592186504741}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33ec9bd3-99d5-5104-8812-7b53252709d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b9b18fd2-40c6-532b-a289-0305c371077f" :question/math-academy-id "q-137090" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=3 \\ 6{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} &=1 \\ 3{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}b \\ c\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $-4a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 \\ -18 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 & -9 \\ -18 & 6 & 3\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}54 & -18 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{9}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}6 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{6} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-4a+\frac{b}{c}=-4\cdot (-\frac{1}{6})+\frac{(\frac{1}{3})}{1}=1.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "fbf9bf75-5bbc-570d-b638-4b8e78bce342" :step/next {:db/id 17592186504713}} {:db/id 17592186049810 :topic/id #uuid "15758f02-6fcf-5bc6-93c8-c4364239ef4c" :topic/knowledge-points $\displaystyle \int 4\sinh 2x \cosh 2x \, \textrm{d}x$." :question/worked-solution "First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\sin {2\theta}=2\sin \theta \cos \theta
$$

Using Osborn's rule, we get the double-angle formula for the hyperbolic sine:

$$
\sinh {2\theta} =2\sinh \theta \cosh \theta
$$

Letting $\theta= 2x$, we get

$$
\sinh {4x} =2\sinh 2x \cosh 2x
$$

Rearranging the above formula, we get

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\sinh {4x}= \sinh 2x \cosh 2x
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int4\sinh 2x\cosh 2xdx &= \int4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\sinh 4xdx \\
&= \int2\sinh 4xdx \\
&= 2\int\sinh 4xdx \\
&= 2 \cdot \frac{1}{4}\cosh 4x + C \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\cosh 4x + C

$$
\cosh{2x} = 1+ 2\sinh^2{x}
$$

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}
\int_{0}^{\ln 2}8\sinh^{2} xdx &= \int_{0}^{\ln 2}8 \cdot \frac{1}{2}(\cosh 2x - 1)dx \\
&= \int_{0}^{\ln 2}4\cosh 2x - 4dx \\
&= \left.(2\sinh 2x - 4x)\right|_{0}^{\ln 2} \\
&= (2\sinh (2\ln 2) - 4\ln 2) - (2\sinh 0 - 4 \cdot 0) \\
&= 2 \cdot \frac{e^{2\ln 2} - e^{-2\ln 2}}{2} - 4\ln 2 \\
&= (2^{2} - 2^{-2}) - 4\ln 2 \\
&= \frac{15}{4} - 4\ln 2
\end{aligned}

"216b7d60-59dd-599b-b414-ed79dbefb05e" :step/math-academy-id 31438} {:db/id 17592186167735 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168120 :tutorial/content "We can compute integrals containing hyperbolic functions using the hyperbolic counterparts of the trigonometric double-angle formulas. We use Osborn's rule to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity.

Osborn's rule states that to convert a trigonometric identity to a corresponding hyperbolic identity, we

- replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function, and
- for any product of two trigonometric sines, change the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

$$
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sinh}{\mathop{\rm sinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\cosh}{\mathop{\rm cosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\tanh}{\mathop{\rm tanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

For example, let's consider the following integral:

$$
\displaystyle{\int} \sinh x \cosh x \, \textrm{d}x
$$

Notice that the corresponding trigonometric integral is

$$
\displaystyle{\int} \sin x \cos x \, \textrm{d}x
$$

One way of solving this trigonometric integral is to use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\sin 2x = 2\sin x \cos x
$$

Applying Osborn's rule, we get an equivalent hyperbolic identity:

$$
\sinh 2x = 2\sinh x \cosh x
$$

Rearranging the above formula, we get

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\sinh {2x}= \sinh x \cosh x
$$

Therefore, we can calculate our original integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int\sinh x\cosh xdx &= \int\frac{1}{2}\sinh 2xdx \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\int\sinh 2xdx \\
&= \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\cosh 2x + C \\
&= \frac{1}{4}\cosh 2x + C
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5aeb4951-903e-5815-85fe-2b3fdd1c992e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5558 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "bfc4d4ca-c5b7-55a0-9d68-e0e086fc3de2" :step/math-academy-id 34434 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167638}}] :activity/title "Integration Using the Hyperbolic Double-Angle Formulas" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186167028} {:db/id 17592186167735 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168120 :tutorial/content "We can compute integrals containing hyperbolic functions using the hyperbolic counterparts of the trigonometric double-angle formulas. 3940} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186189207 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189413 :tutorial/content "Given two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the variance of the sum or difference of these variables is given by

$$
\textrm{Var}[X\pm Y] = \textrm{Var}[X] + \textrm{Var}[Y] \pm 2\textrm{Cov}[X,Y],
$$

where $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$ We'll prove this formula at the end of the lesson.

Note that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y]= 0,$ and we have

$$
\textrm{Var}[X\pm Y] = \textrm{Var}[X] + \textrm{Var}[Y].
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "84bffdf5-551d-52b7-93f3-5c7ba599e972" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6496 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "91e3c205-114c-5ae0-8abd-5bb7f424476e" :step/math-academy-id 39341 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189208}} {:db/id 17592186189208 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188357 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188065 :question/id #uuid "7ea98738-258e-5cc4-9e04-58b0b4638290" :question/math-academy-id "e-10435"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "91379d24-6b6d-5642-8eb8-cbcc8feaf355" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049815} {:db/id 17592186050351}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188780} {:db/id 17592186188781} {:db/id 17592186527183} {:db/id 17592186527189} {:db/id 17592186527205} {:db/id 17592186527208}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Variance of a Sum or Difference of Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "8ceb42c5-5f3d-52e4-b3c8-bda0bdf99ba6" :step/math-academy-id 39343 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189211}} {:db/id 17592186189210 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188359 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188067 :question/id #uuid "0bc5206c-e880-5016-9653-49ac54af4d2f" :question/math-academy-id "e-10443"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "96172470-bd90-53eb-aea7-87d08f462ea2" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188782} {:db/id 17592186188783} {:db/id 17592186527126} {:db/id 17592186527134} {:db/id 17592186527198} {:db/id 17592186527210}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Variance of a Sum of Scaled Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "982300e3-8874-58e0-b502-0dd1759d2e87" :step/math-academy-id 39369 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189212}} {:db/id 17592186189211 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189414 :tutorial/content "If $X$ and $Y$ are random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX + bY] = a^2 \textrm{Var}[X] + b^2 \textrm{Var}[Y] + 2ab \textrm{Cov}[X,Y].
$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = 0,$ and we recover the formula

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX + bY] = a^2 \textrm{Var}[X] + b^2 \textrm{Var}[Y] .
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a2319f43-f4e9-5092-93cf-5e5f4f23f4f7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6502 :tutorial/title "The Variance of a Sum of Scaled Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "8153054a-c500-5f13-a328-66eb26fc4fb8" :step/math-academy-id 39370 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189210}} {:db/id 17592186189212 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188360 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188068 :question/id #uuid "04bff442-bf0b-529b-a8d8-14538a1db48f" :question/math-academy-id "e-10444"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "39efc83e-6658-5b7a-979b-dbc35af5dd98" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050327}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188786} {:db/id 17592186188787} {:db/id 17592186527156} {:db/id 17592186527173} {:db/id 17592186527224}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Combined Variance Given Some Moments"} :step/id #uuid "ba8e9c50-818a-52c4-8395-b662c6ac186d" :step/math-academy-id 39371 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189222}} {:db/id 17592186189213 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188361 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188069 :question/id #uuid "d849af65-721a-5a47-b8b7-9446e77046f2" :question/math-academy-id "e-10447"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f512d235-f663-502f-bd8c-6b3b6748913b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048820}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188784} {:db/id 17592186188785} {:db/id 17592186527219}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Variance of a Sum of Three Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "5fad4c43-2456-5538-bc40-e43bafabf67e" :step/math-academy-id 39377 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189223}} {:db/id 17592186189222 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189420 :tutorial/content "Finally, we have the following generalization for the variance of a sum of $n$ random variables.

$$
\textrm{Var} \left[ \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} a_i X_i \right] = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} a_i^2 \textrm{Var}[X_i] + 2\sum\limits_{i < j} a_i a_j \textrm{Cov}[X_i, X_j]
$$

Let's see an example of how this works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "5169e0a6-5da8-51b4-8e84-5154fe8622f5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6535 :tutorial/title "Generalizing to Multiple Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "63b7b972-cc52-5658-b0d3-7a5571d28c29" :step/math-academy-id 39481 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189213}} {:db/id 17592186189223 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189421 :tutorial/content "Let's prove the following formula:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X+ Y] = \textrm{Var}[X] + \textrm{Var}[Y] + 2\textrm{Cov}[X,Y]
$$

Applying the definition of variance and using the linearity of expectation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X+Y] & =\text{E}[((X+Y)-\text{E}[X+Y])^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[((X-\text{E}[X])+(Y-\text{E}[Y]))^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}+(Y-\text{E}[Y])^{2}+2(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])].\end{aligned}
$$

Distributing the expected value, and using the fact that $\textrm{E}[aX] = a\cdot \textrm{E}[X]$ for constant $a,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X+Y] & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}+(Y-\text{E}[Y])^{2}+2(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])] \\  & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}]+\text{E}[(Y-\text{E}[Y])^{2}]+2\cdot \text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])] \\  & =\text{Var}[X]+\text{Var}[Y]+2\text{Cov}[X,Y]\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

as required.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+2y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$

$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0$, we have

$$
{y}^{′}(0)={y}_{c}^{′}(0)\,\text{and}\,{y}^{′}(1)={y}_{c}^{′}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions. 

- Use ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{2}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{2}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).$

$$

$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$

with periodic forcing functions.

As before, we consider a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function $f(x)$, for which the general solution can be written as

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

The main ideas are similar to those of solving IVPs:

- we choose the correct form of the series for the particular solution $y_p$, and then

- use boundary conditions at the endpoints to determine the constants in the homogeneous part $y_c$ of the solution.

When $f(x)$ is periodic, we often look for $y_p$ as a Fourier series on a symmetric interval $[-L,L].$

Recall that for an equation of the form $y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)$ with no (damping) $y'$ term, the particular solution inherits the parity of $f(x)$:

- If $f$ is *even*, then its Fourier series contains only cosine terms.

- If $f$ is *odd*, then its Fourier series contains only sine terms.

For example, consider the boundary value problem

$$
y''+5y=f(x)
$$

on $[-2,2]$, where $f$ is $4$-periodic and odd. We want the appropriate Fourier series form for a particular solution $y_p$.

Because $f$ is $4$-periodic on $[-2,2]$, we have $L=2$, so the Fourier basis on this interval is

$$
\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Next, since $f$ is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. Since the equation has no $y'$ term, the particular solution inherits the same parity and is also odd.

Therefore, the appropriate form for $y_p$ is a sine series:

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

"23fc6608-1b88-5376-be85-f016f7a7fd7f" :step/math-academy-id 601827} {:db/id 17592186231791 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231992 :tutorial/content "Recall that we are considering a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function $f(x)$, for which the general solution can be written as

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

There are many types of boundary conditions (including mixed or Robin-type conditions), but in this lesson, we will focus on the two simplest cases:

- *Dirichlet conditions* (values of $y$ are specified):

$$
y(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=\beta
$$

- *Neumann conditions* (values of $y'$ are specified):

$$
y'(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=\beta
$$

A key simplification is possible if we choose our particular solution $y_p$ to satisfy the corresponding *homogeneous* boundary conditions. For any given $f(x),$ it is always possible to find such a $y_p$. 
This drastically simplifies the computations, as the boundary conditions then determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

- *Dirichlet-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y(a)=y_c(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=y_c(b),
$$

so we can solve for the constants in $y_c$ using only the homogeneous solution.

- *Neumann-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p'(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p'(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y'(a)=y_c'(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=y_c'(b),
$$

so the derivative conditions determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

Let's see how this works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "16e90dd1-2074-5728-ad7b-e05a00c3e171" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14795 :tutorial/title "Using Boundary Conditions"} :step/id #uuid "46704bc7-b368-569c-9ed3-f228bcfd99b9" :step/math-academy-id 601983 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231790}}] :activity/title "Solving BVPs Using Fourier Series" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186231522} {:db/id 17592186231788 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231986 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we will use Fourier series to solve boundary value problems with periodic forcing functions.

As before, we consider a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function $f(x)$, for which the general solution can be written as

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

The main ideas are similar to those of solving IVPs:

- we choose the correct form of the series for the particular solution $y_p$, and then

- use boundary conditions at the endpoints to determine the constants in the homogeneous part $y_c$ of the solution.

When $f(x)$ is periodic, we often look for $y_p$ as a Fourier series on a symmetric interval $[-L,L].$

Recall that for an equation of the form $y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)$ with no (damping) $y'$ term, the particular solution inherits the parity of $f(x)$:

- If $f$ is *even*, then its Fourier series contains only cosine terms.

- If $f$ is *odd*, then its Fourier series contains only sine terms.

For example, consider the boundary value problem

$$
y''+5y=f(x)
$$

on $[-2,2]$, where $f$ is $4$-periodic and odd. We want the appropriate Fourier series form for a particular solution $y_p$.

Because $f$ is $4$-periodic on $[-2,2]$, we have $L=2$, so the Fourier basis on this interval is

$$
\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Next, since $f$ is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. Since the equation has no $y'$ term, the particular solution inherits the same parity and is also odd.

Therefore, the appropriate form for $y_p$ is a sine series:

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Let's see more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "67a0ca11-7450-5f6a-8bdc-4aee6301f209" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14775 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "46d5d3ac-e51c-5772-ac47-f492d00757d3" :step/math-academy-id 601823 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231789}} {:db/id 17592186231986 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we will use Fourier series to solve boundary value problems with periodic forcing functions.

$$
{y}^{″}+2y=f(x),\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=5
$$

where $f(x)$ is $4$-periodic and even. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$" :question/worked-solution "We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+2y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=-A\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+{y}_{p}^{′}(x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0$, we have

$$
{y}^{′}(0)={y}_{c}^{′}(0)\,\text{and}\,{y}^{′}(1)={y}_{c}^{′}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions. 

- Use ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{2}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{2}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).$

- Use ${y}^{′}(1)=5$ with $B=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =-A\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+{y}_{p}^{′}(1) \\ 5 & =-A\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+0 \\ A & =-\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0664f390-8c5d-5111-9629-741058ac23ee"} {:db/id 17592186497436 :step/content {:db/id 17592186372866 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3cafa24e-4543-5b34-90d7-30a196dea194" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)" :db/id 17592186372868} {:answer/id #uuid "e11913eb-e3e1-5f57-a56a-942b4c1c6e23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})" :db/id 17592186372869} {:answer/id #uuid "677af0cd-8fcf-515a-9ae8-5589651ec3f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})" :db/id 17592186372870} {:answer/id #uuid "1ca9f35e-fe96-5630-bbab-c22309b7bc81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)" :db/id 17592186372871}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186372868} :answer-field/id #uuid "426794d2-6862-5438-ba72-af2a254821f3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186372867}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "28c90549-a363-5df9-b9c5-c5f06fe88f4d" :question/math-academy-id "q-344281" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+5y=f(x)
$$

on $[-1,1]$, where $f$ is $2$-periodic and even. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$

$\,$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Because $f$ is $2$-periodic on $[-1,1]$, we have $L=1$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{1})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{1}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5219f94f-df72-53fc-a578-2400b0bec682" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497487}} {:db/id 17592186497453 :step/content {:db/id 17592186372884 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ca1a5ef5-d795-51cc-943c-7a342a6b79ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{\sqrt{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{8})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{8}x)" :db/id 17592186372886} {:answer/id #uuid "e0d3a205-6dc6-5c9e-bac4-a249e8ab4de0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{\sqrt{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{8})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{8}x)" :db/id 17592186372887} {:answer/id #uuid "2853c5b9-37c6-5227-b945-7d1f193fd0b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{\sqrt{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{8})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{8}x)" :db/id 17592186372888} {:answer/id #uuid "83ee3b8e-a567-507f-a915-c7357bb35a78" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{\sqrt{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{8})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{8}x)" :db/id 17592186372889}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186372889} :answer-field/id #uuid "9b894e19-8672-5d3a-ad64-9899ae78c522" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186372885}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d1435ee5-1c1b-550d-94b4-e30eac47db5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-344322" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0.$*

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0$, we have

$$
y(0)={y}_{c}(0)\,\text{and}\,y(1)={y}_{c}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+B(0)+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Use $y(1)=6$ with $A=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 6 & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+0 \\ B & =\frac{6}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼\frac{6}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "de0f6281-e792-51d2-a694-b1b34794e517" :step/next {:db/id 17592186509018}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8db0a3b8-eaf2-565b-a867-fb89aa025843" :answer/type {:db/id #uuid "a82ffc50-94c7-5ef3-8250-c59c884b5c7d" :question/math-academy-id "q-344315" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+5y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)=4
$$

where $f(x)$ is $1$-periodic and odd. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$" :question/worked-solution "We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+5y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0$, we have

$$
y(0)={y}_{c}(0)\,\text{and}\,y(1)={y}_{c}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+B(0)+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).$

- Use $y(1)=4$ with $A=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 4 & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+0 \\ B & =\frac{4}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼\frac{4}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8362d1b1-2815-579d-a7ce-8b445abb4156"} {:db/id 17592186516891 :step/content {:db/id 17592186372860 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fe92f4fa-7615-54d2-a819-127fb1a673f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{10})" :db/id 17592186372862} {:answer/id #uuid "3b55cc73-4e32-591c-bee5-a9d934861abd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{10})" :db/id 17592186372863} {:answer/id #uuid "9f4b6aad-9479-5fcd-b841-a17705d991a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5})" :db/id 17592186372864} {:answer/id #uuid "b3faa44a-d5ae-5692-901c-7fe9f2979668" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5})" :db/id 17592186372865}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186372864} :answer-field/id #uuid "f04ef90f-3003-58fb-a7fe-77d398fbdee2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186372861}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6f67e1f7-be25-5035-9c23-854e909c6a11" :question/math-academy-id "q-344268" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

:question/problem "Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $\mathbf F$ shown below. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is negative

II. The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is zero

III. The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is positive

![](images/7e/7e7fbe6aaf1310b186344a3cf5a127075f11a86b51db2e687ddc7035d5d890f8.png)" :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C\mathbin:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

The outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. From the diagram below we see that $\mathbf F$ acts perpendicular to $\mathbf n$ at every point on $C.$ Therefore, there is no net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

![](images/4a/4a3d9864bb6bada1fd218b299427bc5bb4ffcbcccb1a504fff77416d5d292151.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

- Statement III is false. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/93/9310d17389f61de2984c0e23cfe1060e77d4a87a140d2f1c892bdbab9b99629b.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
\oint\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} {:db/id 17592186049653} {:db/id 17592186050104} {:db/id 17592186180031 :question/id #uuid "a2d693ae-0e11-561b-9b69-4ee74bfcc078" :question/math-academy-id Consider the vector field $\mathbf F = 2x\,\mathbf i + 2y\,\mathbf j$ and a square $C$ with side length $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across all four sides of the square.*" :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/1d/1de4c4c55784b4a84a0493a4cc65082c430cadcc39c3d808001b2fd27665e968.png)

First, consider the side $C_1.$ We have that $\mathbf n_1 = \mathbf i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(2x\,i+2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_1,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \mathbf i + t\,\mathbf j, \quad \Rightarrow\quad \mathbf r'(t) = \mathbf j, \qquad t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =2(1-(-1)) \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides $C_2, C_3,$ and $C_4$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 4\cdot 4 = 16.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180036 :question/id #uuid "ea876586-e09c-5050-847d-bc8b312ea302" :question/math-academy-id "q-126881"} {:db/id 17592186180042 :question/id #uuid :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Flux Across a Rectangle Using Two Symmetry Properties"}] :question/problem "![](images/59/59b5f1676f036f80e6aa2e9e331327ed9ec28e88bacda52a91ee0865736e9ce3.png)

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F = 5x\,\mathbf i - 3y\,\mathbf j$ and a rectangle $C$ with base $4$ and height $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$ 

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*" :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/79/793755cda5243dbb427d8722c21ab150a4821c3957f0ccd0ef0fedbbd576e924.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side $C_1.$ We have that $\mathbf n_1 = \mathbf i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(5x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =5{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_1,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = 2\mathbf i + t\,\mathbf j, \quad \Rightarrow\quad \mathbf r'(t) = \mathbf j, \qquad t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =5{\int }_{-1}^{1}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =10{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =10\cdot 2 \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_3$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s = 20.
$$

- Next, we consider the side $C_2.$ We have that $\mathbf n_2 = \mathbf j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(5x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_2,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = t\,\mathbf i + \mathbf j, \quad \Rightarrow\quad \mathbf r'(t) = \mathbf i, \qquad t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-3{\int }_{-2}^{2}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =(-3)\cdot 4 \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_4$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = -12.
$$

Finally, then

$$
\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s= 2 \cdot 20 + 2 \cdot (-12) = 16.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180037 :question/id #uuid "2e3c5efb-b46d-57f5-8660-cecbe88198e4" :question/math-academy-id "q-126892"} {:db/id 17592186180043 :question/id #uuid Consider the vector field $F=-x\,i+3y\,j$ and a rectangle $C$ with base $6$ and height $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/51/511bae61d710c3362bb18618717b3d44ef5dcedece5f669e0b5237b7b524a054.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-x\,i+3y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=3i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-{\int }_{-2}^{2}3\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =(-3)\cdot 4 \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=-12.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(-x\,i+3y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+2\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-3,3].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =3{\int }_{-3}^{3}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{-3}^{3}\text{d}t \\  & =6\cdot 6 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=36.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot (-12)+2\cdot 36=48.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186290435 :question/id #uuid "a69a7a8b-52c6-5396-ab13-a2f6e97bdfa1" :question/math-academy-id "q-226152"} {:db/id 17592186420496 :question/id #uuid *Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/1d/1de4c4c55784b4a84a0493a4cc65082c430cadcc39c3d808001b2fd27665e968.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(4x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot 2 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=8.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(4x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-3{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =(-3)\cdot 2 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=-6.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot 8+2\cdot (-6)=4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186421470 :question/id #uuid "f9f7d0a1-c461-5247-ab30-95b875686e93" :question/math-academy-id "q-226134"} {:db/id 17592186050793} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid 3715} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180341 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180787 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf F$ be a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. Imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water, and $C$ is a curve that allows water to flow through it (like a fishing net). 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol C$** is a scalar number that tells us how much water is escaping the region bounded by $C.$ 

We have three possible scenarios: 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

![](images/6f/6ff4d006d3fbf4a434f35a13c8591fc166ff6c74adf2b7969752b7541e486df2.png)

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/38/3812148e855a84e3233316acc8bbf59bd7cd802a874c9e4807c6efd7ca6754cf.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero.

The following vector field has zero flux across $C$ because the amount of water flowing in through $C$ equals the amount of water flowing out through $C.$

![](images/56/56aef4f217e9981755826745a97e8389d86b49518ffd7d3ebc75e5ee2dc28f8b.png)

The following two vector fields also have a zero flux across $C$ because the water flow is tangential to $C$ at every point along $C.$

![](images/63/637677324152af3d428e405c89025f35dbe5d71e2e8f0a0797ef3aca30bae7e1.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ecd8591f-8e5b-50b2-91a1-4f15bd97b2c2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9521 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1e80fc64-e097-5e8d-a35c-056416216619" :step/math-academy-id 184955 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180342}} {:db/id 17592186180342 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180788 :tutorial/content "If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ The symbol $\oint\limits$ means integration over the closed curve.

It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below.

![](images/6d/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png)

First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$

![](images/49/498e1afbaac8bc8297213eae09cc8bf8742b29f45dda1dfafff868c67ebb9de9.png)

We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components:

- a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and

- a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$

![](images/ac/ac3aae49f372908f2f9aeb53e3fc98bff117846fca05a8c696009e443390811c.png)

Therefore, the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{n}F & =\frac{F\cdot n}{||n||}=F\cdot n.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression above represents the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at a single point only. Therefore, to calculate the total net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ we sum (integrate) this expression over the entire curve. This gives

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a328d4d8-bfe8-50eb-8bbd-281b3bb07afe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9522 :tutorial/title "Constructing an Integral Formula for the Flux"} :step/id #uuid "9dac0bb5-3a03-56c0-a614-dc9f045cb3e3" :step/math-academy-id 184956 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180343}} {:db/id 17592186180343 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180789 :tutorial/content "Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $\mathbf F$ below. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. 

![](images/e6/e679efaa2612d45bbfe8b918de7148853b64eaf530af34a525ef1735e0946b09.png)

By drawing an outward-pointing unit normal vector, it's clear that there is a net flow *out* through $C.$ 

![](images/fb/fbcd6fd0fadcc955212a145de9edb4654ddb92ddebb8ba31eb775cff676efeeb.png)

Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is positive, and we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s > 0.
$$

When measuring flux through a closed curve, the curve's orientation does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same in either case. 

![](images/a3/a3d398d382e6bc94ddde77e650d50a6b5ec050083f89f64104f6f2fd172a9239.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is also positive, and we have

$$
\oint\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s > 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "36b855d8-9994-5c22-bbc4-e28065875f84" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9523 :tutorial/title "Orientation-Independence"} :step/id #uuid "a000a04f-fdd8-5b25-9b23-e59a14a3592d" :step/math-academy-id 184957 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180344}} {:db/id 17592186180344 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179644 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179482 :question/id #uuid "c427d9b4-2944-5edc-8e19-363de348d23d" :question/math-academy-id "e-15147"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2b7b8782-d1f4-5654-a18f-6ad35de8fb30" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049212} {:db/id 17592186049653} {:db/id 17592186050104}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180031} {:db/id 17592186180032} {:db/id 17592186262687} {:db/id 17592186262688} {:db/id 17592186262690} {:db/id 17592186262691} {:db/id 17592186420910} {:db/id 17592186420911} {:db/id 17592186420912} {:db/id 17592186420914}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining a Flux's Sign From a Diagram"} :step/id #uuid "4f8760a0-8c8e-5ec6-9492-0ecc32789da6" :step/math-academy-id 184958 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180345}} {:db/id 17592186180345 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180790 :tutorial/content "To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+ \cdots +
\int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$

As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. 

![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

 

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
$$

To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by

$$
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below.

![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png)

Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have 

$$
\mathbf n = -\mathbf j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "472c362c-27a5-5041-90c3-4533c63b736d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9524 :tutorial/title "Calculating Flux"} :step/id #uuid "ab771459-c3a6-5f4b-9e75-cfa3f13b9add" :step/math-academy-id 184961 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180346}} {:db/id 17592186180346 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179645 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179483 :question/id #uuid "15426c37-1508-5407-ab49-b26f8761795c" :question/math-academy-id "e-15148"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f9c8ca56-5ea8-547c-80ab-6b1f1347447e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180034} {:db/id 17592186180035} {:db/id 17592186235531} {:db/id 17592186262697} {:db/id 17592186262698} {:db/id 17592186262699} {:db/id 17592186262700} {:db/id 17592186262701} {:db/id 17592186362496} {:db/id 17592186420909} {:db/id 17592186420913}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Integral Expression for Flux"} :step/id #uuid "2c288a88-997c-5ef1-98ff-24092e7506f9" :step/math-academy-id 184962 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180347}} {:db/id 17592186180347 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180791 :tutorial/content "Calculating the flux of a vector field across a rectangle or square requires computing four flux integrals. However, we can often simplify our calculations if the vector field displays symmetry.

To demonstrate, consider the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

![](images/8e/8e1767b9bea45e742df4953f0ec50b2d43c9622994035342307dc2be6abba8de.png)

If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/65/65a8c37c64580f7d1f41f32722f20dfee2b8fd98333920a0feae781ea8d9541e.png)

Since the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ is parallel to $C_2$ and $C_4,$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

This is easy to verify, since, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}-5\,i\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}0\,\text{d}s \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and similarly for the integral along $C_4.$ 

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

Since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through $C_1$ will cancel with the net outflow through $C_3.$ That is

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
=
-\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53e768e4-a3bb-5b89-83b9-a97e9ff4a921" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9525 :tutorial/title "Using  Symmetry to Simplify Flux Calculations"} :step/id #uuid :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179866} {:db/id 17592186180341 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180787 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf F$ be a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. Imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water, and $C$ is a curve that allows water to flow through it (like a fishing net). 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol C$** is a scalar number that tells us how much water is escaping the region bounded by $C.$ 

We have three possible scenarios: 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

![](images/6f/6ff4d006d3fbf4a434f35a13c8591fc166ff6c74adf2b7969752b7541e486df2.png)

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/38/3812148e855a84e3233316acc8bbf59bd7cd802a874c9e4807c6efd7ca6754cf.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero.

The following vector field has zero flux across $C$ because the amount of water flowing in through $C$ equals the amount of water flowing out through $C.$

![](images/56/56aef4f217e9981755826745a97e8389d86b49518ffd7d3ebc75e5ee2dc28f8b.png)

The following two vector fields also have a zero flux across $C$ because the water flow is tangential to $C$ at every point along $C.$

![](images/63/637677324152af3d428e405c89025f35dbe5d71e2e8f0a0797ef3aca30bae7e1.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ecd8591f-8e5b-50b2-91a1-4f15bd97b2c2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9521 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1e80fc64-e097-5e8d-a35c-056416216619" :step/math-academy-id 184955 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180342}} {:db/id 17592186180787 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf F$ be a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. Imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water, and $C$ is a curve that allows water to flow through it (like a fishing net). 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol C$** is a scalar number that tells us how much water is escaping the region bounded by $C.$ 

We have three possible scenarios: 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

![](images/6f/6ff4d006d3fbf4a434f35a13c8591fc166ff6c74adf2b7969752b7541e486df2.png)

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/38/3812148e855a84e3233316acc8bbf59bd7cd802a874c9e4807c6efd7ca6754cf.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero.

The following vector field has zero flux across $C$ because the amount of water flowing in through $C$ equals the amount of water flowing out through $C.$

![](images/56/56aef4f217e9981755826745a97e8389d86b49518ffd7d3ebc75e5ee2dc28f8b.png)

The following two vector fields also have a zero flux across $C$ because the water flow is tangential to $C$ at every point along $C.$

![](images/63/637677324152af3d428e405c89025f35dbe5d71e2e8f0a0797ef3aca30bae7e1.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ecd8591f-8e5b-50b2-91a1-4f15bd97b2c2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9521 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186180342 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180788 :tutorial/content "If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ The symbol $\oint\limits$ means integration over the closed curve.

It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below.

![](images/6d/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png)

First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$

![](images/49/498e1afbaac8bc8297213eae09cc8bf8742b29f45dda1dfafff868c67ebb9de9.png)

We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components:

- a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and

- a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$

![](images/ac/ac3aae49f372908f2f9aeb53e3fc98bff117846fca05a8c696009e443390811c.png)

Therefore, the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{n}F & =\frac{F\cdot n}{||n||}=F\cdot n.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression above represents the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at a single point only. Therefore, to calculate the total net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ we sum (integrate) this expression over the entire curve. This gives

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a328d4d8-bfe8-50eb-8bbd-281b3bb07afe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9522 :tutorial/title "Constructing an Integral Formula for the Flux"} :step/id #uuid "9dac0bb5-3a03-56c0-a614-dc9f045cb3e3" :step/math-academy-id 184956 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180343}} {:db/id 17592186180788 :tutorial/content "If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+ \cdots +
\int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$

As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. 

![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

 

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
$$

To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by

$$
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below.

![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png)

Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have 

$$
\mathbf n = -\mathbf j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "472c362c-27a5-5041-90c3-4533c63b736d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9524 :tutorial/title "Calculating Flux"} :step/id #uuid "ab771459-c3a6-5f4b-9e75-cfa3f13b9add" :step/math-academy-id 184961 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180346}} {:db/id 17592186180790 :tutorial/content "To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula

However, we can often simplify our calculations if the vector field displays symmetry.

To demonstrate, consider the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

![](images/8e/8e1767b9bea45e742df4953f0ec50b2d43c9622994035342307dc2be6abba8de.png)

If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/65/65a8c37c64580f7d1f41f32722f20dfee2b8fd98333920a0feae781ea8d9541e.png)

Since the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ is parallel to $C_2$ and $C_4,$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

This is easy to verify, since, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}-5\,i\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}0\,\text{d}s \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and similarly for the integral along $C_4.$ 

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

Since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through $C_1$ will cancel with the net outflow through $C_3.$ That is

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
=
-\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53e768e4-a3bb-5b89-83b9-a97e9ff4a921" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9525 :tutorial/title "Using  Symmetry to Simplify Flux Calculations"} :step/id #uuid "5c82115b-5b07-5765-b4a2-64382478cffb" :step/math-academy-id 184965 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180348}} {:db/id 17592186180791 :tutorial/content "Calculating the flux of a vector field across a rectangle or square requires computing four flux integrals.
